Hardcoded resource file paths scattered across modules instead of a single configuration point
ARC-E1C.name: hardcoded-identifier-scattered-across-modules

lower_when.condition: Exactly two copies exist, in the same package, and a test asserts they are equal.

ARC-E2A.criteria: Qualifies when durable records (ledgers, audit trails, filed-issue maps) are stored in a location the project treats as disposable (gitignored scratch, temp or cache directories) next to throwaway state, so routine cleanup destroys them. An audit trail destroyed by a delete operation is SEC-C4C; a rewrite with no backup is DAT-F1A.
examples: triage-ledger.jsonl and filed-issues.json - durable audit ledgers - live inside the fully gitignored, run-scratch .panopticon/ directory alongside disposable state
ARC-E2A.name: durable-state-in-ephemeral-scratch-location

lower_when.condition: The project's clean command explicitly excludes the durable files, and the docs name them as durable.

raise_when.condition: The project's own documented cleanup command or workflow deletes that directory, and the durable records have no other copy.

ARC-E2B.criteria: Qualifies when a component writes generated configuration or registrations to a global (user- or machine-wide) location although the project's configuration model is otherwise project-scoped, so projects collide or leak into each other. Silent config auto-discovery is ARC-E2D.
examples: Generated host-native agent registration writes to a global, non-project-scoped directory, in tension with the project's otherwise project-scoped configuration model
ARC-E2B.name: global-scope-write-conflicts-with-project-scoped-model

lower_when.condition: Global writes are namespaced per project (by path hash or project id), so two projects cannot overwrite each other.

ARC-E2C.criteria: Qualifies when documentation states an environmental runtime precondition (working directory, environment, invocation ordering, consistent flags across runs) that the code relies on but never checks, so violating it makes the program fail late or silently misbehave. When the unenforced statement is a policy or verdict whose violation the program simply permits, that is ARC-F1E; startup configuration consumed without validation is OPS-C1A; a path resolved against the wrong base is COD-E2B.
examples: SKILL.md documents that the pipeline MUST run from the repo root where .panopticon/ lives, but nothing in code checks or enforces this precondition at runtime
ARC-E2C.name: implicit-runtime-contract-unenforced

lower_when.condition: Violating the precondition fails immediately with a clear OS or library error naming the missing path or variable.

ARC-E2D.criteria: Qualifies when code silently auto-discovers a config or input file when none is given, with no log line or notice that the fallback fired, so behavior depends on whatever files happen to be present. Configuration behavior that is merely undocumented is QAL-C2F; a missing or corrupt config treated as permissive is COD-B1A.
examples: main() silently auto-discovers .panopticon/groups.json when no --groups argument is given, with no log line indicating the fallback fired
ARC-E2D.name: implicit-config-discovery-action-at-a-distance

lower_when.condition: The discovery rule is documented in --help and the discovered path is echoed in normal output.

raise_when.condition: The auto-discovered file is read from a directory whose contents come from untrusted input (e.g. the tree of a repository being scanned).

ARC-E3A.criteria: Qualifies when two or more independent configuration axes combine into a cross-product that is never enumerated, validated or tested, so some combinations have undefined behavior. A per-host configuration gap is ARC-E3C; a narrow test scenario matrix is TST-A3C.
examples: Write-guard enforcement mode (WHERE writes go) and tool-policy mode (enforcement vs. advisory) are independent axes whose cross-product is never enumerated or tested
ARC-E3A.name: orthogonal-config-axes-increase-complexity

lower_when.condition: Unsupported combinations are rejected at config load with an explicit error.

ARC-E3B.criteria: Qualifies when one domain, lens or component has supporting reference material (checklists, guides, profiles) that a parallel peer lacks, so the peer operates with less guidance. A reference document missing items it should list is ARC-G1C.
examples: There is no architecture-panel equivalent of security-checklists.md, so the architecture lens has less supporting reference material than the security lens
ARC-E3B.name: asymmetric-domain-coverage-across-artifacts

ARC-E3C.criteria: Qualifies when a per-host (or per-platform) configuration exists for some hosts but is missing its fallback, validation or field set for others, so hosts silently diverge. Divergent execution paths across CI and image environments are ARC-B3A; inconsistent field NAMING across hosts is QAL-F3C.
examples: model-profiles.yml's openrouter host profile has no corresponding hardcoded fallback in model_resolver.py, unlike kimi and claude
Tool policy mode has no cross-host validation, so hosts can silently diverge in enforcement behavior
ARC-E3C.name: cross-host-config-parity-gap

lower_when.condition: The missing per-host entry falls back to a shared default whose value is identical to the other hosts' explicit entries.

raise_when.condition: The diverging setting is an enforcement or security policy mode, so one host enforces while another runs advisory.

ARC-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when an enforcement decision trusts a persisted flag or an earlier check instead of re-verifying the live state that flag describes, so the gate passes after the state has changed (a TOCTOU in an enforcement path). A generic check-then-act race outside enforcement is COD-F1B; a control that is never applied to a class of invocations is AGT-B1A.
examples: --emit-kimi-swarm gates on the persisted plan's stale enforced flag instead of live-verifying current registration state
The primary plan-emission path never binds the unenforced-ack to plan content, silently defeating the stale-flag guard it was meant to backstop
ARC-F1A.name: enforcement-relies-on-stale-flag-not-live-verification

lower_when.condition: The flag is written and checked in the same process invocation with no step in between that can change the underlying state.

ARC-F1B.criteria: Qualifies when an audit or accounting record of enforcement covers only some of the actors subject to the policy, so the record understates exposure. A sensitive action with no audit logging at all is SEC-C4B; an audit trail destroyed by deletion is SEC-C4C.
examples: meta.tool_policy_mode audit field excludes scout and advisor from enforcement accounting despite their equal exposure to the same policy
ARC-F1B.name: audit-accounting-excludes-in-scope-actors

lower_when.condition: The excluded actors hold no write or tool capability that the policy governs.

ARC-F1C.criteria: Qualifies when sibling scripts or commands perform comparable privileged actions but only some pin their target and check authorization, so the others rely on ambient defaults. A single operation with no function-level authorization is SEC-C1C; mutation through ambient credentials with no scoping is SEC-C1D.
examples: Only reconcile_apply.py pins --repo and gates on admin permission; triage.py/file_issues.py/file_fixmes.py rely on ambient gh defaults with no equivalent check
ARC-F1C.name: inconsistent-authorization-gate-across-sibling-scripts

lower_when.condition: The ungated siblings perform only read operations against the remote.

ARC-F1D.criteria: Qualifies when a batch of remote or persistent operations has no recovery path (resume, rollback, or a record of progress) for a mid-batch failure, leaving partial state, while a sibling path in the same codebase does recover. A compound operation that is not atomic is COD-F1A; a missing database transaction boundary is DAT-D1B; retry without backoff is OPS-A1B.
examples: reconcile_apply.apply()'s batch loop has no recovery path for a mid-batch GitHub API failure, unlike its sibling function
ARC-F1D.name: partial-batch-operation-lacks-failure-recovery-path

lower_when.condition: Every operation in the batch is idempotent, so a plain rerun completes it.

ARC-F1E.criteria: Qualifies when a stated policy, rule, or verdict is documented or declared but the code does not enforce it (an enforcement gap, not a stale reference). Distinct from a security/enforcement CONTROL that degrades to permit on misconfiguration (ARC-F2E), and from a merely stale doc (QAL-C1x / ARC-G2x).
examples: Enforcement for hostile-corpus reviews is SHOULD-level prose guidance in a doc, not an automated gate
Tool finding verdict handling is not architecturally enforced anywhere in the pipeline
The 'same flags is a requirement, not a convenience' contract in SKILL.md has no programmatic check
ARC-F1E.name: policy-or-verdict-not-enforced-by-code

lower_when.condition: The unenforced rule governs only formatting, naming or report presentation, not any gate, permission or data path.

raise_when.condition: The unenforced rule is the only control between attacker-controlled input (e.g. content of the repository under review) and a write, network or tool action, and that code path executes in a default run with no other gate.

ARC-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when a compensating control exists but its scope exempts exactly the location or class that an attacker or compromised actor would use, so the control misses the case it exists for. A primary mediation control that skips a class of invocations is AGT-B1A; a control that mis-parses an input shape is ARC-F2C.
examples: The post-fan-out clean-tree check only flags modifications 'outside .panopticon/', exempting the exact directory a compromised unenforced reviewer would use to poison downstream synthesis
ARC-F2A.name: compensating-control-has-scope-blind-spot

lower_when.condition: No downstream step reads files from the exempted scope.

ARC-F2B.criteria: Qualifies when an enforcement mechanism (hook, guard) can only apply session- or process-wide and cannot tell which actor triggered it, so per-actor least privilege is impossible. A control missing a class of invocations is AGT-B1A; a tool grant broader than the task needs is AGT-B1D.
examples: A harness spike confirmed the session-wide write-guard hook cannot distinguish which subagent fired it, blocking per-agent tightening as a documented architectural limitation
ARC-F2B.name: enforcement-hook-cannot-scope-to-individual-actor

lower_when.condition: All actors sharing the session are meant to hold the same privilege, so per-actor scoping would grant nothing narrower.

ARC-F2C.criteria: Qualifies when a security control DOES run on an invocation but assumes an undocumented input SHAPE and so mis-evaluates it (e.g. hardcoding tool_input['file_path'] for a NotebookEdit payload that is shaped differently) — the control mis-parses what it sees. A control that fails to cover a whole class of invocations at all (e.g. Bash never reaching the write-guard) is AGT-B1A.
examples: The write-guard hook hardcodes tool_input['file_path'] for Write/Edit/NotebookEdit alike, silently mis-evaluating NotebookEdit's differently-shaped payload
allowlist_from_plan depends on undocumented plan['out_file'] structure with no schema backing it
ARC-F2C.name: security-control-assumes-undocumented-input-shape

lower_when.condition: The mis-shaped payload belongs to a tool that no actor under the control is granted.

ARC-F2D.criteria: Qualifies when a general, non-enforcement component silently SKIPS or tolerates malformed or unexpected-shape runtime INPUT instead of rejecting it — the harm is weakened processing or silent data loss, not an opened security gate. When the failing thing is a security/enforcement control that degrades to permit, that is ARC-F2E (the single home for the write-guard fail-open incident); the config-load fail-open choice viewed as a correctness defect is COD-B1A.
examples: group_runner.py and ingest_tools.py tolerate non-dict plan entries and malformed input by silently skipping them instead of rejecting
ARC-F2D.name: component-fails-open-on-malformed-input

lower_when.condition: Skipped items are counted and reported in the run's output or summary.

ARC-F2E.criteria: Qualifies — and is the single home for the write-guard fail-open incident — when a SECURITY / ENFORCEMENT control (write-guard, tool-policy) degrades to permit, allow, or advisory because its own config or context is missing, malformed, or unregistered: the gate opens. A general, non-enforcement component that skips malformed input is ARC-F2D; the config-loading code's fail-open choice viewed as a correctness defect is COD-B1A; a detection / scan tool that silently loses coverage is SEC-G2B.
examples: Write-guard fails silently open (no deny, no warning) when the allowlist file is missing or malformed
Tool-policy enforcement silently degrades to prompt-only ("advisory") when a host agent isn't registered
ARC-F2E.name: security-control-fails-open-on-misconfiguration

lower_when.condition: The degraded mode emits a visible warning and the run's output is stamped unenforced/advisory.

raise_when.condition: An untrusted input in a normal run can produce the missing, malformed or unregistered condition (e.g. a scanned repository or an agent can delete or corrupt the allowlist), so the gate opens when an attacker wants it to.

ARC-F2G.criteria: Qualifies when the CATCH is structurally overbroad — a bare or blanket handler masking multiple distinct error types (an architecture smell about the handler's shape), regardless of any single missing check. A single unchecked auxiliary failure is COD-B2C; a security-relevant swallow is SEC-F1B.
examples: Multiple functions catch bare Exception (merge-base lookup, fallback-branch resolution), swallowing intentional and accidental errors alike
ARC-F2G.name: overbroad-exception-handling-masks-errors

lower_when.condition: The blanket handler logs the full traceback or re-raises after cleanup.

ARC-G1A.criteria: Qualifies when contributor-facing instructions (CONTRIBUTING, development docs) prescribe test, lint or setup steps that differ from what CI actually runs, so a contributor who follows them gets a different result from CI. A general doc-vs-code disagreement is ARC-G1B; stale CLI flag documentation is QAL-C2C.
examples: CONTRIBUTING.md's test/lint instructions omit dependency installation steps and diverge from what ci.yml actually runs
ARC-G1A.name: contributor-instructions-diverge-from-ci

lower_when.condition: The only divergence is a missing setup step that fails loudly (e.g. a missing dependency import) the first time a contributor follows the instructions.

ARC-G1B.criteria: Qualifies when two independent sources of truth for the same fact diverge — the same logic/constant re-expressed in two runtimes, or a doc that disagrees with the code it documents (specs disagree → ARC). A single document contradicting itself is QAL-C2B; a design doc merely superseded or drifted is ARC-G2A/ARC-G2B.
examples: CHANGELOG.md and DEVELOPMENT.md's History section are two divergent, non-overlapping sources of truth for release history
Documented 'monthly' panopticon-tools rebuild cadence contradicts the actual daily/weekly CI schedule
ARC-G1B.name: divergent-duplicate-source-of-truth

lower_when.condition: One of the two sources is explicitly labelled canonical and the other points to it.

ARC-G1C.criteria: Qualifies when reference documentation (an architecture section, a file inventory) omits components or artifacts that exist, so readers get an incomplete picture. An implemented capability with no documentation at all is COD-D2D; undocumented configuration behavior is QAL-C2F; docs asserting an artifact that does not exist (the inverse) is ARC-D3B.
examples: DEVELOPMENT.md's Architecture section under-describes the Dockerfile's actual tool set
DEVELOPMENT.md's skill/reference/ inventory omits model-profiles.yml despite the versioning contract requiring it to be bumped together
ARC-G1C.name: reference-documentation-incomplete

lower_when.condition: The omitted item is internal-only and the doc states it lists public components only.

raise_when.condition: The omitted item is named by a versioning or release contract that requires it to be updated together with the documented items.

ARC-G2A.criteria: Qualifies when a design/spec document has been superseded but carries no deprecation marker, so a reader can't tell it is obsolete. A design doc that has drifted from the delivered scope (still 'current' but wrong) is the sibling ARC-G2B.
examples: The spec corpus retains superseded and internally-contradictory architecture documents with no deprecation or status marker distinguishing current from historical
ARC-G2A.name: superseded-doc-without-deprecation-marker

lower_when.condition: The superseded doc is not linked from any current README, index or agent prompt, so a reader reaches it only by browsing the tree.

ARC-G2B.criteria: Qualifies when a design/spec document still presented as current has drifted from what was actually delivered. A document explicitly superseded but left unmarked is the sibling ARC-G2A.
examples: The Phase-1 design's phased roadmap drifts from the scope actually delivered by the later scanner-ecosystem-expansion work
A planned Phase-5 integration reuses the static-scan fixture pattern for a corpus that fundamentally differs from static-scan fixtures
ARC-G2B.name: design-doc-drifts-from-delivered-scope

lower_when.condition: The doc is dated and framed as a plan or roadmap rather than a description of the current system.

ARC-G3B.criteria: Qualifies when a file is tracked in version control although the repository's own ignore rules exclude it, so the tree contradicts its declared hygiene. A tracked file that exposes a credential is SEC-B3A; an orphaned, unused asset is QAL-E2C.
examples: skill/.DS_Store is tracked in git despite .gitignore's own 'OS / editor noise' rule listing .DS_Store
ARC-G3B.name: tracked-file-violates-own-gitignore-rule

ARC.guide: ARC covers structure: where a responsibility lives, whether two specifications agree with each other (code vs code, doc vs code, schema vs producer, docs vs the repository's actual layout), and whether declared gates and enforcement are wired and fail closed. Choose ARC when the fix is structural (a new owner, boundary, contract or gate) or when two specs disagree; choose COD when one instance breaks a contract or gives a wrong result, QAL for a per-instance smell or inert staleness, OPS for runtime error-swallowing or a self-inflicted operational failure (a deliberate fail-open design decision stays ARC), and SEC/AGT when the finding is the exploitable flaw itself rather than the architecture around it. Look in A (module boundaries and ownership), B (packaging and images), C (CI/CD gating), D (contracts and interfaces), E (configuration), F (enforcement and fail-open), G (documentation integrity).
ARC.name: architecture

category_guides.1: Handles never released: COD-A1A is the product-code file-handle leak; the test-code form is TST-D1B and operational overload is OPS-D1A.
category_guides.2: Bounds and indexing: COD-A2A is a write past a fixed buffer (memory corruption), COD-A2B an off-by-one index, COD-A2C a read of an absent index or an empty sequence. Choose A2A only for a WRITE that can corrupt memory; a crash on a bad index is A2C (or SEC-F1A when the input is attacker-supplied).

A.guide: Resource lifecycle and memory/bounds safety: a handle that is never released (A1) or an access outside a buffer or sequence's bounds (A2). A leak or out-of-bounds access in test code is TST (TST-D1B, TST-B3A); capacity exhaustion under load with no cap is OPS-D1A.
A.name: resource-lifecycle

category_guides.1: Guard and permission scope: COD-B1A is a config loader that defaults to permissive on missing or corrupt config; COD-B1C is a shared guard whose computed allowed set is too broad. B1A is easy to confuse with ARC-F2E (the enforcement control itself fails open); B1C with AGT-B1C/AGT-B1D (agent tool grants) and ARC-F2B (a hook that cannot tell actors apart).
category_guides.2: Silent failure and diagnostics: COD-B2C is the default home for an unchecked auxiliary failure that leaves wrong or missing data; COD-B2A a null that crashes downstream; COD-B2B an error message that blames the wrong cause; COD-B2D a transformed result not re-checked against its constraint; COD-B2E truncation with no warning; COD-B2F unguarded Web Storage access. B2C, B2D and B2E are the easiest to confuse: unchecked call, unchecked output, and cut-off output. A component that deliberately skips malformed input is ARC-F2D.

B.guide: Defensive checks: guards that grant too much (B1) and failures that are unchecked, misreported, or silently degrade results (B2). A security-relevant swallow is SEC-F1B, an overbroad catch clause ARC-F2G, a security control that degrades to permit ARC-F2E, and an unlogged runtime swallow OPS-E1A.
B.name: defensive-checking-discipline

category_guides.1: Severity/grade mapping: COD-C1A conflates confidence with severity (one source value feeds both fields), COD-C1B ignores the source's value and hardcodes one. An unmapped value silently falling back to a default is COD-C3B.
category_guides.2: Parsing and selection: COD-C2A picks the wrong input file, COD-C2B loses state between lifecycle phases, COD-C2C has a regex that rejects a valid variant, COD-C2D fails a lookup because an identifier is not normalized. C2D and COD-G3D (Unicode normalization) overlap; C2C and COD-D1B (schema stricter than producer) overlap when the regex is a validator.
category_guides.3: Output conformance: COD-C3A emits a required field missing or empty, COD-C3B has an incomplete lookup table with a silent fallback, COD-C3C emits a non-standard key that downstream drops. A mapping that is sparse by design and only undocumented is QAL-C2F; a spec that never tells the producer to emit the field is ARC-D2E.

C.guide: Value mapping and normalization when adapting one tool's or source's output into another's model: grade fields mapped wrongly (C1), wrong parsing or selection logic (C2), and output that does not conform to its own contract (C3). Two specifications disagreeing is ARC; adapter inconsistency with siblings is ARC-A4A.
C.name: tool-adapter-normalization

category_guides.1: Schema definition drift at the field level: COD-D1A value outside its enum, COD-D1B validator stricter than the producer, COD-D1C records in one array with different shapes, COD-D1D schema omits a documented-required field. Wholesale divergence is ARC-D1B; an id format specified differently across artifacts is ARC-D1D.
category_guides.2: Docs versus implementation: COD-D2B a documented feature that does not exist, COD-D2C specification documents that contradict, COD-D2D an implemented capability missing from docs. When the flag exists and only its docs are stale or under-cover it, that is QAL-C2C, not D2B or D2D. Two disagreeing specs are ARC-G1B, a superseded spec with no marker is ARC-G2A, and one self-contradicting document is QAL-C2B.
category_guides.3: Boundary type and protocol: COD-D3A calls an external API with the wrong parameter shape, COD-D3B an adapter that does not satisfy its declared interface, COD-D3C one field emitted with different types across paths. D3C versus COD-D1C: one field's type versus a whole record's shape.

D.guide: Interface contracts that runtime behavior violates: schemas versus actual values (D1), documentation versus implementation where a user following the docs breaks (D2), and type or protocol mismatches across a call boundary (D3). Per the routing rule, spec-vs-spec disagreement is ARC (ARC-D1B, ARC-G1B) and inert doc staleness is QAL (QAL-C2C).
D.name: interface-contract-drift

category_guides.1: Iteration and shortcut logic: COD-E1A dedup that discards a distinct entry sharing a coarse key, COD-E1B a loop that exits before processing all valid entries. Unstable identity keys across runs are ARC-D1C; deliberate capping is COD-B2E.
category_guides.2: Execution context and ordering: COD-E2A production code made unreachable by an earlier guard or exit, COD-E2B a relative path resolved against the wrong base directory. The test-code cwd form of E2B is TST-D2A.

E.guide: Control flow and execution order: loops and shortcuts that drop or skip valid work (E1) and code that runs in the wrong place, order, or context (E2). A test-discovery gap is TST-C1A; a misplaced block that skips nothing is QAL-F2B.
E.name: control-flow-and-execution-order

category_guides.1: Shared state: COD-F1A a compound operation that is not atomic, COD-F1B check-then-act (TOCTOU), COD-F1C shared mutable state with no synchronisation. F1B is a stale check, F1A a non-atomic sequence of writes, F1C an unprotected shared variable; a repeated user action is COD-F3E.
category_guides.2: Liveness and blocking: COD-F2A deadlock from lock ordering, COD-F2B a blocking call on an async loop or UI thread, COD-F2C an unbounded collection rendered in one pass. A missing outbound timeout is OPS-A1A.
category_guides.3: Async correctness: COD-F3A a stale cache read, COD-F3B unsafe lazy initialization, COD-F3C an unawaited async result, COD-F3D an unsafe signal handler, COD-F3E a user action re-entered while in flight. F3B is a special case of COD-F1C, F3E is easy to confuse with COD-F1B, and an enforcement gate trusting a stale cached value is ARC-F1A.

F.guide: Concurrency and asynchrony: unsynchronised shared state and races (F1), deadlock and blocking of a loop or UI thread (F2), and misuse of async primitives, caches, and signals (F3). A race in a database transaction is DAT-D1C, on a flat file DAT-F1C; partial multi-statement writes are DAT-D1B.
F.name: concurrency-and-asynchrony

category_guides.1: Time: COD-G1A DST-unsafe arithmetic, COD-G1B epoch milliseconds vs seconds, COD-G1C naive mixed with aware datetimes, COD-G1D wall clock used for elapsed time. G1B is the time-specific form of COD-G3C.
category_guides.2: Numeric: COD-G2A money held in float, COD-G2B integer overflow or truncation, COD-G2C precision lost in a numeric conversion, COD-G2D floats compared for equality. G2A wins over G2C when the value is monetary.
category_guides.3: Encoding and units: COD-G3A bytes and str conflated, COD-G3B a platform default encoding assumed, COD-G3C a quantity in the wrong unit, COD-G3D strings compared without Unicode normalization. G3D overlaps COD-C2D; user-facing byte-vs-character length is LNG-E1A.

G.guide: Data representation: time (G1), numbers (G2), and text encoding and units (G3). User-facing text length and locale formatting is LNG (LNG-E1A, LNG-B1A); a database column whose type cannot hold the value is DAT-A1A.
G.name: data-representation-and-time

COD-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when product code opens a file handle (open(), a stream, a reader) with no context manager, try/finally, or explicit close on every path, so release depends on garbage collection or process exit. Evidence names the open site and the path that skips the close. The same leak in test code is TST-D1B; unbounded growth of connections, threads or memory under load with no cap is OPS-D1A.
examples: File opened without a context manager; handle never explicitly closed, relying on GC
json.load(open(...)) pattern never closes the underlying file handle
File resource leak in apply subcommand
COD-A1A.name: unclosed-file-handle-leak

lower_when.condition: the handle is opened once in a short-lived process that exits right after, and the runtime closes it promptly by reference counting

raise_when.condition: the handle is opened once per request or loop iteration in a long-running service and is kept referenced (stored on a long-lived object or in a list) or the runtime does not reclaim it promptly, and any client can trigger the path, so open descriptors grow until the process hits its fd limit and refuses work; evidence shows the per-request open and the retained reference

COD-A2A.criteria: Qualifies when code writes into a fixed-size buffer a number of bytes taken from input or a computed length with no check against the buffer's capacity, so the write can go past the end and corrupt adjacent memory (unsafe/native code, CWE-787/120). Evidence names the buffer, its size, and the source of the length. A read past the end or a crash on a bad index is COD-A2C; an index off by one that stays in bounds is COD-A2B; an integer overflow that produces the bad length is COD-G2B.
examples: Unsafe code writes user_input.len() bytes into a fixed 8-byte buffer with no bounds check
COD-A2A.name: unbounded-buffer-write

lower_when.condition: the write length comes from a value the program computes itself (not from input) and can exceed the buffer only on a path the evidence shows is reachable but not caller-controlled
the language or runtime bounds-checks the write in the shipped build, so an overrun panics or aborts instead of corrupting memory

COD-A2B.criteria: Qualifies when an index, range end, loop bound or count is off by exactly one (using 1 where 0 is right, <= where < is right, nth(1) where the value is already shifted), so the code reads or processes the wrong element or misses the first or last one, while staying inside the sequence. Evidence names the expression and the element it should have reached. An access that goes outside the sequence or reads an empty one is COD-A2C; a write past a buffer is COD-A2A; a loop that stops early for a reason other than its bound is COD-E1B.
examples: env::args().nth(1).unwrap() used to fetch the second CLI arg, but the function actually receives the first argument as its own parameter
COD-A2B.name: off-by-one-argument-index-error

lower_when.condition: the wrongly selected element only changes a display value or log line, not the data the code goes on to process

COD-A2C.criteria: Qualifies when code indexes a sequence, reads argv, or calls min/max/first on a collection without checking that the index exists or the collection is non-empty, including a .get default that cannot fire because the key is present but its list is empty. Evidence names the access and the input that makes it empty or short. A null value dereferenced downstream is COD-B2A; when the short or empty input comes from an untrusted source and the result is a crash, SEC-F1A; unsafe indexing inside a test assertion is TST-B3A; an off-by-one that stays in bounds is COD-A2B.
examples: Missing bounds check on argv access
min() called on a potentially empty sequence in _max_severity
pip-audit adapter indexes fix_versions[0] with a default that never fires when the list is present-but-empty
COD-A2C.name: unchecked-index-or-empty-sequence-access

lower_when.condition: the resulting exception is caught by an enclosing handler that reports the bad input and the run continues with the remaining items

COD-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when config-LOADING code chooses a permissive default on a missing or corrupt config artifact (treats absent and corrupt alike, or resolves a bad path and returns allow) — a correctness fail-direction defect in the loader itself. The specific write-guard / security-control fail-open incident single-homes in ARC-F2E; a general component that skips malformed runtime input is ARC-F2D.
COD-B1A.name: fail-open-on-missing-or-corrupt-config

lower_when.condition: the permissive default only controls a non-enforcement behavior (a feature toggle, output format, verbosity), so failing open grants no action that would otherwise be refused

COD-B1C.criteria: Qualifies when a guard shared by several actors or callers computes its allowed set too broadly, for example as the union of every actor's permissions instead of the current actor's, so one actor may act on resources that belong to another. Evidence names how the allowed set is built and the cross-actor action it permits. An agent tool whose write scope is missing altogether is AGT-B1C, and a grant of more tools than the task needs is AGT-B1D; a hook that has no way to tell actors apart is ARC-F2B.
examples: Write-allowlist is built from the union of every dispatch-plan-*.json across the fan-out, so one reviewer can overwrite a sibling reviewer's findings file
COD-B1C.name: overly-broad-permission-scope-in-shared-guard

lower_when.condition: the extra scope only allows actions that cannot change another actor's resources (reads, or creating new paths that no other actor reads)

raise_when.condition: the over-granted scope lets a lower-trust actor overwrite or delete another actor's output that a downstream step treats as authoritative, with no other copy kept

COD-B2A.criteria: Qualifies when a value that can be null/None/undefined (an explicit JSON null, a .get(key, default) whose default does not fire because the key is present with null, an optional return) is used without a check, so a later operation raises or the record is silently skipped. Evidence names where the null comes from and the operation that fails. An empty sequence or missing index is COD-A2C; when the null arrives in attacker-supplied input and crashes a service, SEC-F1A; an auxiliary load whose failure is not checked is COD-B2C.
examples: .get(key, default) + .startswith() crashes on an explicit JSON null, silently dropping the record instead of handling it
COD-B2A.name: unguarded-null-crashes-downstream

lower_when.condition: the null makes the program fail loudly with an error that names the record, and it does not drop or skip the record

COD-B2B.criteria: Qualifies when an error message or exit diagnostic names a cause that is not the one that actually failed (for example, it reports 'not a git repository' when a merge-base lookup failed), sending the operator to the wrong fix. Evidence names the real failing call and the message shown. A message that is accurate but too vague is QAL-I1B; a docstring that promises the wrong exception type is QAL-C2D; a failure that produces no message at all is COD-B2C or OPS-E1A.
examples: --changes mode's error message blames 'not a git repository' when the real failure is a merge-base lookup
COD-B2B.name: error-message-misattributes-root-cause

lower_when.condition: the real cause is also reported in the same output (a chained exception or traceback shown next to the misleading message)

COD-B2C.criteria: The default home for a swallowed or missing error whose consequence is a WRONG or MISSING RESULT — an auxiliary load/call whose failure is not checked, so the program proceeds on bad or absent data. When the swallowed failure is specifically security-relevant it is SEC-F1B; when the defect is an OVERBROAD catch clause masking multiple error types it is ARC-F2G; a config-loader that fails open is COD-B1A. A Web Storage call with no handling for its throws is COD-B2F.
examples: load_report has no error handling around meta.parts continuation files, and its confinement check diverges from the primary path
COD-B2C.name: missing-error-handling-around-auxiliary-load

raise_when.condition: the data the failed load should have supplied feeds a gate verdict, pass/fail status, or persisted record, and the run reports success with no marker that the data is absent

COD-B2D.criteria: Qualifies when code transforms a result to meet a constraint (it splits, shrinks, filters, or re-encodes it) and does not check the transformed result against that constraint again, so a single pass that is not enough leaves output that still breaks the limit. Evidence names the constraint and the transform that is not re-checked. Output cut short with no warning is COD-B2E; a required field that ends up missing or empty in the output is COD-C3A.
examples: write_report()'s oversize split does one unbounded halving pass and never re-validates the result against the original size constraint
COD-B2D.name: result-not-revalidated-after-transform

raise_when.condition: the over-limit result is passed on to a consumer that rejects or truncates it without telling anyone (an API size cap, an issue body limit), so the data is lost

COD-B2E.criteria: Qualifies when code caps, pages or truncates a result set or value (a --limit, a first-N slice, a fixed-size buffer) and does not detect or report that more data was there, so the caller treats a partial result as complete. Evidence names the cap and why the source can exceed it. A missing cap on an endpoint or query is OPS-D1B; a scanner that drops findings silently is SEC-G2B; a persisted mirror left durably partial is DAT-E1D; a loop that exits early by mistake, not because of a cap, is COD-E1B.
examples: recover_linkage_from_github caps at --limit 1000 with no detection or warning that results were truncated
COD-B2E.name: silent-truncation-without-warning

raise_when.condition: the truncated result is used for a completeness claim or decision: a count, an 'all items processed' status, a reconciliation, or a gate

COD-B2F.criteria: Qualifies when a client path calls the Web Storage API (localStorage or sessionStorage getItem, setItem, removeItem, or the property access itself) with no handling for its documented throws, SecurityError when storage is blocked and QuotaExceededError when it is full, so a browser that denies or fills storage breaks a render, boot or persistence path instead of degrading. Evidence names the call and the path it aborts. A generic auxiliary load whose failure goes unchecked is COD-B2C.
examples: A theme hook reads localStorage in its state initializer and writes it in a layout effect with no try/catch, so a blocked or full storage throws and aborts the app's first render
A draft-persistence path updates in-memory state, then calls sessionStorage.setItem unguarded, so a quota error leaves the two diverged
COD-B2F.name: unguarded-web-storage-access

raise_when.condition: the unguarded call runs in the application's root initialisation or first render, so a browser with storage blocked gets a blank or broken app and not just one degraded widget

COD-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when an adapter or normalizer takes one source value and uses it for both confidence and severity, or puts the source's confidence/priority into the severity field, so the two axes stop being independent and findings are graded by certainty instead of impact. Evidence names the source field and both target fields. Ignoring the source's severity and hardcoding one value is COD-C1B; an unmapped value that silently falls back to a default grade is COD-C3B.
examples: Brakeman has no real severity field; adapter derives both confidence and severity from the same High/Medium/Weak vocabulary via a map missing a 'low' entry
SpotBugs BugInstance.priority (its confidence) is mapped onto our severity field, while our confidence field is hardcoded
osv-scanner adapter silently downgrades known vulnerabilities to INFO severity
Shared severity normalizer silently defaults unmapped/un-rated severity strings to INFO across every dependency
COD-C1A.name: analyzer-confidence-conflated-with-severity

lower_when.condition: the wrongly derived severity only affects display or sort order and does not feed a gate, filter threshold, or suppression rule

COD-C1B.criteria: Qualifies when an adapter sets a constant severity for every finding from a source that provides its own per-finding severity or level (a SARIF level, a CVSS score), so the real spread of grades is lost. Evidence names the source field that is ignored and the constant. Using the source's confidence as the severity is COD-C1A; a mapping table that lacks some values and silently falls back is COD-C3B; inconsistency between sibling adapters in fail-safe direction is ARC-A4A.
examples: roslyn_secguard's parse() hardcodes severity to 'HIGH' for every SecurityCodeScan finding instead of reading the SARIF 'level' field
pip-audit adapter hardcodes severity to MEDIUM for essentially all findings, masking the true severity
COD-C1B.name: severity-hardcoded-ignoring-tool-value

lower_when.condition: the hardcoded value is at or above every grade the source can emit, so findings can only be graded too high (noise) and none can fall below a gate

COD-C2A.criteria: Qualifies when code picks which input file to process by a heuristic (the first glob match, sort order, a name pattern) that can pick a secondary file (dev or test requirements, a backup, a fixture) over the primary one, so the run analyses the wrong input and reports nothing about the right one. Evidence names the heuristic and the competing candidate it can pick. A correct name resolved against the wrong directory is COD-E2B; a scan tool that runs on no input at all and stays silent is SEC-G2B.
examples: pip-audit's _find_requirement globs requirements*.txt and takes the first sorted match, silently picking a dev/test requirements file over the primary requirements.txt
COD-C2A.name: incorrect-source-file-selection-heuristic

lower_when.condition: the file it can wrongly pick is a superset of the intended one (for example it includes the primary requirements), so results are noisier but nothing from the primary input is missed

COD-C2B.criteria: Qualifies when one lifecycle phase (init, invoke, run) stores state on an instance or in a process and a later phase reads it from a different instance, process or worker that never received it, so the later phase falls back to a default or computes a wrong result. Evidence names where the state is written, where it is read, and why they do not share it. A deviation from a stateless convention with no wrong result is ARC-A4A; state shared between concurrent threads with no lock is COD-F1C.
examples: PipAuditAdapter records the manifest into self._manifest_path in invoke(), but parse() runs in a separate process/instance and never sees it
PipAuditAdapter maintains mutable instance state, deviating from the stateless adapter pattern
COD-C2B.name: instance-state-not-propagated-through-lifecycle

lower_when.condition: the later phase rebuilds the missing state on its own from the same inputs, so only efficiency is lost

COD-C2C.criteria: Qualifies when a parsing regex or pattern match fails on a legitimate variant of its input (more than one item per line, an optional line that is absent, alternative quoting or ordering), so valid records are silently not matched or fail to parse. Evidence names the pattern and the valid variant it rejects. A schema or validator that rejects real producer output is COD-D1B; a pattern with catastrophic backtracking is SEC-H4A; an identifier that matches only after normalization is COD-C2D.
examples: LABEL_RE.fullmatch() only matches a single backtick-quoted label, silently failing on multi-label lines
bundle-audit block regex requires a CVE: line unconditionally while treating the sibling GHSA: line as optional, though either may be absent
COD-C2C.name: regex-rejects-valid-input-variant

lower_when.condition: a non-match raises a parse error that names the line, so the rejected variant is not silently dropped

COD-C2D.criteria: Qualifies when an identifier (a path, key, name, id) is compared or looked up without first being put into the same form as the table it is matched against (a ./ prefix, a trailing slash, letter case, separators), so equal identifiers fail to match and the record is misclassified or dropped. Evidence names both forms. A mismatch caused by Unicode normalization is COD-G3D; a fingerprint that changes between runs is ARC-D1C; a scrub applied on one path but not its recovery path is ARC-D1A.
examples: diff_map.classify() does not normalize a ./-prefixed location.file before matching it against the hunk map
COD-C2D.name: unnormalized-identifier-causes-lookup-mismatch

lower_when.condition: a lookup miss falls back to a conservative classification (treats the item as in scope or unmatched-but-kept), so nothing is dropped

COD-C3A.criteria: Qualifies when a producer emits a record that lacks a field its output contract marks as required, or fills it with an empty string or empty object, so consumers get a non-conforming record. Evidence names the field, the contract that requires it, and the code path that leaves it empty. A schema whose required list omits a documented field is COD-D1D; a specification that never tells the producer to emit the field is ARC-D2E; one field emitted with different types is COD-D3C.
examples: Findings F-DUP-1/F-DUP-2 lack the required location.line_start field
Findings contain empty-string values for structurally required panel/category/title fields
sarif_to_findings() can emit an empty location object when a SARIF result has no locations
COD-C3A.name: required-output-field-missing-or-empty

COD-C3B.criteria: Qualifies when a lookup or mapping table that the code relies on (CWE to OWASP, a severity map, a catalog) is missing entries for values the program actually produces, and a lookup miss silently falls back to a default or empty value, so enrichment or classification is quietly lost for those values. Evidence names the missing keys and the fallback. A mapping that is sparse by design and only lacks documentation of that is QAL-C2F; a handler that silently skips an unregistered format or extension is ARC-A4D; the same table duplicated in two places is ARC-A3B.
examples: CWE-to-OWASP mapping in the reference catalog is incomplete
cwe-catalog.json is missing CWE-16, CWE-778, CWE-693 needed by citations.py's category-derived CWE fallback
The cwe_owasp mapping omits 8 of the 34 CWEs listed in the main catalog, silently dropping OWASP derivation for those findings
COD-C3B.name: incomplete-lookup-catalog-silent-fallback-gap

lower_when.condition: a miss leaves the field empty and visibly marked unknown, and nothing downstream decides anything from it

raise_when.condition: the fallback value is a grade or classification that a gate or filter acts on (for example unmapped severities default to INFO and INFO is below the gate), so real findings pass the gate unseen

COD-C3C.criteria: Qualifies when a producer emits a key or field name outside the shared vocabulary (a tool-specific citation key, a renamed field) and a downstream stage silently discards it, so the information is lost without an error. Evidence names the key, the producer, and the stage that drops it. A shared lookup table that lacks a value is COD-C3B; a schema field nobody populates is ARC-D2D; sibling adapters that use different conventions are ARC-A4A.
examples: cargo-audit adapter's non-standard 'rustsec' citation key is dropped by the downstream citation pipeline with no error
COD-C3C.name: nonstandard-key-silently-dropped-downstream

lower_when.condition: the same information also travels in a standard field of the same record, so dropping the non-standard key loses nothing

COD-D1A.criteria: Qualifies at the FIELD level when a value exists (or is referenced as valid) that lies outside that field's own declared enum — an enum-completeness or value-validity violation for one specific field. A specific documented-required field omitted from the schema is COD-D1D; a wholesale, multi-field contract-vs-schema divergence is ARC-D1B.
examples: confirmation_status field carries a value outside its own schema enum
summary.gate enum is [PASS, FAIL, OFF] but SKILL.md references INCONCLUSIVE as a valid gate value in six places
COD-D1A.name: schema-enum-incomplete-vs-actual-values

lower_when.condition: the out-of-enum value appears only in documentation or prompts and no producer emits it at runtime, so no real instance is rejected or misread

COD-D1B.criteria: Qualifies when a LIVE schema, pattern, or validator is stricter than what the producer legitimately emits, so real output is actively REJECTED (an invalid instance is produced at runtime) — a correctness harm. If the over-precision is inert and nothing is actually rejected, it is QAL-C2A; if the stricter artifact is a dead, unimported duplicate, QAL-E1B; if the defect is the id/format being specified inconsistently across two or more artifacts with no single authority, ARC-D1D.
examples: report-schema.json's finding-id pattern (2-4 letters) is stricter than what agents/synthesize.py actually emit
COD-D1B.name: schema-pattern-stricter-than-producer-output

lower_when.condition: the validator runs in advisory or warn-only mode, so real output is flagged but not dropped, rejected, or blocked

COD-D1C.criteria: Qualifies when the elements of one array or collection in an emitted document have different shapes (different key sets, nested structure, or optional sub-objects), so a consumer written for one shape mishandles the others. Evidence names two elements and how their shapes differ. One field with a different type across return paths is COD-D3C; a value outside an enum is COD-D1A; one equivalent edge case (missing versus empty) handled differently is ARC-D2B.
examples: Finding object schema is inconsistent across the findings array
Provenance object field structure varies across findings
COD-D1C.name: inconsistent-record-shape-across-array

lower_when.condition: every shape present is valid under the published schema and the consumers in the repo handle all of them, so the inconsistency is cosmetic

COD-D1D.criteria: Qualifies at the FIELD level when the schema's required list OMITS a field the documentation mandates as mandatory — a required-field gap for specific fields. A field carrying a value outside its enum is COD-D1A; a wholesale contract-vs-schema divergence spanning many fields or behaviors is ARC-D1B.
examples: report-schema.json's required list omits provenance/citations despite docs mandating 'MUST include provenance/citations'
Schema is missing an integrity object for fields that are actually emitted
COD-D1D.name: schema-omits-documented-required-fields

lower_when.condition: every producer in the repo always emits the field, so the gap only weakens validation and no non-conforming record has been or can be produced by current code

COD-D2B.criteria: Qualifies when documentation describes a feature, flag, or mode that is NOT IMPLEMENTED at all, so a user following the docs invokes something that does not exist and the run breaks — behavioral, HIGH. If the flag exists but its documentation is merely stale, renamed, or under-covered, that is QAL-C2C (doc hygiene); if the whole CLI interface contract has drifted structurally, ARC-D2A.
examples: README Quick Start documents a --mode flag that doesn't exist in the CLI
SKILL.md documents an -e/--explore mode with no corresponding implementation in orchestrator.py
HTML artifact is only auto-derived when --out is passed explicitly, contradicting the documented default synthesize invocation
COD-D2B.name: documented-feature-or-flag-not-implemented

lower_when.condition: invoking the missing feature fails at once and loudly (an unknown-flag or usage error), so no run continues on a wrong assumption

COD-D2C.criteria: Qualifies (until re-homed) only when two specification documents that both claim to be current prescribe incompatible behavior for the same feature and code was, or will be, implemented from one of them. A single document that contradicts itself is QAL-C2B; two sources of truth that disagree in general are ARC-G1B; a design document that drifted from what was delivered is ARC-G2B; a superseded document left unmarked is ARC-G2A.
examples: A spec's Advisor Confirmation Flow prescribes a severity-downgrade behavior that the same-day epistemics-core spec explicitly supersedes/contradicts
COD-D2C.name: self-contradicting-specification-documents

lower_when.condition: no code has been implemented from the losing document yet
one of the two documents is explicitly dated or marked as superseded by the other, so a reader can tell which applies

COD-D2D.criteria: Qualifies (until re-homed) when a capability that exists in code (a host profile, flag, or mode) is absent from the user-facing documentation that lists its siblings, so users cannot discover it. Reference documentation that is incomplete in general is ARC-G1C; undocumented configuration behavior is QAL-C2F; a documented capability that does not exist is COD-D2B.
examples: 'openrouter' host profile has no corresponding documentation in SKILL.md's Host dispatch section
Step 5's --host hint omits 'codex', the newest first-class host
COD-D2D.name: implemented-capability-missing-from-docs

lower_when.condition: the capability is listed in --help or another shipped reference that users see, and only the narrative documentation omits it
the capability is marked experimental or internal in code

COD-D3A.criteria: Qualifies when code calls an external API, library, CI action or CLI with an argument whose shape, type or kind differs from what that interface documents (a directory where a file is expected, a list where a scalar is expected, a wrong unit or enum), so the call fails or quietly does something else. Evidence cites the external interface's documented parameter. An internal adapter that does not satisfy its own declared protocol is COD-D3B; a field whose type differs across the repo's own return paths is COD-D3C; a quantity in the wrong unit is COD-G3C.
examples: security.yml passes a directory path to the SARIF-upload action's sarif_file parameter, which expects a single file
COD-D3A.name: external-api-invoked-with-wrong-parameter-shape

lower_when.condition: the wrong shape makes the call fail with an error on every invocation, so the defect shows up on the first run and cannot produce wrong results unseen

COD-D3B.criteria: Qualifies when a concrete adapter or implementation does not satisfy the protocol, interface, or abstract base it is registered or typed as (missing or wrong-signature methods, wrong return type), so the dispatcher's calls through that interface fail or misbehave. Evidence names the protocol member and how the implementation differs. Adapters that satisfy the protocol but follow different conventions are ARC-A4A; two documents describing incompatible protocols are ARC-G1B; a wrong call into a third-party API is COD-D3A.
examples: LegacySarifAdapter violates the ToolAdapter protocol structure
Phase 1's module-level-function adapter protocol conflicts with the class-based protocol actually adopted elsewhere
COD-D3B.name: adapter-violates-declared-protocol-interface

lower_when.condition: the dispatcher never calls the missing or mismatched member on this adapter in the paths the repo uses (it is structural non-conformance only)

COD-D3C.criteria: Qualifies when one field crossing a function, module, or serialization boundary has different types on different paths (a string on one path and an int on another, a list or a scalar, a string or null), so consumers that compare, sort, or do arithmetic on it get wrong results or raise. Evidence names the field and two paths with their types. Whole records with different shapes are COD-D1C; a value outside its declared enum is COD-D1A; bytes and text mixed up is COD-G3A.
examples: derive_evidence() returns 'verified_by' as inconsistent types across return paths
location.line_start is emitted as a string instead of an integer
COD-D3C.name: inconsistent-field-type-across-boundary

lower_when.condition: every consumer in the repo coerces the field to one type before use

COD-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when deduplication or merge logic uses a key coarser than the entries' real identity (or falls back to one after an exact match), so two different entries that share the coarse key collapse and one is silently discarded. Evidence names the key, the two distinct entries, and the drop site. An identity key that changes between runs is ARC-D1C; an id format specified inconsistently across artifacts is ARC-D1D; a deliberate cap is COD-B2E.
examples: build_diff silently drops a run3 finding that shares a coarse key with an already-exact-matched run2 fingerprint
COD-E1A.name: dedup-logic-drops-entry-sharing-coarse-key

lower_when.condition: the discarded entry is also kept in a raw or unmerged output that is shipped next to the deduplicated one

raise_when.condition: the discarded entries are records with no other copy (findings, transactions, user data), the run reports success, and the evidence shows two distinct real or representative inputs that share the coarse key

COD-E1B.criteria: Qualifies when a loop meant to process every valid entry (search paths, candidates, pages) exits early, through a break, a return, or a first-match condition, before reaching later valid entries, so coverage is incomplete. Evidence names the exit and an entry it skips. An off-by-one in the loop bound is COD-A2B; a deliberate cap with no warning is COD-B2E; dedup that discards entries is COD-E1A.
examples: NODE_PATH loop breaks after the first global_node, leaving incomplete directory coverage
COD-E1B.name: loop-exits-before-exhausting-valid-entries

raise_when.condition: the skipped entries are inputs a security or completeness check is supposed to inspect, so the check passes without examining them

COD-E2A.criteria: Qualifies when a guard, return, or exit placed before later definitions makes PRODUCTION code unreachable — the skipped code would run in normal operation but now never executes (a reachability defect). If the silently skipped definitions are test cases (a test-discovery gap), that is TST-C1A; if nothing after the guard is actually skipped (pure misplacement), QAL-F2B.
COD-E2A.name: unreachable-code-due-to-guard-placed-before-definition

lower_when.condition: the unreachable code is neither a security control, a data-write path, nor a validation step (for example a reporting or feature path), so its absence gives wrong or missing output but no exposure or data loss
the unreachable code's absence is visible to the user at once (a command that does nothing, a missing section), so it cannot go unnoticed

COD-E2B.criteria: Qualifies when a relative path is resolved against a base the code does not intend (the process cwd instead of the module or skill directory, or the repo root instead of the target), so the read or write hits a different or missing file whenever the program is launched from somewhere else. Evidence names the path, the base it resolves against, and the base intended. A hardcoded absolute path is ARC-E1A; the test-fixture form is TST-D2A; a search path an attacker can plant files in is SEC-D1B; picking the wrong file among several candidates is COD-C2A.
examples: Security-checklists reference is relative to the skill directory, but the reviewing agent's cwd is the target repo
COD-E2B.name: path-resolved-against-wrong-base-directory

lower_when.condition: the only supported launch method (a documented wrapper or entry point) always sets the base to the intended directory

raise_when.condition: the mis-resolved path is used as the target of a write, overwrite, or delete, so launching from another directory changes or removes files outside the intended tree

COD-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when a compound in-memory operation that must be indivisible (update two related fields, increment then publish, pop then push) runs as separate steps that another thread or task can interleave with, so observers see or produce an inconsistent intermediate state. Evidence names the steps and the invariant that holds between them. A stale check followed by an act is COD-F1B; a single shared variable with no lock is COD-F1C; related multi-statement database writes with no transaction are DAT-D1B; a file write that can tear on crash is DAT-F1B.
COD-F1A.name: atomicity-violation-compound-operation

lower_when.condition: the inconsistent intermediate state is only visible to readers that display it (a progress or status view) and is never read by code that writes or decides from it

COD-F1B.criteria: Qualifies when code checks a condition (existence, type, symlink status, permission, value) and later acts on the result as a separate step, so the state can change between the check and the act and the act proceeds on a stale premise. Evidence names the check, the act, and what can change the state between them. A repeatable user action with no in-flight guard is COD-F3E; a DB or KV read-modify-write with no lock or CAS is DAT-D1C, and the flat-file form is DAT-F1C; a copy that dereferences attacker-controlled symlinks is SEC-D1C; an enforcement gate that trusts a persisted flag instead of re-verifying is ARC-F1A.
examples: decide() validates a write target via os.path.islink()/os.path.realpath(), but the actual write happens later in a separate tool-call step, leaving a window for the target to change
COD-F1B.name: check-then-act-race

raise_when.condition: the check is a security decision (path confinement, symlink, permission) and a less-trusted party can write the checked object during the window

COD-F1C.criteria: Qualifies when state shared between threads, tasks, or concurrent async continuations is read and written without synchronisation, so an interleaving corrupts or overwrites it, including an older async result applied over a newer one. Evidence names the shared state and two concurrent writers. A user action that can be re-entered while its own request is in flight is COD-F3E; one-time lazy initialization that races is COD-F3B; database rows are DAT-D1C and shared flat files are DAT-F1C.
COD-F1C.name: shared-mutable-state-without-synchronization

lower_when.condition: the shared state is a cache or counter used only for display or metrics, and a lost update is corrected the next time it is read

raise_when.condition: the corrupted state is persisted or sent on (written to storage or returned to a client), and the code runs with two or more concurrent writers in its default deployment (a thread pool, multiple async tasks, or several workers sharing the state), as the evidence shows

COD-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when two or more code paths acquire the same locks (mutexes, DB row locks, file locks) in different orders, or a path re-acquires a non-reentrant lock it already holds, so concurrent execution can block forever. Evidence names the locks and the two acquisition orders. A blocking call that stalls an event loop is COD-F2B; a missing timeout on an outbound call is OPS-A1A; a long-held DB transaction that causes contention is DAT-D1D.
COD-F2A.name: deadlock-lock-ordering

lower_when.condition: the lock acquisitions use a timeout or try-lock, so the cycle ends in an error and retry and not a permanent hang

COD-F2B.criteria: Qualifies when a synchronous blocking call (I/O, sleep, lock wait, or heavy CPU work) runs on an async event loop or UI thread and stalls it. Rendering an unbounded collection in one pass is COD-F2C.
COD-F2B.name: blocking-call-in-async-context

lower_when.condition: the blocking call runs only at startup or shutdown, before or after the loop serves any request or UI event

COD-F2C.criteria: Qualifies when one interaction renders every item of a collection that grows with user data (rows, messages, participants, search results) into the UI in a single pass, with no paging, virtualisation, windowing or cap, so the interaction's main-thread time and DOM size scale with the data. Evidence names the collection's source, why it is unbounded, and the render site. Loading an unbounded collection into memory is QAL-G2A; an endpoint or query returning an unbounded result set is OPS-D1B; a synchronous blocking call on an async path is COD-F2B.
examples: A table view renders every row of a user-data collection in a single render pass, with no paging, virtualisation or cap, so render time and DOM size grow with the data
A chat panel maps a session's full message history to rendered message components when it opens
COD-F2C.name: unbounded-collection-rendered-in-one-pass

lower_when.condition: the collection is bounded by an enforced product limit (for example a server-side cap on members or messages per view) small enough that one pass stays cheap

COD-F3A.criteria: Qualifies when code reads a cached or memoized value after the underlying source has changed and there is no invalidation, versioning, or expiry tied to that change, so callers get an outdated result. Evidence names the cache, the write that should invalidate it, and the read that returns the old value. A copy of data kept in sync with a source of record that has drifted is DAT-E1D; missing memoization (the opposite) is QAL-G1B; a race between concurrent writers to the cache is COD-F1C.
COD-F3A.name: stale-cache-read-without-invalidation

lower_when.condition: the cache has a short time-to-live that the evidence shows, and a stale read only delays a non-critical display update

COD-F3B.criteria: Qualifies when a value is created on first use (a singleton, a cached client, a module-level lazy global) by a check-if-unset then set step with no lock or once-guard, so concurrent first callers can each create it, or one can see a partly built instance. Evidence names the lazy site and the concurrent callers. General unsynchronised shared state is COD-F1C; a check that goes stale before the act on external state is COD-F1B; a cache that is never invalidated is COD-F3A.
COD-F3B.name: thread-unsafe-lazy-initialization

lower_when.condition: creating the value twice is idempotent and side-effect free, and the language's memory model publishes the reference only after construction, so the only cost is duplicate work

COD-F3C.criteria: Qualifies when an async call's coroutine, promise, or future is created and never awaited or otherwise handled (a missing await, a fire-and-forget with no error handler), so its work may not run, may finish after the caller has moved on, or may fail with nobody seeing the rejection. Evidence names the call and what depends on its result. A user action that can be re-triggered while in flight is COD-F3E; an error that is caught and dropped is COD-B2C; a blocking call inside async code is COD-F2B.
COD-F3C.name: unawaited-async-result

lower_when.condition: the unawaited work is meant to be fire-and-forget (telemetry, a prefetch), and nothing later reads its result or depends on its finishing

COD-F3D.criteria: Qualifies when a signal handler does work that is not async-signal-safe (allocating, taking locks, doing I/O, calling non-reentrant library functions) or changes shared state that the interrupted code may be using, so a signal arriving at the wrong moment deadlocks or corrupts that state (CWE-479). Evidence names the handler and the unsafe operation. Missing graceful-shutdown draining on SIGTERM is OPS-B1A; general unsynchronised shared state is COD-F1C.
COD-F3D.name: unsafe-signal-handler

lower_when.condition: the runtime defers the handler to a safe point (for example, Python runs signal handlers between bytecodes on the main thread) and the handler only sets a flag or exits

COD-F3E.criteria: Qualifies when a user-triggered asynchronous action (a mutation, submit or create) can be activated again while an earlier activation is still in flight, because nothing disables the control, tracks a pending state, or deduplicates the request, so repeated activation issues duplicate side effects. Evidence names the trigger, the async call, and the missing guard. Threads or tasks racing on unsynchronised shared state are COD-F1C; a check that is stale by the time it is acted on is COD-F1B.
examples: A Save button calls an async upload mutation and stays enabled until the success callback navigates away, so a second click submits a duplicate
A confirm handler starts a permission change without recording or checking an in-flight state, so repeated activation fires the request again
COD-F3E.name: async-action-without-in-flight-guard

lower_when.condition: the server treats the request as idempotent (an idempotency key, upsert, or unique constraint), so a repeat yields one effect and at most a redundant call

raise_when.condition: the duplicated side effect is a payment, charge, or transfer that cannot be reversed, and the server takes no idempotency key and has no dedup for the request

COD-G1A.criteria: Qualifies when code adds or subtracts calendar spans (days, months) as fixed numbers of seconds or hours in local time, or builds local times that may not exist or may occur twice, so results are an hour off or invalid across a DST change. Evidence names the arithmetic and the time zone. Comparing naive and aware datetimes is COD-G1C; using the wall clock to time intervals is COD-G1D; user-facing date formatting is LNG-B1A.
COD-G1A.name: dst-unsafe-time-arithmetic

lower_when.condition: the time zone the computation runs in is pinned to UTC or another zone with no DST, as shown by the code or deployment config

COD-G1B.criteria: Qualifies when an epoch timestamp produced in one unit (milliseconds, microseconds) is read as another (seconds), or the reverse, so dates land decades off or durations are off by a factor of 1000. Evidence names the producer's unit and the consumer's assumption. Unit confusion in a quantity that is not a timestamp is COD-G3C; precision lost when converting the timestamp is COD-G2C.
COD-G1B.name: epoch-unit-confusion-ms-vs-s

lower_when.condition: the value is only displayed, and the resulting date is so far off that a reader cannot miss it

raise_when.condition: the misread timestamp decides when data is deleted or retained, or when a credential or token expires, so records are deleted early or access outlives its intended expiry

COD-G1C.criteria: Qualifies when time-zone-aware and naive datetimes are compared, subtracted, or stored together, so the code raises, or treats a naive value as local time when it was UTC (or the reverse), and ordering or durations come out wrong. Evidence names both values' origins. DST-unsafe calendar arithmetic is COD-G1A; a wrong epoch unit is COD-G1B.
COD-G1C.name: naive-aware-datetime-mixing

lower_when.condition: mixing them raises an exception every time (Python's naive/aware comparison TypeError), so it cannot produce a wrong ordering unseen

COD-G1D.criteria: Qualifies when elapsed time, timeouts, or rate limits are measured with the wall clock (time.time(), Date.now()) instead of a monotonic clock, so NTP adjustments, manual changes, or leap smearing make intervals negative, too long, or too short. Evidence names the measurement and the decision it drives. A test whose result depends on the wall clock is TST-F1E; DST arithmetic on calendar time is COD-G1A.
COD-G1D.name: wall-clock-used-for-elapsed-time

lower_when.condition: the measured interval is only logged or reported as a duration

raise_when.condition: the measured interval drives a timeout, lockout, rate limit, or token-expiry decision, so a clock step can expire or extend it

COD-G2A.criteria: Qualifies when monetary amounts are stored, summed, or compared as binary floating point (float, double, JS number used for fractional currency), so rounding error builds up into wrong totals or failed equality. Evidence names the money value and the arithmetic. A database column type that cannot hold the amount exactly is DAT-A1A; precision lost in a non-monetary numeric conversion is COD-G2C; comparing floats for equality in general is COD-G2D.
COD-G2A.name: monetary-value-in-float

lower_when.condition: the float only holds a value computed exactly elsewhere (integer minor units or decimal) and is used for display or formatting, never fed back into arithmetic or storage
the amounts are whole currency units well within 2^53 and are never divided or multiplied by fractions

COD-G2B.criteria: Qualifies when integer arithmetic or a narrowing cast can go past the target type's range (a fixed-width add, multiply, or shift, int64 to int32, signed to unsigned), so the value wraps, saturates, or is truncated without notice. Evidence names the operation, the type, and the input range that overflows it. When the overflowed value then sizes a buffer write, the memory corruption is COD-A2A; loss of fractional or low-order precision without a range overflow is COD-G2C.
COD-G2B.name: integer-overflow-or-truncation

lower_when.condition: the language traps on overflow in the shipped build (checked arithmetic), so overflow aborts instead of wrapping

raise_when.condition: the overflowed value is used as an allocation size, length, or index, or as a balance or quantity that is persisted, and the overflowing input can arrive through normal use

COD-G2C.criteria: Qualifies when a numeric value is converted to a representation that cannot hold it exactly (a 64-bit integer through a JSON or JS double, a decimal through float, a high-precision value through a narrower float) and the code goes on to rely on the exact value. Evidence names the conversion and a value that changes. Money in float is COD-G2A; integer range overflow or truncation is COD-G2B; a database column too narrow for the value is DAT-A1A.
COD-G2C.name: precision-loss-in-numeric-conversion

lower_when.condition: the converted value is only displayed or rounded for presentation, and no comparison, key, or later calculation uses it

raise_when.condition: the converted value is an identifier or key (a 64-bit id through a double), so distinct records collide or point to the wrong record without notice

COD-G2D.criteria: Qualifies when floating-point values produced by arithmetic are compared with == or != (or used as dict or set keys) instead of within a tolerance, so mathematically equal results compare unequal. Evidence names the comparison and how the operands were computed. Money stored in float is COD-G2A; precision lost in a conversion is COD-G2C.
COD-G2D.name: float-equality-comparison

lower_when.condition: both operands are exactly representable constants or integers stored as floats, so equality is exact

raise_when.condition: the equality result ends a loop or decides a branch that changes persisted data or a gate verdict

COD-G3A.criteria: Qualifies when raw bytes and decoded text are mixed up: bytes concatenated with or compared to str, a str written to a binary stream, len() of bytes treated as a character count in data processing, or a repr like b'...' ending up in output. Evidence names the value and where its kind changes without notice. Decoding with an implicit platform encoding is COD-G3B; user-facing text length or truncation by bytes is LNG-E1A; one field with different types across return paths is COD-D3C.
COD-G3A.name: bytes-string-conflation

lower_when.condition: the mix-up raises a TypeError on every run, so it cannot produce corrupted output silently

COD-G3B.criteria: Qualifies when text is read from or written to files, subprocesses, or sockets without naming an encoding, so the platform or locale default (cp1252, ASCII, the LANG setting) is used and non-ASCII content is garbled or raises on other machines (CWE-176). Evidence names the I/O call and the content that can be non-ASCII. Mixing bytes and str is COD-G3A; strings compared without Unicode normalization is COD-G3D; locale-aware formatting of UI text is LNG-B1A.
COD-G3B.name: default-encoding-assumption

lower_when.condition: the runtime's default is UTF-8 on every supported platform (for example Python UTF-8 mode is forced, or the supported OS list has only UTF-8 locales)

COD-G3C.criteria: Qualifies when a quantity (a size, duration, distance, rate, currency) produced in one unit is used as another (KiB as bytes, minutes as seconds, cents as dollars) with no conversion, so limits, thresholds, or results are off by a constant factor. Evidence names the producer's unit and the consumer's assumption. An epoch timestamp read in the wrong unit is COD-G1B; an external API passed a value in the wrong unit is COD-D3A.
COD-G3C.name: unit-confusion-in-quantity

lower_when.condition: the mis-scaled quantity only feeds a log line or a display label

raise_when.condition: the mis-scaled quantity is a money amount, a dosage or physical control value, or a safety limit (a size cap or rate limit made 1000x looser), so the error causes financial loss or disables a protection

COD-G3D.criteria: Qualifies when strings that can contain composed or decomposed Unicode forms (NFC vs NFD, compatibility characters) are compared, hashed, or used as keys without normalizing them to one form, so visually identical text fails to match or duplicates get past a uniqueness check (CWE-176). Evidence names the comparison and the source of non-normalized text. Non-Unicode identifier normalization (case, ./ prefixes, separators) is COD-C2D; byte-vs-character length is LNG-E1A.
COD-G3D.name: unicode-normalization-mismatch

lower_when.condition: every input reaching the comparison is restricted to ASCII by an earlier validation step

raise_when.condition: the compared string is an identity or uniqueness key (a username, file path, permission or role name), so distinct forms of the same text slip past a uniqueness or match check

COD.guide: COD (correctness) is the home for an instance that produces a WRONG RESULT, crashes, hangs, or breaks a contract at runtime: memory and bounds errors, unchecked failures, wrong parsing or value mapping, schema-vs-output mismatches, control-flow and ordering mistakes, races and async misuse, and numeric/time/encoding errors. Choose ARC instead when two specifications disagree with each other or the defect is structural (ARC-D*, ARC-F2*, ARC-G1*), QAL when the problem is inert staleness or readability with no wrong behavior (QAL-C*, QAL-E*), DAT when the wrong state is in a database or durable file (DAT-D*, DAT-F*), SEC when the input is attacker-reachable and the harm is exploitation (SEC-F1A, SEC-D1C), OPS when the failure is a capacity, timeout, or telemetry gap in production operation (OPS-A1A, OPS-D1A, OPS-E1A), and TST when the defect lives in test code. Look in A for leaks and bounds, B for guards and swallowed failures, C for value mapping and parsing, D for schema/doc/interface contracts, E for loop and ordering logic, F for concurrency and async, G for time, numbers, encoding and units.
COD.name: correctness

category_guides.1: Integrity-and-modeling: a type that cannot hold the value set is DAT-A1A; an invariant the type can hold but no CHECK/UNIQUE/NOT NULL constraint enforces is DAT-A1B; a parent reference with no FK is DAT-A1C; a NULL with no single meaning is DAT-A1D. The easy confusions are A1A/A1B (range invariants), A1B/A1C (membership via FK), A1B/A1D (a required field left nullable) and A1B/DAT-E1C (a unique constraint wrong under soft delete).

A.guide: Schema-design: the declared shape of stored data and whether it enforces the domain's rules. Covers column types, constraints, foreign keys and NULL semantics; see category 1.
A.name: schema-design

category_guides.1: Safety-and-reversibility: apply-time data loss is DAT-B1A (it outranks B1C irreversibility and B1D re-run safety); heavy locks during apply are DAT-B1B; no faithful down path is DAT-B1C; an unsafe re-run is DAT-B1D; a migration that applies nothing is DAT-B1E; a first-run failure swallowed and recorded as applied is DAT-B1F. The usual confusions are B1A/B1C, B1D/B1F, B1E/B1F and B1B/DAT-D1D (migration vs runtime locus).

B.guide: Migrations: what applying, re-running, reversing or silently skipping a schema migration does to production data and schema. Everything here is migration-scoped: a non-migration rewrite of stored data is DAT-F1A, and startup code that runs a migration unconditionally on every boot is OPS-C1B. See category 1.
B.name: migrations

category_guides.1: Efficiency-and-scale: no index for a hot read is DAT-C1A; a query per row in a loop is DAT-C1B; no LIMIT on a growing set is DAT-C1C; too many columns fetched is DAT-C1D. C1C/C1D co-occur (rows vs columns), and C1C overlaps OPS-D1B and QAL-G2A.

C.guide: Query-patterns: the cost and shape of reads and writes issued against a store. Covers missing indexes, per-row query loops, unbounded result sets and over-fetched columns; see category 1. An API endpoint lacking pagination is OPS-D1B; in-memory growth after the read is QAL-G2A.
