C.name: query-patterns

category_guides.1: Isolation-and-atomicity: a transaction whose isolation level is too weak for its invariant is DAT-D1A; no transaction around writes that must be all-or-nothing is DAT-D1B; concurrent writers racing on a read-modify-write with no lock or CAS is DAT-D1C; a transaction held open across expensive work is DAT-D1D. The easy confusions are D1A/D1C, D1B/DAT-E1B, and D1D/DAT-B1B (runtime vs migration). For a check-then-insert race with no unique constraint, cite DAT-A1B when the fix is the constraint and D1C when the finding is the race window.

D.guide: Transactions-and-concurrency: whether multi-statement database or KV work is atomic, isolated and short. Covers isolation choice, missing transaction boundaries, read-modify-write races and long-held transactions; see category 1. The flat-file analogue is area F; in-memory races are COD-F.
D.name: transactions-and-concurrency

category_guides.1: Retention-and-drift: ORM model vs migration DDL drift is DAT-E1A; a delete path that strands rows is DAT-E1B; soft delete applied inconsistently is DAT-E1C; a mirror or derived store that durably contradicts its source is DAT-E1D. The easy confusions are E1A/DAT-B1E (a disabled migration causing drift), E1B/DAT-A1C (orphans), E1B/DAT-D1B (mid-sequence failure) and E1C/DAT-A1B (unique constraints).

E.guide: Data-lifecycle: stored data that becomes inconsistent over time, through ORM-vs-DDL drift, deletes, soft-delete semantics, or mirrors that diverge from their source; see category 1. Retention of personal data is SEC-B4C, and audit records destroyed by a delete cascade are SEC-C4C, not here.
E.name: data-lifecycle

category_guides.1: Write-durability-and-atomicity: an overwrite with no backup is DAT-F1A; truncate-in-place with no temp+rename is DAT-F1B; a concurrent read-modify-write with no file lock is DAT-F1C. F1B prevents torn files, not lost updates (F1C). The DB analogue of F1C is DAT-D1C, and the migration analogue of F1A is DAT-B1A.
category_guides.2: Format-and-read-safety: no version marker in a persisted format is DAT-F2A; reading a persisted file into memory with no size bound is DAT-F2B. An unversioned data contract exchanged between pipeline phases or components is ARC-D1F; a network response read unbounded is SEC-F2A.

F.guide: Durable-file-and-local-state: persistence to flat files and embedded stores (config, caches, state files, BoltDB, on-disk JSON). Category 1 is how such files are written; category 2 is their format and how they are read back. Durable state written to an ephemeral scratch location is ARC-E2A; a schema migration's data loss is DAT-B1A, not F.
F.name: durable-file-and-local-state

DAT-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when a column's declared type cannot represent the domain's value set, so valid values are rejected, truncated, rounded or wrapped: too narrow a width or precision, an INT for a value that exceeds its range, a FLOAT/REAL column for money, a string length shorter than the documented maximum, a DB enum type lacking a value the code writes. A type that CAN hold every valid value but lets invalid ones in for lack of a CHECK/UNIQUE/NOT NULL is DAT-A1B. Money held in a float in application code is COD-G2A; overflow or truncation in arithmetic rather than storage is COD-G2B; a JSON/spec schema enum missing a produced value is COD-D1A.
DAT-A1A.name: inappropriate-type-for-domain

lower_when.condition: The database rejects out-of-range writes with an error (strict mode, typed driver) rather than silently truncating, so the defect surfaces as a visible write failure, not wrong data.

raise_when.condition: The column holds monetary or ledger amounts that are summed, compared or settled from the stored value, and its type rounds or truncates them (FLOAT/REAL, or a DECIMAL scale smaller than the currency's minor unit).

DAT-A1B.criteria: Qualifies when an invariant the application relies on (uniqueness, a per-row range or format rule the column type can represent, NOT NULL for a required field, membership in a lookup set) has no backing DB constraint, so any write path that bypasses the application check (a second service, a bulk import, a concurrent request) violates it. When the same check-then-insert locus could be cited as a race, PREFER A1B when the fix is the missing constraint and DAT-D1C when the finding is the exploitable race window. A type that cannot represent the value set at all is DAT-A1A; a missing foreign key specifically is DAT-A1C; a unique constraint that fails to exclude soft-deleted rows is DAT-E1C.
examples: Unique constraint enforced in app code but absent from schema (check-then-insert)
Spec invariant unique(org,slug) has no backing DB constraint
Domain membership invariant left as TODO, FK unenforced
Column type does not enforce documented value-range invariant
DAT-A1B.name: missing-constraint-for-invariant

lower_when.condition: Every write to the table goes through a single serialized writer (single process holding a lock, or a single-writer embedded store), so no bypassing or concurrent write path exists today.

DAT-A1C.criteria: Qualifies when a logical parent reference is stored as a bare column with no foreign key, so orphan rows survive parent deletion and referential integrity is unenforced (including ORM belongs_to/dependent declarations with no DB-level FK). The fix is the schema FK. Other uniqueness/range invariants with no constraint are DAT-A1B; a delete code path that strands rows regardless of the schema (mid-sequence failure, bulk soft delete bypassing a cascade) is DAT-E1B; an ON DELETE CASCADE that never fires because the model soft-deletes is DAT-E1C.
examples: Parent reference stored as bare UUID column with no foreign key
Join/counter table missing FK, orphans survive parent deletion
Spec'd FK implemented as plain column, no referential integrity
ORM belongs_to/dependent: :destroy with no DB-level FK or index
DAT-A1C.name: missing-foreign-key-relationship

lower_when.condition: No code path deletes or re-keys parent rows (the parent table is insert-only), so orphans cannot arise today even though the FK is absent.

DAT-A1D.criteria: Qualifies when a nullable column's NULL has no single defined meaning: it contradicts a 'required' contract (NULL rows silently drop out of equality filters and joins) or is overloaded as a wildcard/'matches all' (conflating unset with global). The finding is the ambiguous semantics; when the fix is simply adding NOT NULL to a field the application already treats as required, cite DAT-A1B. Code that dereferences the NULL and crashes is COD-B2A. The mirror image (a NOT NULL column filled with sentinel placeholders like 'unknown') is noted for future coverage.
examples: Nullable column contradicts 'required' contract; NULL rows silently unqueryable
NULL overloaded as wildcard/global, conflating 'unset' with 'matches all'
DAT-A1D.name: nullable-column-ambiguous-semantics

DAT-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when APPLYING the migration destroys existing production data that was not preserved or backfilled — data loss at deploy time. Precedence: when apply-time data loss and irreversibility coincide, code B1A (data loss outranks rollback impossibility). A migration with no working reverse path but no apply-time data loss is DAT-B1C; one that is unsafe to re-run is DAT-B1D. Grade by blast radius: a targeted cleanup of known-invalid rows is lower-severity than a whole-table wipe. Destructive RESTORE/backup or non-migration config rewrites are out of scope here (see DAT-F1A).
examples: DELETE/TRUNCATE whole table to satisfy a new NOT NULL column, no backfill
DROP+re-ADD column resets stored values while paired data survives
Unconditional dropIfExists of production auth/token tables
Mass .update() overwrites per-user values with default, no backfill + noop reverse
DAT-B1A.name: destructive-migration-without-backfill

lower_when.condition: The destroyed rows are a targeted set the migration identifies as already invalid or unreachable (orphans, known-corrupt rows), not a whole table or column of live values.

DAT-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when a schema migration holds heavy locks on a hot or large table while it applies: an unbatched mass UPDATE inside one transaction, or a DDL that forces a full-table rewrite or blocking index build under an exclusive lock (e.g. ADD NOT NULL with a volatile default, CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY). Severity assumes production concurrency; a single-writer/embedded target lowers it. The same long transaction in application runtime code (not a migration) is DAT-D1D; a migration that destroys data is DAT-B1A.
examples: Unbatched UPDATE over hot table inside one transaction holds row locks
ADD NOT NULL column with volatile default forces full-table rewrite under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE
DAT-B1B.name: table-lock-heavy-migration

lower_when.condition: The DDL is metadata-only on the target engine version (e.g. ADD COLUMN with a constant default on PostgreSQL 11+, ALGORITHM=INSTANT) and the remaining hazard is a brief exclusive lock taken without a lock_timeout.
The locked table is a small bounded lookup or config table, or the target is a single-writer/embedded store with no concurrent traffic during the migration.

DAT-B1C.criteria: Qualifies when the migration has no working reverse path — down() absent, a no-op, or untested — regardless of whether apply-time data loss occurs. If applying it also destroys un-backfilled production data, code DAT-B1A instead (data loss outranks irreversibility); if the defect is that re-running fails or double-applies, that is DAT-B1D. Also qualifies when a reverse path EXISTS but is unfaithful/lossy (drops columns/timestamps, over-drops rows) — 'has a downgrade, downgrade is wrong' is still effectively irreversible.
examples: Empty down()/pass downgrade leaves migration unrewindable
Rollback uses invalid SQL (DELETE TABLE), errors on execution
Forward-only migration runner with no reverse steps
Downgrade exists but is lossy — effectively irreversible
DAT-B1C.name: irreversible-migration-no-rollback

lower_when.condition: The migration is purely additive (creates a table, column or index that no released code yet reads or writes), so a corrective forward migration fully undoes it.

raise_when.condition: The reverse path exists but is lossy (drops columns, rows or values) and the deploy pipeline runs it automatically on rollback, so a routine rollback destroys production data.

DAT-B1D.criteria: Qualifies when re-running the migration against an already-applied state fails or double-applies (re-run / idempotency safety, e.g. CREATE TABLE without IF NOT EXISTS) — often fully reversible and non-destructive, hence distinct. Apply-time data destruction is DAT-B1A; an absent or broken rollback path is DAT-B1C. Weight whether the migration runner already prevents re-application: if a re-run is only reachable by operator error, grade lower; if a destructive step precedes the idempotency marker (retry re-destroys) or a data rewrite double-applies, it qualifies at full severity.
examples: Destructive step runs before idempotency marker is written; retry re-destroys
Data-rewrite migration double-applies on re-run (no current-shape guard)
DAT-B1D.name: non-idempotent-migration

lower_when.condition: The migration runner records applied versions and refuses re-application, so a re-run is only reachable by an operator manually resetting the version table.

DAT-B1E.criteria: Qualifies when a migration silently does nothing (an empty or commented-out up() body, or a migration excluded from the run) while permanently occupying a version slot, so the intended change is never applied and cannot be re-applied under that name. Distinct from DAT-B1A (destructive), DAT-B1C (no working down path; B1E is a missing UP path) and DAT-B1F (the up() ran and failed, but the failure was swallowed). When the resulting gap shows up as model-vs-DDL drift, cite B1E for the migration and DAT-E1A only if no migration is responsible.
examples: immich migration up() fully commented out, occupies a version slot doing nothing
DAT-B1E.name: no-op-or-disabled-migration

DAT-B1F.criteria: Qualifies when a migration wraps its DDL in a try/catch (or matches error-text substrings) and is recorded as applied despite the change failing, producing partial or absent schema that masquerades as migrated with no signal at deploy time. Distinct from DAT-B1D (non-idempotent = fails on RE-run) — B1F swallows the FIRST-run failure; and from SEC-F1B (generic silent-exception-swallowing) — B1F is migration-state-specific.
examples: firefly-iii migration wraps DDL in catch(QueryException) and is still marked applied
Temporal changeset marked applied when a real failure's message matches 'already exist'
Beekeeper migration failure logged and skipped, leaving partial schema
DAT-B1F.name: migration-error-swallowed-marked-applied

lower_when.condition: The swallowed DDL only adds an optional object (an index, a comment, a view) whose absence degrades performance but not correctness.

DAT-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when a frequently-run read path (status polling, an append-only table's ORDER BY/WHERE reads) has no supporting index, forcing sequential scans. 'Hot' means called on a request/execution hot path or over an only-grows table; a rare admin call does not qualify. The finding is a missing index, not the query's shape: a query issued once per row is DAT-C1B, a query with no LIMIT is DAT-C1C, and a foreign key column lacking an index alongside a missing FK is DAT-A1C.
examples: Composite index absent for status-polling query on hot execution table
Append-only table lacks index on ts/event columns used by ORDER BY + WHERE
DAT-C1A.name: missing-index-for-hot-query

lower_when.condition: The table has a documented small bound (configuration, lookup, per-user rows capped by the product) so a sequential scan stays cheap as data grows.

DAT-C1B.criteria: Qualifies for per-row queries issued in a loop instead of a set-based query: a count via len(lazy_relationship) instead of SQL COUNT, per-row .get()/update in a serializer or merge loop, a constant lookup re-queried per row. The query count must scale with the row count. Repeated filesystem stat calls are QAL-G1C; a non-query value recomputed per iteration is QAL-G1A/QAL-G1B; a single query lacking an index is DAT-C1A.
examples: Collection count via len(lazy_relationship) instead of SQL COUNT
Per-row .get(pk=...) in serializer loop, no prefetch, on hot endpoint
Per-row update_attribute in find_each instead of update_all
DAT-C1B.name: n-plus-one-query
DAT-C1B.notes: moved at the 0.1 seeding session from the draft QAL-G1D (a code that did not survive the 0.2.0 identity-base reset)

lower_when.condition: The loop is bounded by a small fixed or product-capped count (a page of at most N items) or runs only in a batch job off the request path.

DAT-C1C.criteria: Qualifies when a database or store query has no LIMIT/pagination and its result grows unbounded with data (.all() materializing a whole table, history that grows per event, a Redis keyspace or etcd prefix scan pulled into memory). The fix is in the query: SQL LIMIT, keyset pagination, or a cursor. Deliberate, bounded full-table exports/projections do NOT qualify. An API endpoint whose contract exposes no page size or cap is OPS-D1B; in-memory growth of a collection not fed by a query is QAL-G2A; fetching too many columns rather than rows is DAT-C1D.
examples: Query has no LIMIT/pagination; result grows unbounded with entity history
List endpoint returns full rows (incl heavy text column) with no pagination
.all() materializes entire table, filtered/sliced in application code
DAT-C1C.name: unbounded-result-set

lower_when.condition: The queried set is bounded by a product rule enforced at write time (a per-user cap, a fixed enumeration), even though the query itself has no LIMIT.

DAT-C1D.criteria: Qualifies for SELECT * (or fetching a whole wide/blob column) on a production read path where only some fields are needed. Often co-occurs with DAT-C1C; cite C1D when over-fetching columns is the defect, C1C when the unbounded row count is.
examples: SELECT * across multiple production read helpers, pulls wide/body columns
Join selects entire JSON blob column instead of needed fields (TODO acknowledged)
DAT-C1D.name: select-star-in-production-path

lower_when.condition: The table is narrow (no blob, large text or JSON column) so SELECT * fetches little beyond the needed fields.

DAT-D1A.criteria: Qualifies when an explicit multi-statement transaction exists but its isolation level is too weak for its invariant (a read-modify-write or a read-then-insert that needs SERIALIZABLE/REPEATABLE READ or row locks running at READ COMMITTED). Presupposes a settable isolation level; stores using advisory-lock + single atomic upsert give this no surface. When there is no transaction at all, cite DAT-D1B; when the race is a read-modify-write with no lock or CAS and the fix is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE or a version check rather than raising isolation, cite DAT-D1C. No corpus instance yet, prior-art only; enrich when observed.
DAT-D1A.name: isolation-level-mismatch

lower_when.condition: The invariant the weak isolation can violate is an advisory counter or statistic that no write-path decision (balance, quota, entitlement, uniqueness) reads.

DAT-D1B.criteria: Qualifies when related multi-statement writes that must be all-or-nothing run with no surrounding transaction (or a write runs on the outer connection instead of the open transaction handle), so a mid-sequence failure leaves partial state. Also covers loop-exit/cancellation paths that exit an open transaction without commit/rollback. A single non-transactional external side-effect leg lowers severity (no transactional fix available).
examples: Multi-write merge across repositories with no surrounding transaction
Write runs on outer connection instead of the open transaction handle
Delete-then-recreate without transaction.atomic (IntegrityError swallowed)
Multi-row financial mutation with manual delete-on-error instead of a DB transaction
DAT-D1B.name: missing-transaction-boundary

lower_when.condition: One leg of the sequence is a non-transactional external side effect (an API call, a file write), so no database transaction could make the whole sequence atomic.

DAT-D1C.criteria: Qualifies for a read-modify-write in a DB/KV transaction with no row lock or optimistic-concurrency guard, so concurrent writers race. Scope note: a read-modify-write on a FLAT FILE belongs to DAT-F1C, not here. Also covers a broken/absent CAS (an optimistic WHERE version=? that binds a stale/zero version, or a blind last-writer-wins Update with no ResourceVersion) — same harm class as a transient race. When the same check-then-insert locus lacks a unique constraint, prefer DAT-A1B for the fix and D1C for the exploit.
examples: CAS on a stale/self-read revision instead of the caller's observed version
Read-modify-write toggle without row lock or optimistic locking
Read-decide-write across two separate transactions (once-guard runs twice)
DAT-D1C.name: read-modify-write-race

lower_when.condition: The racing writers are all the same single-instance background job (no concurrent request path can reach the read-modify-write).
The raced value is a cosmetic or advisory field (a view count, a last-seen timestamp) where a lost update has no downstream decision.

DAT-D1D.criteria: Qualifies when application runtime code holds a single transaction open across expensive work (an unbounded mass UPDATE, or network I/O and thousands of row writes before one commit) so it holds locks on a hot table for the duration. An unbounded remote-call batch inside one DB transaction routes here (vs DAT-C1C for the unbounded set alone). The same lock-heavy pattern inside a schema migration is DAT-B1B; a missing timeout on the network call itself is OPS-A1A.
examples: Unbounded mass UPDATE in a single transaction holding locks on a hot table
Network I/O and thousands of row writes held inside one open transaction
DAT-D1D.name: long-running-transaction

lower_when.condition: The transaction touches only rows no other path reads or writes and its duration is bounded by a fixed small batch size, so it neither blocks writers nor pins the MVCC snapshot horizon for long.

DAT-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when the code's schema view (ORM model metadata) drifts from the migration DDL with no reconciling migration, in EITHER direction: code ahead of migrations, or a migration ahead of the model (tests permanently diverging from prod). Drift built live via metadata.create_all is corroborating. When a specific migration that should have carried the change is empty or disabled, cite DAT-B1E; when a committed generated artifact (not the DB schema) is stale with no build check, that is ARC-C1F; a schema-vs-documentation divergence with no runtime break is ARC-D1B; a persisted file format with no version marker is DAT-F2A.
examples: ORM model metadata drifted from migration DDL with no reconciling migration
DAT-E1A.name: code-schema-drift-without-migration

lower_when.condition: The drift is in an object the running code never reads or writes (an unused column, an index or constraint declared on one side only), so no query fails or returns wrong data.

DAT-E1B.criteria: Qualifies when a delete code path leaves rows or objects that should have been removed: a delete spanning the database and another store (object storage, search index) where a mid-sequence failure strands a parent/index row, or a bulk soft delete that bypasses the cascade/enqueue that removes children. When all steps are in one database and a transaction would make them atomic, cite DAT-D1B; when the orphans exist only because the schema has no FK, cite DAT-A1C; when the cascade never fires because of soft-delete semantics in the schema, cite DAT-E1C.
examples: Multi-step delete leaves index/parent row when a mid-sequence storage step fails
Bulk soft-delete bypasses cascade, orphaning child records
DAT-E1B.name: orphaned-rows-on-delete

DAT-E1C.criteria: Qualifies when soft-delete semantics are applied inconsistently within a schema: a unique constraint that does NOT exclude soft-deleted rows (full-unique vs partial-unique within one soft-delete schema), so recreate-after-delete collides; an accessor filtering for soft-deleted rows inverted vs its siblings; or an ON DELETE CASCADE that never fires because the model uses soft delete. A unique invariant with no constraint at all is DAT-A1B; a bulk delete path that skips the cascade/enqueue code is DAT-E1B; a missing FK is DAT-A1C.
examples: Unique constraint does not exclude soft-deleted rows (full-unique vs partial-unique within one schema)
Soft-delete tombstones one key column but a non-partial unique constraint still collides on re-create
FK ON DELETE CASCADE never fires because the model uses soft delete
Accessor filters for soft-deleted rows, inverted vs its sibling queries
DAT-E1C.name: soft-delete-inconsistency

lower_when.condition: The inconsistency only causes a loud failure (a unique-violation error on re-create) on an admin-only path, with no wrong data returned to readers.

DAT-E1D.criteria: Qualifies when a mirror or derived store durably contradicts its system-of-record with no reconciliation or self-heal path, so reads serve stale/wrong data indefinitely. Includes silent partial mirroring (truncation with no warning) and fabricated provenance (substituting run-time values for missing source fields). Durable is the test: an in-process cache that serves stale data until restart or TTL is COD-F3A; a one-off truncation of output with no persisted mirror is COD-B2E; the ORM model drifting from migration DDL is DAT-E1A.
examples: Mirror row stuck at status=open while GitHub says verified-pass, never reconciled
Issue mirror silently truncates at --limit 1000 with no partial-mirror warning
Mirror fabricates created-at timestamp when source value is missing
DAT-E1D.name: mirror-source-divergence

lower_when.condition: The mirror is display-only and each view links to or shows the source of record, so a reader can see the authoritative value.

raise_when.condition: A billing, payout or invoicing computation reads the diverged mirror instead of the system of record, so the wrong value is charged or paid for every affected record.

DAT-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when a persisted store's data is overwritten or replaced with no snapshot, backup, or prompt, so a mistake or crash is unrecoverable. Distinct from DAT-B1A, which is migration-scoped (apply-time data loss during a schema migration); F1A is non-migration persistence (config/state/cache rewrites). A corrupt-input path that silently discards then overwrites recoverable data also qualifies.
examples: chezmoi init overwrites hand-edited chezmoi.toml with no backup or prompt
Corrupt brew JSON cache silently overwritten with empty {} on next write
Truncated strix cli-config.json ignored then clobbered by next persist
Empty menu snapshot accepted as truth, soft-deletes every product in one shot
DAT-F1A.name: destructive-rewrite-without-backup

lower_when.condition: The overwritten file holds a handful of user-set preference values rather than accumulated data (documents, history, inventory, state), so the loss is a re-entry cost, not lost records.

DAT-F1B.criteria: Qualifies when a persisted file is written via truncate-in-place with no temp-file + atomic rename (and no fsync), so a crash or ENOSPC mid-write leaves torn, truncated, or zero-length state. This is crash-durability of a single writer — distinct from COD-F1A (in-memory concurrency-atomicity / races). The presence of a correct atomic-write helper elsewhere in the same codebase that this path bypasses is corroborating evidence.
examples: PrusaSlicer ConfigBase::save truncates preset INI in place, no temp+rename
Terraform filesystem state written via Seek0/Truncate0 in place, torn on crash
Logseq :writeFile page save truncates in place with no atomic replace
curl truncates cookie jar in place before temp+rename, zero-length on crash
DAT-F1B.name: non-atomic-file-write

lower_when.condition: The reader detects a torn or empty file (checksum, parse failure) and falls back to defaults with a visible warning, and the file holds only settings the user can re-enter.

raise_when.condition: The file is the only copy of user-authored content (notes, documents, infrastructure state) and the truncate-in-place path runs on every save, so a crash or full disk destroys that content.

DAT-F1C.criteria: Qualifies when a read-modify-write cycle on a shared flat file uses no file lock or atomic replace, so concurrent writers silently lose each other's updates. The file analogue of DAT-D1C (which is the DB-transaction read-modify-write race, fixed by a transaction / optimistic concurrency); F1C is fixed by a file lock (flock/fcntl) or atomic rename. Atomic-write that prevents torn files does NOT prevent lost updates.
examples: curl shared cookie jar read-modify-write with no lock loses concurrent writer's cookies
Homebrew CacheStoreDatabase read-modify-write without flock loses cache entries
DAT-F1C.name: lost-update-on-unsynchronized-file

lower_when.condition: Concurrent writers are only possible if the user runs two instances by hand, and the program does not document or support that mode.

DAT-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when an on-disk or embedded-store format (flat files, BoltDB/bbolt, on-disk JSON) that the program writes and later reads back carries no schema/format version marker, so format evolution silently misreads or corrupts pre-existing files (versions are then sniffed heuristically). Relational schemas versioned by a migration history are out of scope; their drift is DAT-E1A. An unversioned data contract exchanged between pipeline phases or components is ARC-D1F. A read of the file with no size bound is DAT-F2B; deserialising an untrusted file into objects is SEC-A2B.
examples: qBittorrent RSS feeds.json has no version field, format sniffed heuristically
curl Netscape cookie file has no schema-version header
PrusaSlicer INI config persisted with no schema version for cross-version migration
DAT-F2A.name: unversioned-persisted-format

lower_when.condition: The format has never changed shape across releases and the reader rejects unknown fields or shapes with an error instead of misreading them.

DAT-F2B.criteria: Qualifies when a persisted file is read wholly into memory with no size bound (or an element count is read from the file and used to allocate unchecked), so a crafted or naturally-large file exhausts memory. Distinct from SEC-F2A (unbounded read of a network response — different sink) and QAL-G2A (in-memory collection growth, not a file read).
examples: qBittorrent reads fastresume file with readFile(-1) unbounded into memory
PrusaSlicer loadvector allocates from an unbounded file-supplied element count
DAT-F2B.name: unbounded-persisted-file-read

raise_when.condition: The file is received from another party (downloaded, imported, shared, or written by a peer) rather than written only by this program, so a crafted size or element count reaches the read.

DAT.guide: DAT covers persisted data: schema shape, migrations, query cost, transaction boundaries and DB/KV concurrency, consistency over time (schema drift, deletes, mirrors), and durable files and embedded local stores. Choose DAT when the defect sits in the persistence layer; choose COD when the same hazard is in in-memory logic (process-state races COD-F, numeric and encoding representation COD-G), OPS when it is an endpoint or service capacity limit or a startup side effect (OPS-D1B, OPS-D1A, OPS-C1B), SEC when an attacker triggers it or the data is personal data under privacy rules (SEC-B4C), and ARC when two specifications other than the live schema and its migrations disagree. Look in A for schema shape, B for migrations, C for query cost, D for transactions, E for consistency over time, and F for files and embedded stores.
DAT.name: data-and-persistence

category_guides.1: A complete user-facing literal written at point-of-use is LNG-A1A; a message built by concatenating or interpolating in code outside the catalog is LNG-A1B. Easy to confuse: when the pieces ARE translated but glued together, that is LNG-C1A, and a key that exists in code but not in the catalog is LNG-D1A.

A.guide: Externalization: user-facing text that does not go through the i18n layer at all, so it cannot be translated. Category 1 separates a whole hardcoded literal (LNG-A1A) from a message assembled in code (LNG-A1B).
A.name: externalization

category_guides.1: Hardcoded separators, date patterns or currency placement are LNG-B1A; an n==1-else-'s' plural rule is LNG-B1B. Easy to confuse: a naive/aware datetime mix is COD-G1C and a wrong unit or currency conversion is COD-G3C; a time shown in the right zone but the wrong pattern is still LNG-B1A.

B.guide: Locale formatting: values whose rendering depends on locale conventions (number separators, date order, currency, plural forms). Category 1 holds number/date/currency formatting (LNG-B1A) and plural rules (LNG-B1B).
B.name: locale-formatting

category_guides.1: Separately translated fragments glued or interpolated into a sentence are LNG-C1A. Easy to confuse: untranslated pieces assembled in code are LNG-A1B, and a count-based plural branch is LNG-B1B.

C.guide: Grammar: messages whose translated parts are composed in code so word order, gender or agreement breaks in other languages. Category 1 holds the concatenated-translation code (LNG-C1A).
C.name: grammar

category_guides.1: A referenced key missing with no fallback, or a renamed or unused key left behind, is LNG-D1A. Easy to confuse: a string that was never given a key is LNG-A1A.

D.guide: Key drift: the translation catalog and the keys code references fall out of sync. Category 1 holds the key-lifecycle code (LNG-D1A).
D.name: key-drift

category_guides.1: Text limited, truncated or split mid-character for display is LNG-E1A. Easy to confuse: bytes and str mixed in logic is COD-G3A, decoding with an implicit default encoding is COD-G3B, NFC/NFD mismatch in comparison or lookup is COD-G3D, and a silent truncation of a result set is COD-B2E.

E.guide: Encoding: user-facing text measured, truncated or indexed at the wrong unit (bytes or UTF-16 code units instead of characters or graphemes). Category 1 holds LNG-E1A; encoding defects in program logic belong to COD area G, and a stored column sized in bytes rather than characters is DAT-A1A.
E.name: encoding

category_guides.1: Hardcoded left/right, a missing dir attribute, physical instead of logical CSS properties, or un-isolated user-supplied mixed-direction text is LNG-F1A. Easy to confuse: a missing document or element language attribute is not F1A, and bidi control characters used to disguise code or identifiers are a spoofing hazard, not a layout defect.

F.guide: Directionality: UI that assumes left-to-right text and layout, including user-supplied mixed-direction text that is not isolated. Category 1 holds the RTL/bidi code (LNG-F1A).
F.name: directionality

LNG-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when a complete user-facing string (a label, prompt, button text, error or notification shown to an end user) is written as a literal at point-of-use in a codebase that has an i18n layer or a stated localisation requirement, so it bypasses the catalog and cannot be translated. Evidence names the literal and the i18n mechanism it bypasses. Log lines, developer diagnostics and machine-read identifiers are not user-facing and do not qualify. A message assembled in code from pieces is LNG-A1B; translated fragments glued together are LNG-C1A; a key referenced in code but missing from the catalog is LNG-D1A; a spelling error in shipped text is QAL-C2E.
examples: hardcoded-user-facing-string
hardcoded-ui-strings-bypassing-i18n
LNG-A1A.name: hardcoded-user-facing-string

lower_when.condition: the surface showing the string is not offered in any non-source locale today (the product publishes no translations, or this operator/admin surface is excluded from localisation), so no user currently sees it untranslated

LNG-A1B.criteria: Qualifies when a user-facing string is built by interpolation or concatenation outside the i18n layer, so the composed message is never a single translatable unit (i18n externalization). Distinct from a fully hardcoded literal (LNG-A1A); the grammatical breakage of concatenating already-translated fragments is LNG-C1A.
examples: user-facing-string-dispatched-outside-template
label-built-in-code-not-catalog
LNG-A1B.name: string-assembled-outside-i18n

LNG-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when a number, date, time or currency amount shown to users is formatted with hardcoded separators, patterns or symbol placement instead of a locale-aware formatter (CLDR/ICU, Intl, babel), so output is wrong or ambiguous in other locales. Evidence names the value, the hardcoded pattern and the display site. A deliberately locale-neutral machine-read format (ISO-8601, a CSV or API field) does not qualify, and neither does its inverse (locale-dependent formatting leaking into a machine-read field), which is a parsing/correctness defect outside LNG. Pluralization is LNG-B1B; a naive/aware datetime mix is COD-G1C; a wrong unit or currency conversion is COD-G3C.
examples: locale-unaware-date-formatting
hardcoded-number-format
LNG-B1A.name: locale-unaware-number-date-format

raise_when.condition: the rendered string parses as a different valid value under the convention of a non-source locale the product publishes (a grouping/decimal swap such as 1,234 vs 1.234 on an amount, or a day/month-ambiguous date such as 03/04), so a reader in that locale takes it for a different amount or date

LNG-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when plurals use a naive rule (e.g. n==1 else add 's'), ignoring the target language's CLDR plural categories (zero/one/two/few/many/other), so many locales render grammatically wrong counts. Distinct from number/date formatting (LNG-B1A).
examples: naive-plural-s-suffix
count-based-if-else-plural
LNG-B1B.name: naive-pluralization

lower_when.condition: the n==1 branch selects between two translated catalog strings (no suffix appended in code) and every locale the product publishes has CLDR plural categories of exactly one (n==1) and other, so the selection is correct for all current users

LNG-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when a sentence is built by concatenating separately translated fragments or interpolating values into split strings, so word order, gender, and agreement break in languages that differ from the source (i18n message grammar). Distinct from bypassing i18n entirely (LNG-A1B); here fragments are translated but composed ungrammatically.
examples: concatenated-translation-fragments
sentence-built-by-string-glue
LNG-C1A.name: translation-assembled-by-concatenation

LNG-D1A.criteria: Qualifies when translation keys drift out of sync with the catalog — a referenced key is missing with no fallback, or a renamed/unused key lingers — so users see a raw key or blank instead of text (i18n catalog integrity). The key-lifecycle form; a string that never entered the catalog is LNG-A1A.
examples: translation-key-drift
missing-locale-fallback
LNG-D1A.name: translation-key-drift-or-missing-fallback

lower_when.condition: the drift is only an orphaned key that no code path references (drop this lower and set floor LOW if the orphaned-key half is re-homed to QAL-E2C)

raise_when.condition: the missing key renders blank (not a visible raw key) in the source locale as the only text of a control, error or confirmation message, so the user cannot tell what the action does or what failed

LNG-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when user-facing text is measured, truncated, limited or indexed by bytes or UTF-16 code units as if they were characters, so multi-byte, surrogate-pair or multi-codepoint grapheme text (emoji, combining marks, CJK) is split mid-character or held to a lower effective limit than documented (CWE-176). Evidence names the length/index operation and the text it is applied to. Bytes and str mixed in program logic is COD-G3A; decoding with an implicit default encoding is COD-G3B; NFC/NFD mismatch in comparison or lookup is COD-G3D; a result set or output cut off with no warning is COD-B2E; a stored column sized in bytes rather than characters is DAT-A1A.
examples: utf8-byte-length-conflated-with-char-count
unnormalized-utf8-path-handling
LNG-E1A.name: byte-vs-codepoint-length-confusion

raise_when.condition: the mid-character split produces an invalid UTF-8 sequence or a lone surrogate that is then persisted or sent onward (stored in a column, emitted in an API or protocol field), so the corruption outlives the display

LNG-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when a UI that is offered, or stated to be offered, in a right-to-left language assumes left-to-right layout or direction (hardcoded left/right positioning, no dir attribute, physical instead of logical CSS properties, user-supplied mixed-direction text not isolated with bdi/dir=auto), so Arabic, Hebrew, Persian or Urdu render mirrored or bidi-broken (Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm; CSS logical properties). Evidence names the direction assumption and the surface. A missing document or element language attribute is not this code; bidi control characters used to disguise source code or identifiers are a spoofing hazard, not a layout defect.
examples: rtl-layout-support-missing
bidi-directionality-assumption
LNG-F1A.name: missing-rtl-bidi-support

raise_when.condition: the direction assumption breaks a primary layout in a published RTL locale (navigation, form field order, or the reading flow of main content), not an isolated widget or icon

LNG.guide: LNG (language and internationalization) covers defects that make user-facing text untranslatable, ungrammatical, wrongly formatted or wrongly rendered for users in a locale, language or script other than the source one. Choose LNG over ACC when the problem is translation, locale formatting or text direction rather than what assistive technology can announce (an untranslated aria-label is LNG-A1A, a missing accessible name is ACC-A1A). Choose COD area G (temporal, encoding-and-units) or DAT (column types and persisted formats) when encoding, normalization or time handling produces a wrong result in program logic or stored data rather than in displayed text, and QAL for inert hygiene in strings (typos, style-only concatenation, orphaned assets). Look in A for strings that never reach the i18n layer, B for numbers, dates and plurals, C for sentence composition, D for catalog keys, E for character-level measurement and truncation, F for right-to-left layout.
LNG.name: language-and-internationalization

category_guides.1: A call with no bounded timeout is OPS-A1A; a retry with no backoff or jitter is OPS-A1B. Easy to confuse: a test that shells out with no timeout is TST-G3B, an unbounded response body read is SEC-F2A, and a blocking call on an async path is COD-F2B.

A.guide: Resilience of outbound calls to backing services (network, IPC, subprocess): whether a call is bounded in time and whether failures are retried safely. Category 1 holds the timeout code and the retry-amplification code.
A.name: resilience

category_guides.1: Dropping in-flight work on SIGTERM/stop is OPS-B1A, including a stop sequence that never flips readiness before draining. A health or readiness endpoint that reports healthy without checking anything real (a static 200, or liveness standing in for readiness) is OPS-B1B. A signal handler that does unsafe work is COD-F3D, and a torn file left by a kill mid-write is DAT-F1B.

B.guide: Process lifecycle as an orchestrator sees it: how a service stops and how it reports health. Category 1 points at the shutdown-drain and health-check codes.
B.name: lifecycle

category_guides.1: Config consumed at boot without validation, failing late, is OPS-C1A; an unconditional side effect on every boot is OPS-C1B. A loader that picks a permissive default on missing or corrupt config is COD-B1A; a migration that is not safe to re-run is DAT-B1D, and one whose failure is swallowed and recorded as applied is DAT-B1F.

C.guide: What happens at boot: whether configuration is validated before serving and whether startup performs unguarded side effects. Category 1 points at the config-validation and startup-side-effect codes.
C.name: deployment-config

category_guides.1: General unbounded growth of a concurrency, capacity or in-process memory resource (connections, threads/tasks, queues, caches, CPU fan-out) is OPS-D1A; a list endpoint or query with no pagination or cap is OPS-D1B (until the OPS-D1B/DAT-C1C overlap is resolved, cite DAT-C1C when the fix is the query's LIMIT and OPS-D1B when the fix is the endpoint's page/limit contract). Easy to confuse: QAL-G2A (whole collection loaded into memory), DAT-F2B (unbounded file read), SEC-H4B / SEC-F2A (unbounded request / response size), AGT-E1A / AGT-E1B (agent loop or tool budget), and COD-A1A (a leaked file handle).

D.guide: Capacity bounds under load: memory, connections, threads, CPU and result-set size with no cap, quota or backpressure. Category 1 points at the general unbounded-consumption code and the result-set code.
D.name: resource-limits

category_guides.1: A runtime failure that is handled or ignored and emits no log, metric or trace is OPS-E1A. When the swallow makes the program proceed on wrong or missing data it is COD-B2C; a security-relevant swallow is SEC-F1B; an overbroad catch is ARC-F2G; a swallowed CI step is ARC-C2B; a migration failure swallowed and marked applied is DAT-B1F; a log that exists but is vague is QAL-I1B.

E.guide: Failure visibility at runtime: an error is handled or swallowed and leaves no log, metric or trace for operators. Category 1 points at the silent-failure code; diagnostic log quality and trace propagation belong to QAL area I.
E.name: observability

OPS-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when an outbound network, IPC or subprocess call in production code has no bounded timeout or deadline (none passed, none inherited from a configured client default), so a slow or hung dependency can stall the caller indefinitely and hold its worker, thread or connection. This is the single home for a missing outbound deadline until SEC gains a slow-request code. Exclusions: the same call in a test harness is TST-G3B; reading an unbounded response body (size, not time) is SEC-F2A; a synchronous call blocking an async event loop is COD-F2B; retrying with no backoff is OPS-A1B.
examples: missing-timeout-on-outbound-http-call
unbounded-fetch-without-deadline
no-timeout-on-subprocess-invocation
OPS-A1A.name: missing-timeout-on-external-call

lower_when.condition: The call runs in a one-shot process (CLI command, batch job) or once on the boot path before the process reports ready, and holds no shared worker, connection pool or request queue, so a hang stalls only that run or that start.

OPS-A1B.criteria: Qualifies when a failed operation is retried with no exponential backoff or jitter, so retries amplify a dependency failure into a retry storm / thundering herd (SRE retry practice). The retry-amplification form; a missing bounded timeout is OPS-A1A.
examples: retry-without-backoff-or-jitter
tight-retry-loop-amplifies-dependency-failure
OPS-A1B.name: retry-without-backoff-or-jitter

lower_when.condition: The retry count is small and fixed (for example 3 or fewer) and the retried target is a local resource (file lock, local socket) rather than a dependency shared by many clients.

OPS-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when a long-running service does not drain in-flight work on SIGTERM/stop: requests, jobs or writes in progress are dropped instead of being completed or cleanly rejected before exit, including a stop sequence that keeps accepting traffic because readiness is never failed first (12-Factor IX Disposability). Evidence names the stop path and the work it abandons. Exclusions: a health endpoint that never checks anything real (static 200, liveness as readiness) is OPS-B1B; a signal handler that does async-signal-unsafe work is COD-F3D; a persisted file torn by a kill mid-write is DAT-F1B.
examples: no-graceful-shutdown-drain
sigterm-drops-in-flight-requests
OPS-B1A.name: no-graceful-shutdown-drain

lower_when.condition: The only work in flight at stop is read-only or idempotent requests that callers retry, so nothing is lost, only failed.

OPS-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when a liveness/readiness endpoint reports healthy without checking real dependencies or readiness (a static 200, or liveness standing in for readiness), so orchestrators route traffic to an unready instance (health-check semantics; K8s liveness-vs-readiness). Distinct from failing to drain on shutdown (OPS-B1A).
examples: fake-health-check-always-200
liveness-masquerading-as-readiness
OPS-B1B.name: fake-or-noop-health-check

lower_when.condition: The repository's deployment manifests are present and no probe, load-balancer health check or service-discovery rule in them references the endpoint, so nothing in the shipped deployment routes traffic on its answer.

OPS-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when configuration is consumed at startup without validating required values, types or ranges, so a missing or malformed setting surfaces as a late runtime failure instead of failing fast at boot (12-Factor III Config). Evidence names the setting and the later point where it fails. Exclusions: a loader that substitutes a permissive default for a missing or corrupt config artifact is COD-B1A (fail-open direction, not lateness); a component that skips malformed runtime input is ARC-F2D; an unguarded side effect at boot is OPS-C1B.
examples: unvalidated-startup-configuration
missing-required-env-var-fails-late
OPS-C1A.name: unvalidated-startup-configuration

lower_when.condition: The unvalidated setting is read only by an optional, off-by-default feature path, so a bad value fails late only when that feature is enabled and the core serving path is unaffected.

OPS-C1B.criteria: Qualifies when startup performs an unconditional, unguarded side effect on every boot (a migration, data mutation or external write) instead of an explicit, once-only deployment step, so restarts repeat it and concurrently booting replicas race it. Evidence names the boot hook and the side effect. Exclusions: a migration that is itself unsafe to re-run is DAT-B1D (the migration defect; cite OPS-C1B only for running it on boot); a migration that destroys data is DAT-B1A; replicas racing a shared check is COD-F1B; boot-time config not validated is OPS-C1A.
examples: container-boot-runs-unconditional-migration
startup-mutates-state-without-guard
OPS-C1B.name: unconditional-startup-side-effect

lower_when.condition: The side effect is idempotent (a no-op when already applied) and the deployment runs a single instance, so the only cost is boot time.

raise_when.condition: The side effect is a non-migration data mutation or external write that is not idempotent, and the deployment manifest runs more than one replica with no lock or leader election around the step, so concurrently booting replicas duplicate it.

OPS-D1A.criteria: Qualifies when a long-running code path can grow a concurrency, capacity or in-process memory resource without bound under load (open connections, goroutines/threads/tasks, queued work, a cache or buffer that grows per request or key, CPU fan-out) because there is no cap, quota, pool limit, eviction or backpressure. Evidence names the resource and the input that drives its growth. Exclusions: a file handle that is never released is COD-A1A; a whole data-sized collection loaded into memory at once is QAL-G2A; an unbounded query or endpoint result set is DAT-C1C / OPS-D1B; an unbounded file read is DAT-F2B; an attacker-sized request or response is SEC-H4B / SEC-F2A; an agent loop or tool-call budget is AGT-E1A / AGT-E1B.
examples: unbounded-realtime-connection-growth
unbounded-goroutine-fanout
OPS-D1A.name: unbounded-resource-consumption

lower_when.condition: The process is a single-tenant worker or batch job whose exhaustion kills only its own run, with no shared serving pool or co-tenant workload.

OPS-D1B.criteria: If kept rather than merged: Qualifies when a list or query API endpoint exposes no pagination, limit or cap in its contract (no page/cursor/limit parameters and no server-side maximum), so response size and client memory scale with the data. Evidence names the endpoint and the collection behind it. Exclusions: the database query with no LIMIT is DAT-C1C (fix in the query); loading the collection whole into memory is QAL-G2A; rendering it in one pass is COD-F2C; general unbounded connection/thread/CPU growth is OPS-D1A.
examples: missing-query-result-limit
unpaginated-list-endpoint
OPS-D1B.name: missing-pagination-or-result-cap

OPS-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when a runtime failure is caught or ignored and the program continues as designed (degrades or skips) but emits no log, metric or trace, so operators cannot see the failure. The finding is the missing signal, not the handling choice. Exclusions: when the swallow makes the program proceed on wrong or missing data it is COD-B2C; a swallowed security-relevant failure (auth, verification) is SEC-F1B; a blanket catch masking many error types is ARC-F2G; a CI step whose failure is ignored is ARC-C2B; a migration failure swallowed and marked applied is DAT-B1F; a log line that exists but lacks context is QAL-I1B; a sensitive action with no audit record is SEC-C4B.
examples: panic-recovery-bypasses-logging
error-swallowed-without-telemetry
OPS-E1A.name: silent-failure-without-telemetry

lower_when.condition: The silenced failure is on a best-effort auxiliary path (cache warm-up, metrics emission, optional enrichment) whose failure changes no output and no persisted state.

OPS.guide: OPS (production-readiness) covers how running code behaves as a deployed service under real operating conditions: hung or failing dependencies, start/stop lifecycle, boot-time configuration, capacity limits, and whether failures are visible to operators at all. Choose OPS when the failure is internal or systemic (self-inflicted load, a slow dependency, a restart). Route an attacker-sized request or response to SEC, a swallow that leaves the program on a wrong or missing result to COD, a migration or query-shape defect to DAT, a deliberate architectural fail-open decision to ARC, poor-quality diagnostics (a log that exists but is vague) to QAL area I, and agent loop or tool budgets to AGT. Look in A (resilience) for outbound calls and retries, B (lifecycle) for shutdown and health checks, C (deployment-config) for boot-time config and side effects, D (resource-limits) for unbounded growth, and E (observability) for failures that leave no signal.
OPS.name: production-readiness

category_guides.1: Naming problems. QAL-A1B is a mixed naming style. QAL-A1C is a name that clashes with an existing domain concept. A misleading test or helper name is TST-C3B or TST-C3C, and a cross-host field-name mismatch is QAL-F3C.
category_guides.2: Clarity of an expression or literal. Use QAL-A2B for precedence a reader can misread, QAL-A2C for an unexplained number or a fixed index, and QAL-A2D for comments that only restate the code. A hardcoded index that is actually wrong is COD-A2B, and an out-of-range access is COD-A2C. A precedence bug that actually evaluates wrongly has no specific code yet (COD-X0X). The same magic value in a test is TST-C5D.

A.guide: Readability of names, expressions and comments at a single site, where the code is correct but a reader can misread it. Names go in A1 and expressions, numbers and comments in A2. Convention mismatches across files go in F3.
A.name: readability

category_guides.1: Import statements within one file. QAL-B1A is several imports on one line, QAL-B1B is an import placed mid-file or inside a function, and QAL-B1C is an import repeated or shadowed. Inconsistent import style across modules is QAL-F1B. The test-code forms are TST-C5C and TST-G2A.
category_guides.2: Whitespace and line layout. QAL-B2A is an overlong line, QAL-B2B is an awkward continuation, QAL-B2C is missing blank lines and QAL-B2D is inconsistent spacing inside literals. These are pure formatting, so pick whichever names the visible symptom.
category_guides.3: String-building idioms. QAL-B3B is f-strings and %-formatting mixed in one file, and QAL-B3C is + concatenation where the file otherwise uses f-strings. QAL-B3A covers the prefix convention of diagnostic messages, not the formatting idiom. A message lacking identifying context is QAL-I1B.

B.guide: Mechanical style: import statements, whitespace and layout, and string-building idioms. Most entries here can be caught by a linter (automated_by). Choose B only when the finding is about how a line is written. Where code is placed belongs in F2, and conventions shared across modules belong in F1 or F3.
B.name: style-and-formatting

category_guides.1: Stale pointers that break nothing. QAL-C1A is a URL, QAL-C1C is a file path and QAL-C1D is a version number. A stale packaging-manifest URL is ARC-B1C, a doc describing an artifact the repo lacks is ARC-D3B, and a path filter that no longer matches what it should is ARC-C1B. QAL-C1B covers documentation lists in an inconsistent order.
category_guides.2: Doc text that has drifted. QAL-C2A is a schema or example stricter than reality but inert, QAL-C2B is one document contradicting itself, QAL-C2C is CLI docs lagging real flags, QAL-C2D is a docstring error contract that is wrong, and QAL-C2F is config behavior left undocumented. Easy to confuse: QAL-C2A vs COD-D1B (live rejection), QAL-C2B vs COD-D2C (contradictory spec documents), and QAL-C2C/QAL-C2F vs COD-D2D (a capability missing from the docs entirely). QAL-C2E (typos) is text hygiene, not drift.

C.guide: Documentation hygiene: references that have gone stale, and doc text that lags the code without breaking anything. Under the routing principle, inert staleness homes here. Stale pointers are C1 and inert doc-text drift is C2. If a missing reference breaks the code or build, it is ARC-D3A. If a doc and the code are competing sources of truth for the same fact, it is ARC-G1B. If a documented feature does not exist at all, it is COD-D2B.
C.name: documentation

category_guides.1: Duplicated code. QAL-D1A is an inline block of business logic, QAL-D1B is a constant or literal table and QAL-D1C is a named helper function. A dead, drifted duplicate validator is QAL-E1B. Duplication left alone on purpose because it is tangled with an open correctness finding is QAL-H2B.

D.guide: Copy-paste duplication that can be consolidated within the existing structure. The finding is the copies themselves. If the fix needs a new shared module or a canonical owner, use ARC-A3A or ARC-A5A. Duplicated test helpers are TST-C2B or TST-G1B.
D.name: duplication

category_guides.1: Config or rule definitions that nothing reads. QAL-E1A is a setting whose consumer is off or absent. QAL-E1B is an unused, drifted duplicate of a validator, regex or constant. A setting that implies an enforcement that does not happen is ARC-F1E, and contradictory lint settings are ARC-B1E.
category_guides.2: Artifacts a past change left behind. QAL-E2B is a retired component that is still registered (compare ARC-A4C, shadow registries without parity), and QAL-E2C is CSS or asset rules with no referencing markup.
category_guides.3: Unused code. QAL-E3A is a function with no callers. Unreachable code is COD-E2A, and an unused duplicate validator is QAL-E1B.

E.guide: Leftovers that nothing uses: dead config, retired registrations, orphaned assets and unused functions. If the code cannot run because of a misplaced guard or return, it is COD-E2A. Unused test fixtures are TST-E1B.
E.name: dead-code

category_guides.1: How imports resolve across modules. QAL-F1A is an implicit sys.path or caller-provided import dependency, and QAL-F1B is import style varying between modules. Easy to confuse: ARC-A2C (packaging-level resolution hack), TST-G1A (the test-suite form) and TST-G2A (inconsistent imports inside test methods).
category_guides.2: Code placed in the wrong spot. QAL-F2A is logic embedded in a non-standard host such as CI YAML, and QAL-F2B is a cosmetic __main__ guard sitting mid-file. When the guard hides code, it is COD-E2A for production code and TST-C1A for tests. When embedded CI logic is also untested, that untested path is ARC-C1C, not a higher grade of QAL-F2A.
category_guides.3: Divergence from the codebase's own convention. QAL-F3B is noqa usage, QAL-F3C is per-host field names and QAL-F3D is partial type-hint adoption. A naming-style mix inside one module is QAL-A1B. A cross-host parity gap in content (rather than naming) is ARC-E3C.

F.guide: Where code lives and whether it follows the codebase's own conventions: how imports resolve across modules, code in an unusual location, and convention drift (noqa usage, field naming, type-hint adoption). Single-line import style is B1. A missing package structure that forces path hacks is ARC-A2C, and the test-suite form is TST-G1A.
F.name: structure-and-convention

category_guides.1: Work repeated for no reason. QAL-G1A is loop-invariant work not hoisted, QAL-G1B is a pure or idempotent load repeated across calls, and QAL-G1C is the narrow case of repeated filesystem stat or realpath calls on an unchanging path. Pick QAL-G1C only for filesystem-metadata calls and QAL-G1A for other per-iteration work. A query issued per row is DAT-C1B, and a stale cache after memoizing is COD-F3A.
category_guides.2: Memory growing with the data. QAL-G2A is an in-memory collection loaded whole. The neighbours are DAT-C1C (DB result set), DAT-F2B (persisted file read), COD-F2C (UI rendering) and OPS-D1B (API response cap).

G.guide: Avoidable work and memory use in-process: recomputation, missing caches and whole-collection loads. Repeated database queries are DAT-C1B, unbounded query results are DAT-C1C, attacker-reachable resource use is SEC-H4B or SEC-F2A, and capacity under load is OPS-D1A.
G.name: efficiency

category_guides.1: Local complexity. QAL-H1A is a whole function that is too long or has too many branches. QAL-H1B is a single construct nested too deeply (nested ternaries, arrow code). Pick H1B when one construct is the problem and H1A when the function as a whole is.
category_guides.2: Simplification judgment. QAL-H2A is a simplification that made code worse, and QAL-H2C is an abstraction that adds no value. QAL-H2B applies only when near-duplicate code was explicitly deferred from unification because of an open correctness finding. Without a recorded deferral, cite QAL-D1A or QAL-D1C.

H.guide: Complexity, and how judgment is applied when simplifying. H1 covers code that is too complex, and H2 covers simplification that goes wrong or abstraction that adds nothing. A function mixing separable concerns is the structural ARC-A1C.
H.name: complexity-and-simplification

category_guides.1: Diagnostic content. QAL-I1A is trace context dropped across a call, and QAL-I1B is a log message with no identifying context. An error message that names the wrong cause is COD-B2B, and a mixed message-prefix convention is QAL-B3A.

I.guide: Diagnostics quality: logs and traces that exist but help too little. An error swallowed with no telemetry at all is OPS-E1A, sensitive data in logs is SEC-B4A or SEC-B2B, and a missing audit record is SEC-C4B.
I.name: observability

QAL-A1B.criteria: Qualifies when identifiers in one module or package mix naming conventions (snake_case and camelCase, singular and plural collection names) with no rule that explains the split. A per-host config field-name mismatch is QAL-F3C. A name that clashes with an existing domain concept is QAL-A1C. A test or helper name that misstates behavior is TST-C3B or TST-C3C.
examples: maintain consistent naming conventions across a module
QAL-A1B.name: inconsistent-naming-convention

raise_when.condition: The inconsistent names are part of an exported API, CLI flag set or config-key surface that external callers must type.

QAL-A1C.criteria: Qualifies when a file, module or identifier reuses a term that already names a different, established concept in the project's code or docs, so a reader conflates the two. A name that misstates what a test or helper does is TST-C3B or TST-C3C. A term that is defined ambiguously in a spec is ARC-D2F. A naming-style mix is QAL-A1B.
examples: Filename orchestrator.py collides with the unrelated 'orchestrator' concept used throughout the pipeline docs/agent naming
Same collision flagged again independently in a later review pass on the same file
QAL-A1C.name: name-collision-with-domain-concept

QAL-A2B.criteria: Qualifies when an expression evaluates correctly but its operator precedence or line breaks let a reader misread which operand a ternary, boolean or arithmetic operator binds. If the precedence actually gives the wrong result, it is a correctness defect (COD; no specific code exists yet, so use COD-X0X). Deeply nested conditional expressions are QAL-H1B.
examples: `"**Found by:** %s%s" % (src, "  \u00b7  model: %s" % prov["model"] if prov.get("model") else "")` reads, at a glance, as if the ternary applies to the wrong operand
Awkward line break in a conditional expression obscures which branch a continuation line belongs to
QAL-A2B.name: confusing-expression-precedence

lower_when.condition: The expression is already parenthesised or split so each operand's binding is explicit, and only the line break is awkward.

QAL-A2C.criteria: Qualifies when a numeric literal or positional index in production code has no name or comment explaining it, or positional inserts and indexes depend on an unstated layout that a nearby edit would silently shift. The value must currently be correct. Self-evident literals (0, 1, 60 seconds, 1024 bytes, a standard HTTP status code) do not qualify. A wrong index or off-by-one is COD-A2B, and an empty or out-of-range access is COD-A2C. The same unexplained value in test code is TST-C5D.
examples: title_for() truncates with `room = 240 - len(suffix)`, no comment explaining where 240 comes from
render_summary() prepends banner lines via three independent lines.insert(<fixed index>, ...) calls with undocumented, fragile hardcoded indices
QAL-A2C.name: magic-number-or-fragile-hardcoded-index

lower_when.condition: The literal is defined once next to a comment or adjacent docstring that states its origin, and only its name is missing.

QAL-A2D.criteria: Qualifies when comments only restate what the adjacent code plainly does and add no intent or rationale. A comment that has gone stale and now misstates the code is ARC-G1B, or QAL-C2D for a docstring's error contract. A comment that points at a path that no longer exists is QAL-C1C. Commented-out code is not covered here.
examples: removing comments that describe obvious code
QAL-A2D.name: comment-noise

QAL-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when several modules are imported in one import statement (PEP 8 E401). Imports placed mid-file or inside functions are QAL-B1B. Imports repeated or re-aliased are QAL-B1C. Import style differing across modules is QAL-F1B.
examples: `import contextlib, io, os, sys, json, tempfile, unittest` violates PEP 8's one-import-per-line guidance
`import sys, os` on a single line (PEP 8 E401), inconsistent with every sibling test file's one-import-per-line style
QAL-B1A.name: combined-imports-single-line

lower_when.condition: The file's own sibling modules use the same combined style, so the instance departs only from PEP 8, not from the codebase.

QAL-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when an import sits mid-module or inside a function or method body in production code with no lazy-import reason, unlike the file's top-level imports. The test-code form is TST-C5C. An import in a function used to break an import cycle is ARC-A2A.
examples: `import fnmatch` and `from scripts.tools import ADAPTERS` done inside a function body instead of module top-level, unlike the rest of the file
Import statements placed inside test methods rather than at module level
QAL-B1B.name: mid-file-or-inline-import-placement

QAL-B1C.criteria: Qualifies when a module is imported more than once in a file, under different aliases or again in a local scope, while it is already bound at module scope (F811). Test methods re-importing modules already imported at the top are TST-G2A. Import style differing across modules is QAL-F1B.
examples: `scripts.evidence` imported twice under two different aliases (`evidence` and `ev`) in the same file, used inconsistently across classes
10+ test methods locally re-import io/contextlib/tempfile that are already imported at module scope
QAL-B1C.name: redundant-shadowing-import

lower_when.condition: The re-import binds the identical name with no new alias, so no reader can reach the module under two names.

QAL-B2A.criteria: Qualifies when a source line exceeds the project's configured line-length limit (PEP 8 or the repo's ruff/black setting). A long line that is long because of a nested conditional is better cited as QAL-H1B or QAL-A2B when the readability problem is the expression itself.
examples: A nested ternary conditional expression spans ~107 characters, exceeding PEP 8's line-length guideline
Line exceeds an 88-character limit
QAL-B2A.name: line-too-long

lower_when.condition: The line is a URL, a single string literal or a generated data row that cannot be wrapped without hurting readability.

QAL-B2B.criteria: Qualifies when a statement continues across lines with a backslash or with misaligned hanging or visual indentation, where parenthesised implicit continuation is the codebase norm. Overlong single lines are QAL-B2A, and missing blank lines between definitions are QAL-B2C.
examples: Backslash line continuation used instead of implicit (parenthesized) continuation
Misaligned continuation line in a tuple return statement
QAL-B2B.name: misaligned-or-awkward-continuation

QAL-B2C.criteria: Qualifies when top-level or nested definitions lack the blank-line separation the project's style requires (PEP 8 E301/E302/E305). Spacing inside literals is QAL-B2D.
examples: Missing blank line before a module-level function definition
Missing PEP8 two-blank-line separation between top-level definitions
QAL-B2C.name: missing-blank-line-separation

QAL-B2D.criteria: Qualifies when spacing after ':' and ',' (or around operators) inside literals departs from the file's dominant formatting. Missing blank lines between definitions are QAL-B2C.
examples: Dict literals throughout a test file consistently omit whitespace after ':' and ',', breaking from the file's dominant formatting style
QAL-B2D.name: inconsistent-literal-whitespace

QAL-B3A.criteria: Qualifies when stderr or log diagnostics depart from the package's established message-prefix convention (for example '<module>: message' versus 'WARNING:'). Mixing f-string and %-formatting in the message body is QAL-B3B. A message that lacks identifying context is QAL-I1B.
examples: model_resolver.py's 'WARNING:' stderr prefix diverges from the package-wide '<module>: message' convention used by dispatch.py, ingest_tools.py, etc.
load_findings() mixes four different stderr diagnostic-prefix conventions in a dozen lines
QAL-B3A.name: inconsistent-diagnostic-prefix-convention

QAL-B3B.criteria: Qualifies when one file or function mixes f-strings and %-style (or .format) formatting for similar messages, against the file's dominant idiom. Logger calls that pass arguments for lazy %-interpolation (logger.info('%s', x)) do not qualify. + concatenation where f-strings are the norm is QAL-B3C. A diagnostic-prefix mismatch is QAL-B3A.
examples: run_adapters() mixes f-string and %-style diagnostic messages while every sibling function in the same file uses %-formatting
Mixed f-string and %-formatting used for near-identical diagnostics in one file
QAL-B3B.name: mixed-fstring-percent-formatting

QAL-B3C.criteria: Qualifies when a string is built with + concatenation of interpolated values where the file otherwise uses f-strings. Mixing f-string and %-formatting is QAL-B3B. Translatable UI text assembled by concatenation is LNG-C1A.
examples: String built with the + operator instead of an f-string, inconsistent with the file's dominant idiom
QAL-B3C.name: string-concatenation-instead-of-fstring

lower_when.condition: The concatenation joins only literals or constants, with no interpolated runtime value.

QAL-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when a URL or reference in documentation or code is STALE — it points to an outdated org, host, or target — as a single per-instance staleness defect. Does NOT apply to packaging-manifest URLs (project identity), which are ARC-B1C, nor to the same identifier hardcoded across multiple modules so copies diverge, which is ARC-E1C (scatter).
QAL-C1A.name: stale-external-url-reference

lower_when.condition: The stale URL still redirects (HTTP 301/302) to the correct current target.
The URL appears only in a historical record (a CHANGELOG entry, a dated ADR) where it was correct when written.

QAL-C1B.criteria: Qualifies when an ordered documentation list (version history, changelog, numbered steps) follows neither ascending nor descending order, or an order the document itself states. A CHANGELOG version that disagrees with another doc's description is QAL-C1D. Self-contradictory content is QAL-C2B.
examples: DEVELOPMENT.md's version History list is in neither ascending nor descending order
QAL-C1B.name: inconsistent-ordering-in-docs

lower_when.condition: Every entry carries an explicit version or date, so a reader can recover the order without relying on position.

QAL-C1C.criteria: Qualifies for a file-path reference (in a comment, doc, or config) that no longer resolves but breaks nothing — inert staleness of a POINTER per the routing principle. A stale VERSION number is the sibling QAL-C1D; a code/build reference whose absence breaks is ARC-D3A; documentation asserting a structural artifact or component the repository lacks (a doc-vs-repo structural gap, not a drifted pointer) is ARC-D3B.
examples: CODEOWNERS 'CI / security tooling' and 'Schemas and reference data' sections list paths that no longer exist post-restructure
A module docstring's Usage: line names the wrong path for the script it documents
QAL-C1C.name: stale-file-path-reference

lower_when.condition: The stale path appears only in a historical record (a changelog entry, a dated plan) where it was correct when written.

QAL-C1D.criteria: Qualifies for a version number in docs/metadata that no longer matches reality but breaks nothing — inert staleness. A stale file-PATH reference is the sibling QAL-C1C.
examples: pyproject.toml [project].version reads 3.0.0 while the project's actual current version is 4.2.0
CHANGELOG.md's only versioned entry doesn't match DEVELOPMENT.md's description of the same version
QAL-C1D.name: stale-version-number

lower_when.condition: The version appears only in a historical narrative (a dated plan or release note) describing a past state.

QAL-C2A.criteria: Qualifies when a schema, example, or placeholder is more precise or strict than the real convention but the over-specification is INERT — no valid output is actually rejected and nothing breaks (precision hygiene). If a live constraint rejects real producer output, that is COD-D1B (correctness); if the stricter copy is dead and unimported, QAL-E1B; if the format is defined inconsistently across artifacts, ARC-D1D.
examples: report-schema.json constrains finding IDs to a 2-4 letter prefix pattern, but the real convention elsewhere in the codebase is 2-8 letters
A CVE ID format placeholder implies a fixed 6-digit sequence number, imprecise relative to the real CVE ID grammar
QAL-C2A.name: schema-or-example-stricter-than-reality

lower_when.condition: The over-strict artifact is a prose example or placeholder, not a schema that any validator loads.

QAL-C2B.criteria: Qualifies when a SINGLE document contradicts itself (one section states X, another not-X) about behavior that is not normative for an implementation. When two independent sources of truth disagree (code vs code, doc vs code), it is ARC-G1B. When specification documents prescribe contradictory required behavior that an implementer must choose between, it is COD-D2C.
examples: SKILL.md's 'Notes' section makes a blanket self-write claim that directly contradicts the Codex and generic-host sections of the same file
QAL-C2B.name: self-contradictory-documentation

lower_when.condition: One of the contradicting passages is explicitly marked as superseded, historical or non-authoritative inside the same document.

QAL-C2C.criteria: Qualifies when CLI or flag documentation is STALE relative to an implementation that DOES exist: the flags are real, but the docs lag, misname or under-cover them (doc hygiene, LOW). If a documented feature is entirely unimplemented, so a user following the docs breaks, it is COD-D2B. If an implemented flag or capability is absent from the docs altogether, it is COD-D2D. If the documented invocation syntax or arguments manifest as a whole is unreliable as a spec, it is ARC-D2A.
examples: README Quick Start examples use a --mode/--target CLI syntax that no longer matches the documented flags
SKILL.md frontmatter's `arguments` list is stale relative to the much larger, differently-named flag surface documented in the body
QAL-C2C.name: cli-docs-out-of-sync-with-implementation

lower_when.condition: Only secondary metadata is stale (a frontmatter summary list) while the body docs a user reads are correct.

QAL-C2D.criteria: Qualifies when a docstring or API doc names exception types, return sentinels or failure behavior that the implementation does not produce on some path. If a caller relying on the documented contract fails to handle the real failure, so the program proceeds on bad data or crashes, that is a correctness defect (COD-B2C where it is an unchecked auxiliary failure, otherwise COD-X0X). If an error message names the wrong cause, it is COD-B2B.
examples: acquire_pr()'s docstring promises a loud RuntimeError on any failure, but a missing gh/git binary actually raises a different, undocumented exception
QAL-C2D.name: docstring-inaccurate-error-contract

lower_when.condition: The function is private (underscore-prefixed) and every caller in the repo handles a common base exception.

QAL-C2E.criteria: Qualifies when text that ships to users or downstream tools (templates, messages, published docs) contains a spelling error. A misspelt identifier, key or command that breaks a lookup or invocation is a correctness defect (COD-X0X), not this code.
examples: Shipped commit-message template contains the typo 'kim port' instead of 'kimi port'
QAL-C2E.name: typo-in-shipped-text

lower_when.condition: The typo is in prose and changes no name, command or term that a reader would copy or search for.

QAL-C2F.criteria: Qualifies when a config file's deliberate behavior (intentional sparseness, omitted keys, defaults that differ between sections) is not documented, so a maintainer would read it as a mistake. An implemented capability missing from the docs is COD-D2D. Docs that under-describe the architecture are ARC-G1C. A real parity gap between hosts is ARC-E3C.
examples: cwe_owasp mapping's intentional sparseness (8 of 34 catalog CWEs unmapped) is undocumented
model-profiles.yml's claude host entries silently omit max_context_size/max_output_size present on the other two hosts
QAL-C2F.name: undocumented-configuration-behavior

lower_when.condition: A code comment next to the config value already explains the intent, and only user-facing docs omit it.

QAL-D1A.criteria: Qualifies per-instance when the same block of business logic is duplicated and should be consolidated within the existing structure — the finding is the copies themselves (a maintainability / DRY smell). When the hazard is the STRUCTURAL absence of a shared module or owner that a proper fix must create, that is ARC-A3A.
examples: run_tools()'s legacy-SARIF and Phase-1-adapter dispatch blocks duplicate ~20 lines of subprocess invoke/error-handling logic
QAL-D1A.name: duplicated-business-logic-block

lower_when.condition: Both copies are in the same file and each is under 10 lines.

QAL-D1B.criteria: Qualifies per-instance when the same constant is defined in two or more places and should be unified — the finding is the duplicate definitions themselves. When the hazard is the STRUCTURAL lack of a canonical owner that a proper fix must establish (an ownership / aliasing change), that is ARC-A5A. A dead, unimported stricter duplicate is instead QAL-E1B.
QAL-D1B.name: duplicated-constant-definition

lower_when.condition: The duplicated value is fixed by an external standard (a protocol port, a spec-defined header or magic number) and cannot drift independently.

QAL-D1C.criteria: Qualifies when two or more named helper functions in production code are identical or near-identical and could be one shared function. Inline duplicated blocks of business logic are QAL-D1A. Duplication with no structural home, where the fix needs a new module, is ARC-A3A. Duplicated test helpers are TST-C2B. Duplication left unmerged deliberately because it is entangled with an open correctness finding is QAL-H2B.
examples: load_ledger() and record() are nearly identical, copy-pasted across file_fixmes.py and file_issues.py
_severity_class and _panel_class implement the exact same strip/lowercase transform, differing only in a CSS-class prefix string
QAL-D1C.name: duplicated-helper-function

lower_when.condition: The duplicated helper is a trivial transform (a single expression with no branching, for example strip/lower).
