QAL-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when a config setting has no effect because the feature, rule set or consumer that reads it is not enabled or does not exist. If the setting makes a reader believe a policy or gate is enforced when it is not, it is ARC-F1E. Contradictory lint settings are ARC-B1E. A lint gate whose scope misses files is ARC-C1D.
examples: Ruff's `[tool.ruff.lint.pydocstyle] convention = "google"` is dead configuration because the "D" rule set that would consume it is never selected
QAL-E1A.name: dead-configuration-setting

lower_when.condition: The dead setting restates the tool's own default, so enabling the consumer would not change behavior either.

QAL-E1B.criteria: Qualifies when a duplicated validator, regex, or constant is DEAD — an unused, un-imported stricter copy of a canonical rule that has drifted from it (dead code plus duplication). If the drifted duplicate is live and rejects real output, elevate to COD-D1B; if it is live-but-cosmetic over-precision, QAL-C2A; if two live copies simply diverge as a duplication smell, QAL-D1B.
examples: base.py declares ID_RE, an unused, stricter duplicate of the canonical finding-ID regex actually used in synthesize.py; nothing imports or calls it
QAL-E1B.name: unused-duplicate-validator-left-in-code

QAL-E2B.criteria: Qualifies when a component that its own module, docs or a later change mark as retired is still registered in a dispatch table, registry or prefix map. If a second registry duplicates the live one with no enforced parity, it is ARC-A4C. If the retired component is still selected and run by default, producing output it should not, it is a behavioral defect (COD-X0X). An unused function with no registration is QAL-E3A.
examples: "eslint" stays registered in ADAPTERS as a LegacySarifAdapter after being explicitly retired in the module's own comments
sarif_utils.PREFIX still maps "brakeman": "BR" though the only Brakeman findings actually come from the dedicated BrakemanAdapter
QAL-E2B.name: retired-component-still-registered

QAL-E2C.criteria: Qualifies when stylesheet rules, templates or static assets have no remaining reference in any markup or code that could render them. Unused functions are QAL-E3A. Unused test fixtures are TST-E1B.
examples: .grades and .heatmap-more CSS classes in html_report.py with no referencing template markup
QAL-E2C.name: orphaned-asset-rules

QAL-E3A.criteria: Qualifies when a production function, method or class has no caller, registration or export a consumer could reach. Code that cannot run because a guard or return precedes it is COD-E2A. An unused duplicate validator is QAL-E1B. A retired component still registered is QAL-E2B. Unused test fixtures are TST-E1B.
examples: run_adapters: no production caller
model_resolver.role_config: zero callers
QAL-E3A.name: dead-code-unused-function
QAL-E3A.notes: receiving-code-review treats unused/dead code as a YAGNI defect, not merely an opportunity — character is contested across sources

QAL-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when a single production module imports a sibling package only because the caller or a launcher has already set up sys.path or PYTHONPATH, so it fails when imported or run from elsewhere. A project-wide resolution hack that replaces proper packaging is ARC-A2C. The test-suite-wide sys.path.insert pattern is TST-G1A. Import style differing across modules is QAL-F1B.
examples: group_runner.py imports scripts.evidence without ensuring the parent directory is on sys.path, relying implicitly on the caller's setup
Two incompatible sys.path bootstrap conventions coexist in the test suite, making import success order-dependent
QAL-F1A.name: implicit-sys-path-or-import-dependency

QAL-F1B.criteria: Qualifies when sibling production modules use different import conventions for the same kind of dependency (absolute vs relative, module vs from-import, aliasing) with no rule for the split. Problems inside one file are QAL-B1*. The test-method form is TST-G2A. A referenced symbol that is never imported is TST-C5A or a correctness defect, not this code.
examples: Adapter modules use inconsistent import patterns from one file to the next
unittest.mock.patch used without importing the mock submodule, an inconsistent stderr-capture idiom relative to sibling tests
QAL-F1B.name: inconsistent-import-style-across-modules

QAL-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when real program logic is embedded in a host not meant for it (an inline heredoc in CI YAML, a shell one-liner in a Makefile, code in a config string) instead of a reusable, testable source file. A main guard misplaced within a file is QAL-F2B. Untested CI integration is ARC-C1C. A script with zero test coverage is TST-A1A.
examples: Gate logic is embedded as an inline Python heredoc inside the CI workflow YAML instead of living in a reusable, unit-tested script
QAL-F2A.name: logic-embedded-in-non-standard-location

lower_when.condition: The embedded snippet is three lines or fewer and has no branching.

QAL-F2B.criteria: Qualifies ONLY when a misplaced `__main__` guard (or top-level block) is purely cosmetic — every definition after it still collects and executes identically, so there is no reachability or discovery impact (layout hygiene, LOW). If production code after the guard becomes unreachable, that is COD-E2A; if test classes after it are silently dropped from discovery, TST-C1A.
examples: Main block misplaced in the middle of a file rather than at the end
QAL-F2B.name: main-guard-or-block-misplaced-mid-file

lower_when.condition: Only constant or import declarations follow the guard.

QAL-F3B.criteria: Qualifies when lint-suppression comments (noqa, type: ignore, nosec) are applied inconsistently to identical patterns, or are unused (RUF100), against the codebase's suppression convention. A swallowed broad exception itself is ARC-F2G or OPS-E1A. Contradictory lint config is ARC-B1E.
examples: Bare except Exception blocks in orchestrator.py omit the codebase's noqa:BLE001 tolerant-by-design convention used elsewhere for the same pattern
# noqa suppressions on identical `class R:` test-double patterns are applied inconsistently within the same file
QAL-F3B.name: inconsistent-noqa-annotation-usage

QAL-F3C.criteria: Qualifies when equivalent settings use different field names across host or profile sections of one config file, and the loader accepts each spelling. If a loader reads only one spelling, so another section's field is silently ignored, it is COD-C3C. A content parity gap between hosts is ARC-E3C. A naming-style mix in code is QAL-A1B.
examples: model-profiles.yml uses a different field-naming convention for model/effort settings depending on which host section it's in
QAL-F3C.name: inconsistent-per-host-field-naming

QAL-F3D.criteria: Qualifies when type annotations cover only some functions in a file or package with no evident rule for which are annotated (such as public API only). A type mismatch across a boundary is COD-D3C.
examples: select_adapters() and run_adapters() carry full PEP 484 type annotations while most other functions in the same file have none, with no apparent rule for which get them
QAL-F3D.name: partial-type-hint-adoption

QAL-G1A.criteria: Qualifies when a value that does not change across a loop's iterations is recomputed inside the loop. A pure or idempotent load repeated across calls (not iterations) is QAL-G1B. A repeated stat/realpath is QAL-G1C. A database query issued per row is DAT-C1B.
examples: eligible_ids set recomputed inside synthesize's per-group loop despite being loop-invariant
QAL-G1A.name: loop-invariant-not-hoisted

lower_when.condition: The loop's iteration count is bounded by a small constant (a fixed enum or literal list).

raise_when.condition: The recomputed work performs I/O (a file read, network call or subprocess), and the loop's iteration count grows with input size.

QAL-G1B.criteria: Qualifies when a pure or idempotent load or computation (template parse, catalog load) is redone on every call although its inputs do not change during the process. A value recomputed per loop iteration is QAL-G1A. A cache that is added but returns stale data is COD-F3A. A lazy cache that is not thread-safe is COD-F3B.
examples: dispatch.load_template re-read and re-parsed advisor.md once per verify-queue entry — 412 times in run-3
synthesize re-loading CWE catalog and verdicts per call site instead of threading loaded values
QAL-G1B.name: missing-memoization

lower_when.condition: The function runs a fixed number of times per process, independent of input size.

QAL-G1C.criteria: Qualifies when filesystem metadata calls (stat, realpath, exists) for the same unchanging path are repeated per item. Other loop-invariant work is QAL-G1A. Path resolution against the wrong base is COD-E2B.
examples: orchestrator._within recomputed os.path.realpath(repo) per candidate file on large expansions; cached via _repo_realpath
QAL-G1C.name: repeated-filesystem-stat

lower_when.condition: The repeated call runs over a set bounded by a small constant, not by repository or input size.

QAL-G2A.criteria: Qualifies when an in-memory collection that grows with the data is loaded whole in-process where streaming, paging or a bound is available. A database query with no LIMIT is DAT-C1C. A persisted file read whole is DAT-F2B. An unbounded network response read is SEC-F2A. Rendering the collection into the UI in one pass is COD-F2C. An endpoint returning it unbounded is OPS-D1B. Overload of memory or connections under load is OPS-D1A.
QAL-G2A.name: unbounded-collection-load

lower_when.condition: The collection's size is capped by a documented upstream limit (a schema maxItems, a config cap, a fixed retention window).

QAL-H1A.criteria: Qualifies when a function as a whole is too long or too complex for a SINGLE concern (high cyclomatic complexity, many branches, many locals), a local problem whose fix simplifies in place. When the problem is one deeply nested construct inside an otherwise reasonable function, it is QAL-H1B. When the function mixes several SEPARABLE concerns that belong in different units, it is the structural ARC-A1C.
examples: function flagged for high cyclomatic complexity / too many responsibilities combined into one function
QAL-H1A.name: overly-complex-function

lower_when.condition: The complexity comes from a flat dispatch, a single match or if/elif over enumerated cases with no nesting.

QAL-H1B.criteria: Qualifies when one construct (nested ternaries, arrow-shaped if-nesting, nested comprehensions) is nested deeper than needed and could be flattened with guard clauses or extraction, while the rest of the function is reasonable. Whole-function complexity is QAL-H1A. Precedence that is merely misreadable is QAL-A2B. Nesting introduced by an over-eager simplification is QAL-H2A.
examples: nested ternary operators flagged for conversion to switch/if-else chains
reducing unnecessary complexity and nesting
QAL-H1B.name: excess-nesting-complexity

QAL-H2A.criteria: Qualifies when a change (typically a refactor or a simplify pass) removes or inlines a helpful abstraction, name or step and leaves the code harder to read, debug or extend than before. The resulting nested or dense construct on its own is QAL-H1B. A function that now mixes separable concerns is ARC-A1C. An abstraction that adds nothing (the opposite judgment) is QAL-H2C.
examples: removing a helpful abstraction that improves organization
combining too many concerns into a single function to save lines
prioritizing fewer-lines over readability (dense one-liners, nested ternaries) making code harder to debug or extend
QAL-H2A.name: harmful-oversimplification

lower_when.condition: The removed abstraction had a single call site and no test or doc referred to it.

QAL-H2B.criteria: Qualifies only when near-duplicate code (QAL-D1A or QAL-D1C) is explicitly deferred from unification because the merge would change behavior covered by an open correctness finding, and the deferral and the linked finding are recorded. Without a recorded deferral, cite QAL-D1A or QAL-D1C.
examples: eslint _strip_prefix vs sarif_utils._norm_uri: two normalization functions look mergeable but intersect an open correctness finding, so unification was explicitly deferred out of a quality-only PR
reconcile.load_report / file_issues parts-merge unification deferred: duplicated confinement logic entangled with an open reconcile-fingerprint correctness finding
QAL-H2B.name: correctness-entangled-duplication-deferred

QAL-H2C.criteria: Qualifies when a wrapper, class, layer or indirection in production code adds nothing beyond direct use of what it wraps. A parallel structure derived byte-for-byte from another is ARC-A5B. An over-engineered test fixture builder is TST-C5B. Removing an abstraction that did help is QAL-H2A.
examples: eliminating redundant code and abstractions
removing indirection that adds no value beyond direct derivation
QAL-H2C.name: needless-abstraction

QAL-I1A.criteria: Qualifies when code making an outbound call, enqueueing work or spawning a task does not forward the incoming trace or correlation context it holds, so the downstream span or log cannot be joined to its origin. An entry point with no upstream context to continue does not qualify. An error swallowed with no telemetry at all is OPS-E1A. A log line lacking identifying context is QAL-I1B.
QAL-I1A.name: missing-trace-context-propagation

QAL-I1B.criteria: Qualifies when a log or diagnostic message omits the identifying context (entity id, path, input, operation) needed to act on it. A message naming the wrong cause is COD-B2B. An error with no log at all is OPS-E1A. Adding context that is PII or a credential is SEC-B4A or SEC-B2B. An inconsistent message-prefix convention is QAL-B3A.
QAL-I1B.name: vague-log-message-without-context

raise_when.condition: The vague message is the only signal on an error path; no exception, exit status or metric accompanies it.

QAL.guide: QAL covers code and docs that work but are harder to read, change or keep consistent: naming, formatting, inert stale references, duplication, dead code, convention drift, avoidable recomputation, complexity and diagnostic quality. Use COD when the instance gives a wrong result or breaks a contract, ARC when two sources of truth disagree or the fix needs a new structural owner, TST when the same hazard sits in test code (for example TST-C5C, TST-C5D, TST-G1A, TST-G2A), ACC for an assistive-technology defect, and OPS, DAT or SEC when the cost is runtime capacity, query volume or attacker-reachable resource use. Start with A (readability) or B (mechanical style) for local text problems, C for documentation, D and E for copies and leftovers, F for placement and convention, G for wasted work, H for complexity and I for logs and traces.
QAL.name: quality-maintainability

category_guides.1: SEC-A1A when untrusted input is shown to reach a shell or argv sink. SEC-A1B for a pattern-only subprocess flag with no dataflow. Bare-name PATH lookup on an attacker-writable path is SEC-D1B.
category_guides.2: SEC-A2A for eval/exec of untrusted strings, SEC-A2B for deserializers that instantiate types (pickle, unsafe YAML). Build files that execute by design are SEC-E3A, not A2.
category_guides.3: SEC-A3A for untrusted input concatenated into SQL text instead of bound as a parameter. A slow query is DAT-C1 (for example DAT-C1B, N+1); an unbounded result set is OPS-D1B.
category_guides.4: SEC-A4A when untrusted XML is parsed with entities or DTDs enabled. SEC-A4B for an XML-library rule hit with no dataflow or configuration evidence.

A.guide: Untrusted data reaching an interpreter: shell/process (A1), language eval and deserialization (A2), SQL (A3), XML entity processing (A4). Where a category pairs a demonstrated-dataflow code with a heuristic sibling, cite the demonstrated code only when untrusted input is shown reaching the sink.
A.name: injection-and-unsafe-execution

category_guides.1: SEC-B1C is the general code for unescaped untrusted content in a generated artifact. SEC-B1A is the auto-posted markdown/@-mention variant and SEC-B1B the unsafe link-scheme variant. SEC-B1D (remote loads) and SEC-B1E (no CSP) are report hardening, not injection.
category_guides.2: SEC-B2A is secrets through a debug endpoint, SEC-B2B credentials written to output or logs, SEC-B2C a redactor that exists but misses cases, SEC-B2D verbose errors with no secret in them. B2B and B2C differ on whether a redaction control exists.
category_guides.3: SEC-B3A only for a confirmed, real credential. Detector hits of unconfirmed validity are SEC-B3C. SEC-B3B is secrets exposed through a subprocess inheriting the full environment.
category_guides.4: SEC-B4A is personal data in logs. SEC-B4B (over-collection), SEC-B4C (retention) and SEC-B4D (subject-rights path) are distinct lifecycle defects; split a finding that cites more than one.

B.guide: Content leaving the system unsafely: injection into generated output (B1), disclosure through debug, errors and logs (B2), secrets at rest or in the environment (B3), personal-data handling (B4). Choose by what leaks: markup or script (B1), runtime detail or credentials (B2), stored credentials (B3), personal data (B4).
B.name: output-handling-and-data-exposure

category_guides.1: SEC-C1C is a missing role/function check and SEC-C1F a missing per-object ownership check; split a finding that cites both. SEC-C1B is a hidden backdoor trigger. SEC-C1D is a mutation through ambient credentials or context in one script; when the finding is that sibling scripts gate inconsistently, cite ARC-F1C. SEC-C1A is excess container privilege; SEC-C1E is root with no other excess.
category_guides.2: SEC-C2A is no throttling, SEC-C2B a non-constant-time compare, SEC-C2C a response-discrepancy oracle. All three often show up on one login endpoint; split them, do not merge.
category_guides.3: SEC-C3A is a weak PRNG for a security value, SEC-C3B a broken standard algorithm or mode, SEC-C3C a non-cryptographic checksum used in a security role.
category_guides.4: SEC-C4B when no audit record is written. SEC-C4C when the record is written but destroyed through the channel it audits.

C.guide: Who may do what, and with what proof: access control (C1), authentication (C2), cryptographic primitives (C3), security audit logging (C4). Agent tool-grant scope routes to AGT-B1; inconsistent gates across sibling scripts route to ARC-F1C.
C.name: identity-access-and-cryptography

category_guides.1: SEC-D1A is a ../ or absolute path escape, SEC-D1C symlink following during copy or extract, SEC-D1B an attacker-writable search path for binaries, modules or plugins.
category_guides.2: SEC-D2B for a user-influenced fetch with no allow-list (the precursor). SEC-D2A only when internal reach or an allow-list bypass is demonstrated.

D.guide: Attacker-influenced names resolved to resources: filesystem and search paths (D1) and server-side URL fetches (D2). Resolving against the wrong base directory with no attacker is COD-E2B.
D.name: untrusted-path-and-resource-resolution

category_guides.1: SEC-E1B is a version with a published advisory, SEC-E1D an unmaintained dependency with no advisory, SEC-E1C a pinned version with no integrity hash, SEC-E1A an update bot with no cooldown.
category_guides.2: SEC-E2A is an unpinned package or image install, SEC-E2B a mutable CI action ref, SEC-E2C a floating branch of third-party source. Floating scanner rulesets are SEC-G2C.
category_guides.3: SEC-E3A is untrusted build files executed by design, SEC-E3B a binary download with no checksum or signature, SEC-E3C a remote script piped to a shell.

E.guide: Third-party code entering the build or runtime: dependency state (E1), pinning of what is fetched (E2), code executed without verification (E3). Choose E1 for what is resolved, E2 for how it is referenced, E3 for how it is executed.
E.name: supply-chain-and-build-integrity

category_guides.1: SEC-F1A for crashes an attacker can trigger (denial of service). SEC-F1B only when a swallowed exception hides a security-relevant failure; generic swallows are COD-B2C and fail-open controls are ARC-F2E.
category_guides.2: SEC-F2A for an unbounded read of an outbound response that an attacker can influence. Inbound request size and ReDoS are SEC-H4B and SEC-H4A. A missing timeout with an internal or systemic trigger is OPS-A1A.

F.guide: Failures an adversary can trigger with crafted input: unhandled exceptions and security-relevant swallows (F1), and resource exhaustion (F2). Per SCHEMA routing, internally or systemically triggered failures go to OPS, and ordinary error swallowing goes to COD-B2C.
F.name: robustness-under-adversarial-input

category_guides.1: SEC-G1B for an imprecise or inconsistent CWE/classification mapping. Severity-vs-confidence conflation and hardcoded severity are COD-C1A and COD-C1B.
category_guides.2: SEC-G2A is a security surface never routed to the security reviewer, SEC-G2B a scan that silently loses coverage at runtime, SEC-G2C an unpinned remote ruleset.
category_guides.3: SEC-G3B is a missing negative test for a security guard, SEC-G3C a security invariant enforced only by assert, SEC-G3D no vulnerability-disclosure policy. Use ARC-D3B instead of G3D when docs promise a disclosure process that is absent.

G.guide: Integrity of the security tooling itself: triage fidelity (G1), scan coverage (G2), security testing and governance (G3). Use G when the defect makes security review under-report or mis-classify, not when the defect is itself exploitable.
G.name: security-tooling-and-scan-integrity

category_guides.1: SEC-H1A is a session id not rotated at login, SEC-H1B missing cookie flags, SEC-H1C no expiry or invalidation.
category_guides.2: SEC-H2A is missing CSRF protection, SEC-H2B permissive CORS, SEC-H2C an open redirect, SEC-H2D no frame protection.
category_guides.3: SEC-H3A is a JWT algorithm chosen by the token header, SEC-H3C missing exp/aud/iss checks, SEC-H3B an OAuth redirect_uri matching gap (an app-level open redirect is SEC-H2C).
category_guides.4: SEC-H4A is a catastrophic-backtracking regex run on attacker input, SEC-H4B an unbounded inbound body, upload or decompression. Outbound response size is SEC-F2A.

H.guide: Web-application boundaries: session lifecycle (H1), cross-site request controls (H2), token and federation validation (H3), and adversarial request processing (H4: ReDoS and unbounded inbound size, from any entry point, not only browsers). An outbound response read with no bound is SEC-F2A.
H.name: web-session-and-browser-boundary

SEC-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when untrusted or attacker-influenced data is shown to reach a shell or process-argument sink without escaping: a shell=True string, an unquoted shell variable, or concatenated argv that enables option/argument injection (CWE-78/88). A subprocess call flagged by pattern with no dataflow from untrusted input is the LOW heuristic SEC-A1B. Untrusted data evaluated as language code is SEC-A2A. An attacker-controlled build file that executes by design is SEC-E3A.
examples: OS Command Injection via Unquoted Shell Variable
Command Injection via Unquoted Docker Build Arguments
Shell command injection via unescaped fixture paths
Command injection via unsanitized user input to shell
OS command injection via unsanitized shell script construction
SEC-A1A.name: os-command-injection

lower_when.condition: only argument injection (CWE-88) is possible, into a binary with no option that executes code or writes files

raise_when.condition: the injected input is reachable from an unauthenticated network request and the command runs with service or host privileges

SEC-A1B.criteria: Qualifies (LOW) for a pattern-level subprocess hazard with no demonstrated untrusted dataflow, flagged by a rule or a reviewer: shell=True, a partial executable path, string-built argv. When untrusted input is shown to reach the sink, it promotes to SEC-A1A (verify-then-grade, R2). Bare-name resolution through a search path an attacker can write to is SEC-D1B.
examples: subprocess call - check for execution of untrusted input.
Consider possible security implications associated with the subprocess module.
Starting a process with a partial executable path
String Concatenation in Command Argument Construction
Brittle Path Substitution Pattern in Tool Command Construction
SEC-A1B.name: unsafe-subprocess-invocation-pattern

SEC-A2A.criteria: Qualifies when a dynamic code-evaluation sink (eval/exec, Function/new Function, or rendering of attacker-controlled template source; CWE-94/95) receives a value that is not a compile-time constant. The CRITICAL default requires untrusted input shown reaching the sink. A rule or pattern hit with no untrusted dataflow shown qualifies only at the lowered grade (see lower_when) until a heuristic sibling exists. Deserializing untrusted bytes into objects is SEC-A2B; a shell sink is SEC-A1A.
examples: Code injection via eval() with unsanitized user input
Known vulnerable code pattern: eval() with user input
Direct eval() of Unvalidated Command-Line Arguments
Dangerous eval() with user input (CWE-95)
SEC-A2A.name: eval-of-untrusted-input

lower_when.condition: the sink is reachable only by an authenticated non-admin user and evaluation runs in a restricted interpreter (no builtins / isolated VM) with no demonstrated escape
the finding is a rule or pattern hit and no dataflow from an untrusted source to the evaluated value is shown

SEC-A2B.criteria: Qualifies when bytes an attacker can reach are deserialized by a loader that can instantiate arbitrary types or invoke code: pickle, yaml.load without SafeLoader, Java native serialization, BinaryFormatter (CWE-502). A data-only loader (json, yaml.safe_load) on untrusted input is not this code. An XML parser with entity expansion is SEC-A4A; direct eval of strings is SEC-A2A.
examples: Insecure deserialization of untrusted CBOR and YAML input
Known vulnerable code pattern: Unsafe deserialization of untrusted input
SEC-A2B.name: insecure-deserialization-of-untrusted-data

lower_when.condition: the loader enforces an explicit allow-list of instantiable classes (e.g. a Java ObjectInputFilter or a restricted Unpickler.find_class) and no gadget in the allowed set is shown

raise_when.condition: the payload arrives from an unauthenticated network request and the loader executes code directly (pickle, BinaryFormatter) or a gadget chain is present on the classpath

SEC-A3A.criteria: Qualifies when SQL text is built by concatenating or interpolating a non-constant value instead of binding it as a parameter (CWE-89). The CRITICAL default requires untrusted input shown reaching the interpolated value. A rule or pattern hit with no untrusted source shown qualifies only at the lowered grade (see lower_when). Identifier interpolation from a fixed allow-list does not qualify. A slow query is DAT-C1B; an unbounded result set is OPS-D1B; injection into a shell is SEC-A1A.
examples: SQL injection via string concatenation with user input
Known vulnerable code pattern: SQL injection via string concatenation
SEC-A3A.name: sql-injection-via-string-concatenation

lower_when.condition: the injection point is reachable only after authentication and the connection uses a read-only role limited to non-sensitive tables
string-built SQL is flagged by a rule but no untrusted source reaches the interpolated value (internal constants or enum values only)

SEC-A4A.criteria: Qualifies (MEDIUM) when parsing of UNTRUSTED input is demonstrated AND the parser configuration permits external entities/DTD/expansion, or the library in its used configuration is known-vulnerable (CWE-611/776). A bare library import or call flagged by a rule with no dataflow evidence of untrusted input is the LOW heuristic SEC-A4B; if untrusted parsing is shown but entities are disabled, the finding declines to A4B. Verify-then-grade per R2.
SEC-A4A.name: xxe-vulnerable-xml-parsing

raise_when.condition: external-entity resolution is shown to read local files or make outbound requests when fed input from an unauthenticated network source

SEC-A4B.criteria: Qualifies (LOW) on HEURISTIC presence alone — an XML library import or call flagged by a rule with no dataflow evidence that untrusted input reaches it and no confirmation that entity/DTD expansion is enabled. When untrusted-input parsing is demonstrated on an entity-permitting or known-vulnerable configuration, it promotes to SEC-A4A (MEDIUM) per R2.
examples: Using xml.etree.ElementTree to parse untrusted XML data is known to be vulnerable to XML attacks.
XML External Entity (XXE) Injection in XML Parsing
SpotBugs report XML parsed with `xml.etree.ElementTree` instead of a hardened parser
SEC-A4B.name: xml-library-import-flagged

SEC-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when untrusted strings (repo file paths, commit text, finding titles) are interpolated without escaping into markdown that a bot posts automatically to an issue tracker or chat, which allows @-mention pings, link or image injection, or formatting spoofing (CWE-74). Unescaped content in a generated HTML or report file is SEC-B1C. An unsafe URL scheme accepted in rendered links is SEC-B1B.
examples: Scanned-repo file paths flow unescaped into auto-posted GitHub issue comments, enabling markdown/@-mention injection
SEC-B1A.name: markdown-mention-injection-in-automated-comments

lower_when.condition: the comment is posted as a draft or to a holding location that a human reviews before it is published

SEC-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when rendered links or hrefs accept untrusted URLs with no scheme allow-list, so javascript:, data: or vbscript: URLs reach a clickable sink (CWE-79/601). A server endpoint that redirects to an attacker URL is SEC-H2C. General unescaped interpolation into HTML is SEC-B1C.
examples: Unrestricted URL Scheme in Reference Links
SEC-B1B.name: unsafe-url-scheme-allowed-in-links

lower_when.condition: the renderer is not a browser (terminal, PDF, plain-text email) and does not execute script URLs

raise_when.condition: the link renders inside an authenticated web origin, the URL is supplied by a party other than the viewer (stored), and no CSP blocks script URLs, so a javascript: URL runs with the viewer's session

SEC-B1C.criteria: Qualifies when untrusted content (repo-controlled file names, tool output, finding text) is interpolated into a generated artifact (an HTML report, SARIF, markdown, an attribute context) without encoding or neutralization suited to that context, so script or markup is injected when the artifact is viewed (CWE-79/116). Auto-posted tracker comments are SEC-B1A. Unsafe link schemes specifically are SEC-B1B. Untrusted content entering an LLM prompt is AGT-A1B.
examples: Unescaped attribute-context interpolation of finding.evidence.citation_quality enables stored HTML/script injection
Unescaped provenance.confirmation_status enables HTML attribute-injection XSS in generated reports
Untrusted finding text (title/description/impact/remediation) is aggregated with no content neutralization
Repo-controlled file names and messages flow into finding `title`/`location.file`/`description` without control
SEC-B1C.name: untrusted-content-unsanitized-in-generated-output

lower_when.condition: the output format is plain text or JSON consumed only by programs and never rendered as markup

raise_when.condition: the generated artifact is served from an authenticated web origin (dashboard, CI artifact viewer), the injected content is controlled by a party other than the viewer (e.g. a scanned third-party repo), and no CSP prevents inline script

SEC-B1D.criteria: Qualifies when an artifact documented or designed as self-contained or offline fetches remote resources when opened (fonts, scripts, images, analytics), which leaks the viewer's IP and the fact of opening, and contradicts the offline claim (CWE-200). A missing CSP in the same report is SEC-B1E. Untrusted content injected into the report is SEC-B1C.
examples: "Self-contained" HTML report fetches remote Google Fonts on open, contradicting its offline-safety claim
SEC-B1D.name: unintended-external-resource-load-in-offline-report

raise_when.condition: the remote resource is a script, so third-party code runs in the report context with access to its contents

SEC-B1E.criteria: Qualifies when a generated HTML artifact that embeds inline script ships with no Content-Security-Policy, so an injection anywhere in it meets no second line of defence. This is hardening, not an injection: the injection itself is SEC-B1C, remote loads are SEC-B1D, and missing frame protection on a served app is SEC-H2D.
examples: Self-contained HTML report ships an inline <script> with no Content-Security-Policy
SEC-B1E.name: missing-content-security-policy-in-generated-report

raise_when.condition: the same report interpolates untrusted content into HTML (a SEC-B1C sink exists, even if currently encoded)

SEC-B2A.criteria: Qualifies when a debug or diagnostic endpoint or mode that is reachable in a deployed build returns secrets, tokens, or environment values (CWE-215/200). Credentials written to stdout or logs are SEC-B2B. Stack traces or internal detail with no secret in them are SEC-B2D.
examples: Sensitive Token Exposure via Debug Endpoint String Formatting
SEC-B2A.name: debug-endpoint-secret-exposure

lower_when.condition: the exposed values are only the requesting user's own session-scoped token (no service secrets and no other users' data)

raise_when.condition: the endpoint is reachable unauthenticated from the internet and an exposed secret grants production write or admin access

SEC-B2B.criteria: Qualifies when a credential, a token, or a value that carries secrets (including raw subprocess stderr or environment dumps that may contain them) is written to stdout, stderr or logs without redaction (CWE-532). A redaction routine that exists but misses cases is SEC-B2C. Personal data (not credentials) in logs is SEC-B4A. A secret pulled into an AI agent's output or transcript is AGT-D1B. A secret committed to the repository is SEC-B3A.
examples: Hardcoded credentials written directly to standard output
run_tool's F-CAL-1 stderr diagnostic prints raw subprocess stderr with no secret redaction
Unfiltered Stderr Output May Leak Sensitive Information
SEC-B2B.name: credentials-printed-to-output-or-logs

lower_when.condition: the output only might contain secrets (raw stderr passthrough) and no secret-bearing input reaches the process that produces it

raise_when.condition: a live production credential is shown in output that is readable by parties who do not otherwise hold it (public CI logs, a public issue or PR, a log store open to all tenants)

SEC-B2C.criteria: Qualifies when a redaction or masking control EXISTS but misses some sensitive values or forms: a single hardcoded pattern, unmasked alternative encodings, or a path that bypasses the redactor. Sensitive data then leaks despite the control. No redaction at all is SEC-B2B (credentials) or SEC-B4A (personal data). A hardcoded developer path in code or tests with no redaction role is ARC-E1A or TST-E2C.
examples: Public-issue redaction of local absolute paths is a single hardcoded constant that fails open
Test hardcodes the author's local absolute filesystem path instead of computing it dynamically
SEC-B2C.name: incomplete-sensitive-data-redaction

lower_when.condition: the unredacted values are only local absolute paths or the operator's own username, with no credentials or third-party personal data

raise_when.condition: the bypass is shown to publish a live credential to a public sink (public issue, public CI log)

SEC-B2D.criteria: Qualifies when error responses or messages show internal detail to an untrusted caller (stack traces, file paths, SQL text, library versions; CWE-209). The detail helps an attacker but is not itself a secret. Secrets returned by a debug endpoint are SEC-B2A. A response that reveals whether an account exists (account found versus wrong password) is SEC-C2C.
examples: Attempted read of /etc/shadow combined with verbose internal-error disclosure
SEC-B2D.name: verbose-error-message-disclosure

raise_when.condition: the detail is returned to unauthenticated callers and includes internal hostnames/IPs or raw SQL query text (a credential-bearing connection string is SEC-B2A/SEC-B2B instead)

SEC-B3A.criteria: Qualifies (HIGH) when the material is a REAL credential — valid format plus context indicating actual use (a non-placeholder value in production config, a known service-key pattern, or a value verified against the service). Never assign from detector output alone: an unconfirmed pattern/entropy hit (possible-secret, placeholder, fixture, example key) is the LOW SEC-B3C and promotes to B3A only on confirmation (verify-then-grade, R2).
SEC-B3A.name: embedded-credential-or-api-key-in-repo

lower_when.condition: the confirmed credential is scoped read-only to non-sensitive data, or is shown revoked and present only in history

raise_when.condition: the confirmed credential is in a public repository or its history and grants production write, admin, or cloud-account access

SEC-B3B.criteria: Qualifies when a subprocess, especially third-party tooling or tooling that handles untrusted input, is launched with the parent's full environment, so secrets in environment variables (API keys, tokens) are readable by code that does not need them (CWE-200). Printing those values is SEC-B2B. An AI agent's tool grant that exceeds its task is AGT-B1D. Container-level privilege is SEC-C1A.
examples: Shared `run_tool()` subprocess helper inherits the full parent environment for every scanner invocation
SEC-B3B.name: full-environment-inherited-by-subprocess

lower_when.condition: the parent's environment is shown to hold no secrets (a launcher that already strips them, or a CI step with no secret env)

raise_when.condition: the child process runs attacker-controlled code (untrusted build files, plugins from a scanned repo) and the inherited environment holds a live write-scoped credential

SEC-B3C.criteria: Qualifies (LOW) when the evidence is a pattern/entropy DETECTOR hit of unconfirmed validity — possible-secret strings, placeholders, test fixtures, or example keys. When the material is confirmed a real, in-use credential (valid format plus production-use context), it elevates to SEC-B3A (HIGH) per R2.
examples: Possible hardcoded password: 'gate-pass'
Known vulnerable code pattern: Hardcoded secrets in source code
generic-api-key has detected secret for file /src/.env.
SEC-B3C.name: hardcoded-secret-heuristic-flag

SEC-B4A.criteria: Qualifies when personal data (names, emails, addresses, government IDs, health or financial attributes) is written in clear to logs or telemetry (CWE-532/359). Credentials in logs are SEC-B2B. Personal data sent to an LLM provider is AGT-F1A. Over-collection at intake is SEC-B4B.
SEC-B4A.name: pii-in-logs

lower_when.condition: the only personal datum logged is a pseudonymous internal user id or the operator's own identity

raise_when.condition: the logged fields are special-category, financial, or government-identifier data and the logs ship to a store outside the data's access controls

SEC-B4B.criteria: Qualifies when personal data is collected or stored beyond what the stated purpose needs (over-collection at intake). Distinct from SEC-B4C (data kept too long) and SEC-B4D (no path for the subject to access or erase it).
SEC-B4B.name: excessive-data-collection

raise_when.condition: a field collected beyond the stated purpose is special-category data (health, biometrics, government ID)

SEC-B4C.criteria: Qualifies when personal data is kept with no retention window, or with a window that is hardcoded or compile-time and cannot be configured, so the operator cannot bound how long it is kept. Over-collection at intake is SEC-B4B; a missing subject access or erasure path is SEC-B4D. The 0.5.0 widening history belongs in notes, not in criteria.
SEC-B4C.name: missing-retention-limit

raise_when.condition: the data kept without a bound is special-category or financial data

SEC-B4D.criteria: Qualifies when the data model holds a subject's personal data but the product exposes no self-service path for that subject to exercise access, portability (export in a portable form), or erasure (delete or anonymize) — GDPR Art. 15 / 20 / 17. Distinct from SEC-B4B (over-collection) and SEC-B4C (retention window): the data may be minimal and time-bounded and this still qualifies.
examples: The data model holds a subject's personal data but exposes no self-service path for that subject to exercise access / portability (export their own data in a portable form) or erasure (delete or anonymize), so an access/portability/erasure request has no product path
SEC-B4D.name: missing-data-subject-rights-path

SEC-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when a container or sandbox that processes untrusted content has network, filesystem or capability privilege beyond its job, so a compromised workload can exfiltrate data or pivot (CWE-250/1008). Examples: unrestricted egress together with broad read mounts, --privileged, host mounts, added capabilities. Running as root with no other excess is SEC-C1E. An AI agent's tool grant is AGT-B1C or AGT-B1D. Ambient CLI credentials used by a script are SEC-C1D.
examples: Scan container combines full read access to the target repository with unrestricted scan-time network egress
SEC-C1A.name: excessive-container-network-and-filesystem-privilege

lower_when.condition: the container runs only first-party tooling on first-party input (no untrusted code executes inside it), or only one kind of excess (egress or broad mounts, not both) is present

SEC-C1B.criteria: Qualifies when code contains a hidden trigger (a magic input string, hardcoded user, secret header or flag) that bypasses authentication or authorization or enables privileged behaviour (CWE-506/489). A leftover debug endpoint that returns secrets is SEC-B2A. A check that is simply missing, with no trigger, is SEC-C1C.
examples: Hidden backdoor trigger activated by a magic input string
SEC-C1B.name: hardcoded-backdoor-trigger

raise_when.condition: the trigger is reachable from unauthenticated network input and grants admin rights or code execution

SEC-C1C.criteria: Qualifies when an operation, route or function that requires a role or permission can be invoked without that check (CWE-862/285), so any authenticated or anonymous caller can run it. A missing per-record ownership check on an otherwise authorized operation is SEC-C1F. Sibling scripts that gate inconsistently are ARC-F1C. A shared guard that grants too broad a scope is COD-B1C.
examples: Missing authorization check allows any caller to retrieve admin-only data
SEC-C1C.name: missing-function-level-authorization

lower_when.condition: the unguarded operation is read-only and returns only non-sensitive data

raise_when.condition: the unguarded operation is reachable unauthenticated and changes or exports other users' data, or grants admin rights

SEC-C1D.criteria: Qualifies when code changes an external system through ambient credentials or context (the current gh, aws or kubectl context, a repo derived from the cwd) without pinning the target, so it can act on an unintended repo, account or tenant (CWE-284). When the finding is that sibling scripts gate or pin inconsistently, it is ARC-F1C. A write-capable tool granted to an AI agent without scope is AGT-B1C. A container with excess privilege is SEC-C1A.
examples: triage.py mutates GitHub issues via ambient `gh` repo context with no explicit repo pinning
SEC-C1D.name: ambient-authority-unscoped-mutation

lower_when.condition: the mutation is limited to non-destructive annotations (labels) carrying no repository content

raise_when.condition: the mis-targeted mutation is destructive (delete, force-push, permission change) and the ambient context can be set by an attacker (cwd inside an untrusted checkout)

SEC-C1E.criteria: Qualifies when a container image or process runs as root without need (no USER drop; CWE-250) and no other privilege excess is shown. Root combined with egress, host mounts or privileged flags is SEC-C1A.
examples: Fixtures image never drops root privileges before running third-party build tooling
SEC-C1E.name: container-runs-as-root

raise_when.condition: the root process runs untrusted third-party code (build tooling run on scanned or user-supplied input)

SEC-C1F.criteria: Qualifies when the caller is authorized for the operation but the code never verifies the caller owns the specific object/record it acts on (OWASP API1 BOLA, CWE-639/566) — a per-record ownership comparison is missing. Distinct from SEC-C1C missing-function-level-authorization (CWE-862/285), which is whether the caller may invoke the operation at all; the fixes differ (a per-record ownership check vs a route/function guard). A finding citing both should be split, one to each.
examples: BursarBuddy BB-0002: a profile endpoint authenticates the session but never compares the session id to the requested id, so any user reads another user's PII. Proof: proofs/test_bb_0002_profile_idor.py (passing).
SEC-C1F.name: missing-object-level-authorization

lower_when.condition: the operation is read-only and object identifiers are unguessable (128-bit random) and never shown to other users

raise_when.condition: object identifiers are sequential or guessable and the operation changes or deletes another user's record

SEC-C2A.criteria: Qualifies when an authentication endpoint lacks throttling/lockout/backoff against repeated attempts (CWE-307), regardless of how the credential comparison is implemented. The non-constant-time comparison half of the same finding is SEC-C2B; a finding citing both defects should be split, one to each.
examples: Authentication routine has no brute-force protection
SEC-C2A.name: missing-brute-force-protection

lower_when.condition: the credential checked is a high-entropy machine token (at least 128 bits), so online guessing is infeasible

raise_when.condition: the guessed secret is a short code (PIN, OTP, reset code; about 6 digits or fewer) whose full space can be tried online within its validity window at the unthrottled request rate

SEC-C2B.criteria: Qualifies when a credential/token comparison short-circuits on first difference (==, early-exit loop) instead of a constant-time compare (hmac.compare_digest or equivalent), regardless of rate limiting (CWE-208). The missing-rate-limit half of the same finding is SEC-C2A; split a finding that cites both.
examples: Authentication routine uses a non-constant-time comparison
SEC-C2B.name: timing-unsafe-credential-comparison

lower_when.condition: the compared values are a digest or keyed hash of the secret, not the raw secret

SEC-C2C.criteria: Qualifies when an observable response discrepancy (status code, message, or timing) lets an attacker classify whether an identifier (email, username) exists — CWE-203/204/205. The response oracle is the defect, independent of any brute-force protection (SEC-C2A) on the same endpoint.
examples: BursarBuddy BB-0003: login returns 404 "No account found with that email" versus 401 "Incorrect password", classifying any address in one request. Proof: proofs/test_bb_0003_user_enumeration.py (passing).
BursarBuddy BB-0004: signup returns 409 "That email is already registered" versus 201, the same oracle on a different route. Proof: proofs/test_bb_0004_signup_enumeration.py (passing).
SEC-C2C.name: user-enumeration-via-response-discrepancy

lower_when.condition: the identifiers being classified are already public by design (public usernames or profile handles)

SEC-C3A.criteria: Qualifies when a non-cryptographic PRNG (Math.random, random.Random, an LCG, a time-seeded generator) generates a security value: a session token, reset code, CSRF token, key or nonce (CWE-338). A weak hash or cipher algorithm is SEC-C3B. A non-cryptographic checksum used as a hash is SEC-C3C. Unseeded randomness in tests is TST-F1D.
examples: Predictable security token generated from a hand-rolled LCG seeded by wall-clock time
Known vulnerable code pattern: Random() class for token generation
SEC-C3A.name: weak-prng-for-security-token

lower_when.condition: the value is single-use, expires within minutes, and the attacker cannot observe any other output of the same generator

SEC-C3B.criteria: Qualifies when a standard but broken or deprecated algorithm or mode protects a security property: MD5/SHA-1 for signatures or password hashing, a fast unsalted hash for passwords, DES/RC4, ECB mode, RSA without padding (CWE-327). A hand-rolled or non-cryptographic checksum is SEC-C3C. Weak randomness is SEC-C3A. A JWT algorithm chosen by the token is SEC-H3A.
SEC-C3B.name: weak-standard-crypto-algorithm

lower_when.condition: the weak hash is used only inside an HMAC construction (e.g. HMAC-SHA1, HMAC-MD5), where collision resistance is not relied on

SEC-C3C.criteria: Qualifies when a non-cryptographic checksum or ad-hoc hash (CRC32, Adler, the language's hash(), a sum of bytes, an unsalted custom digest) is used where a security property depends on it: integrity checks, deduplication of untrusted content, password storage (CWE-328). A standard but broken algorithm (MD5, SHA-1) is SEC-C3B.
examples: Ad-hoc, unsalted, non-cryptographic checksum used in place of a real hash function
SEC-C3C.name: non-cryptographic-hash-in-security-context

lower_when.condition: the checksum guards only against accidental corruption of first-party data, and no decision an attacker could exploit depends on it

raise_when.condition: the checksum is how stored passwords are hashed, or it is the only integrity check on downloaded executable code fetched over plain HTTP or with TLS verification disabled

SEC-C4B.criteria: Qualifies when a sensitive action (fund transfer, privilege change, data export, deletion) executes with no audit record written at all. If the record IS written but can later be destroyed through the channel it audits, that is SEC-C4C, not this code.
examples: Sensitive fund-transfer action executes with no audit logging
SEC-C4B.name: missing-audit-logging-for-sensitive-action

raise_when.condition: the unaudited action moves money or changes privileges, and the repository's own stated policy or compliance scope requires an audit trail

SEC-C4C.criteria: Qualifies when audit records are destroyed or orphaned through the same channel they audit — a CASCADE from the audited row (e.g. LogEntry.user) wipes the actor's trail on account deletion, or a bulk-deletion workflow purges history — with no append-only store or tamper protection. The log is written, then lost. Distinct from SEC-C4B, where no record is written.
examples: Audit records are destroyed or orphaned through the same channel they audit — a LogEntry.user CASCADE wipes a user's admin-action trail on account deletion, or a bulk-deletion workflow purges Version/Communication/Comment history — with no append-only or tamper protection. (The log IS written, then destroyed; distinct from SEC-C4B missing-audit-logging.)
SEC-C4C.name: audit-trail-not-durable-destroyed-by-deletion

SEC-D1A.criteria: Qualifies when an attacker-influenced path component (a request parameter, an archive entry name, a path controlled by a repo) is joined to a base directory and read or written with no canonicalize-and-contain check, so it escapes the intended root (CWE-22, zip-slip included). Following a symlink planted inside the tree is SEC-D1C. Resolving against the wrong base with no attacker is COD-E2B. A path from an operator-set environment variable falls under the operator-controlled-input modifier.
examples: Path Traversal via Unvalidated FIXTURE_ROOT Environment Variable
Path traversal via unsanitized file path
Known vulnerable code pattern: Path traversal via unsanitized file path
SEC-D1A.name: path-traversal-via-unvalidated-input

lower_when.condition: the escape is read-only and can reach only a directory shown to hold no secrets or other users' data

raise_when.condition: the traversal writes or overwrites files (code, config) from unauthenticated network input

SEC-D1B.criteria: Qualifies when a binary, module or plugin is resolved through a search path (PATH, NODE_PATH, sys.path, the cwd, project-relative plugin directories) that includes a location an attacker can write or supply, for example a tool run on an untrusted checkout that loads plugins from it (CWE-426/427). Bare-name invocation under a trusted PATH is the SEC-A1B heuristic. A sys.path edit made for import convenience, with no attacker-writable element, is QAL-F1A or ARC-A2C. Picking the wrong file by heuristic is COD-C2A.
examples: NODE_PATH inheritance allows plugin hijacking despite cwd defense
eslint-security's own code comment confirms plugin resolution is project-root-relative
Unsafe sys.path Manipulation
Silent Selection of First Alphabetically Sorted Requirements File
External tool binaries (`git`, `gh`, `codex`, `docker`) are invoked by bare name, relying on `$PATH` resolution
SEC-D1B.name: uncontrolled-search-path-element

lower_when.condition: planting needs local write access to a shared-host directory on the path, and the location cannot be supplied through repository or request content

SEC-D1C.criteria: Qualifies when code that copies, archives, reads or deletes an untrusted directory tree follows symlinks (copytree with default symlink handling, tar extraction, recursive reads), so a planted link can read or write outside the tree (CWE-59/61). A path string that escapes via ../ is SEC-D1A.
examples: shutil.copytree dereferences symlinks in the scanned target before building it
Unguarded `shutil.copytree(target, tmp, dirs_exist_ok=True)` dereferences attacker-controlled symlinks
Unvalidated Directory Copy Operation Before Analysis
SEC-D1C.name: unsafe-symlink-following-on-copy

lower_when.condition: following the link only reads, and the copied content is never published, uploaded or returned to the attacker

SEC-D2A.criteria: Qualifies (HIGH) only when server-side URL fetching is DEMONSTRATED to reach internal targets — loopback/link-local, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), RFC1918 services — or an existing allow-list is bypassable (DNS rebinding, redirect laundering, alternate IP encodings). Absent demonstrated internal reachability, a user-influenced fetch without allow-listing is the LOW precursor SEC-D2B. Elevation rule (R2): demonstrated internal reach or bypass promotes D2B to D2A.
SEC-D2A.name: server-side-request-forgery-to-internal-service

raise_when.condition: the fetch reaches a cloud metadata credential endpoint (or an unauthenticated internal admin API) from unauthenticated input

SEC-D2B.criteria: Qualifies (LOW) when a URL/feed/webhook target is user-influenced and fetched without scheme/host allow-listing, with NO demonstrated internal reachability — a latent SSRF precursor. Once a fetch is shown to reach loopback/link-local/metadata/RFC1918 or bypass an allow-list, it elevates to SEC-D2A (HIGH) per R2.
examples: User-controlled URL dispatch pattern without allow-listing (latent SSRF precursor)
SEC-D2B.name: unvalidated-url-fetch-target-ssrf-precursor

SEC-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when an automated dependency-update bot (Dependabot, Renovate, or similar) is set to propose newly published versions with no minimum age or cooldown, so a freshly published malicious release can be merged before it is detected (CWE-1357). A version that is outdated and has a known advisory is SEC-E1B. An unpinned install in a build is SEC-E2A.
examples: This Dependabot configuration does not set a cooldown period. Newly published packages can be malicious.
SEC-E1A.name: dependabot-missing-cooldown-period

lower_when.condition: auto-merge is disabled for bot PRs, so every update gets human review before it merges

SEC-E1B.criteria: Qualifies when a resolved dependency version is covered by a published advisory (CVE, GHSA, RUSTSEC) for the version range in use (CWE-1104). An unmaintained dependency with no advisory is SEC-E1D. A version that is unpinned and could drift is SEC-E2A.
examples: requests 2.25.1: GHSA-9hjg-9r4m-mvj7
lodash 4.17.20: GHSA-35jh-r3h4-6jhm
Known vulnerable dependency: serde_yaml 0.8.25 with RUSTSEC-2024-0327
Package: lodash Installed Version: 4.17.20 Vulnerability CVE-2021-23337 Severity: HIGH Fixed Version: 4.17.21
Known vulnerable dependency: regex 1.4.0 with RUSTSEC-2022-0013
SEC-E1B.name: known-vulnerable-dependency

lower_when.condition: the advisory's affected function or feature is shown not to be used by this codebase

raise_when.condition: the vulnerable function is shown reachable from untrusted input in this codebase and the advisory is rated high or critical
the advisory is on a known-exploited list (e.g. CISA KEV) and the vulnerable path is reachable unauthenticated

SEC-E1C.criteria: Qualifies when a lockfile or requirements file pins versions but has no integrity hashes (legacy lockfile formats, pip requirements without --hash), so a compromised registry or mirror can substitute content (CWE-494). No version pinning at all is SEC-E2A. A direct binary download with no verification is SEC-E3B.
examples: Legacy lockfileVersion 1 lockfile carries no subresource-integrity hash for its dependency
SEC-E1C.name: missing-lockfile-integrity-hash

SEC-E1D.criteria: Qualifies when a dependency is unmaintained and has no known advisory: the repository is archived, there has been no release or response to security reports for a long period, or OpenSSF Scorecard flags it on maintenance. A dependency with a published advisory is SEC-E1B.
SEC-E1D.name: abandoned-unmaintained-dependency

raise_when.condition: the unmaintained dependency parses untrusted input or implements crypto or auth on a production path

SEC-E2A.criteria: Qualifies when a build, CI or image step installs a package or base image by name or by a floating tag with no version or digest pin (pip install x, npm i -g x, FROM image:latest), so the build runs whatever is current (CWE-1357/829). A mutable CI action ref is SEC-E2B. A floating git branch of third-party source is SEC-E2C. Versions pinned without integrity hashes are SEC-E1C.
examples: Unversioned pip package installs enable known vulnerability injection
Unversioned cargo-audit installation enables known vulnerability injection
Unversioned npm package installs enable known vulnerability injection
Base Docker image uses version tag without digest, allowing known vulnerabilities in base layers
SEC-E2A.name: unpinned-build-dependency-install

lower_when.condition: the step runs in a job that holds no secrets and its output is not shipped in a release artifact, or the floating reference is a version tag rather than latest/no version

SEC-E2B.criteria: Qualifies when a CI workflow references a third-party action or reusable workflow by a mutable tag or branch instead of a full commit SHA, so a repointed tag runs new code with the job's token and secrets (CWE-829). Scoping of workflow token permissions is ARC-C1E. Unpinned package installs inside steps are SEC-E2A.
examples: GitHub Actions step uses a mutable tag or branch reference. Tags and branch names can be silently repointed.
GitHub Actions pinned to mutable version tags, not immutable commit SHAs
Third-party GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags in a workflow holding write-scoped tokens
SEC-E2B.name: mutable-ci-action-reference

lower_when.condition: the action is published by the same organization, or the job has a read-only token and no secrets

SEC-E2C.criteria: Qualifies when third-party source (a git repo, submodule or fixture project) is fetched by a floating branch or HEAD instead of a commit SHA and is then built or executed. Package installs are SEC-E2A, CI actions SEC-E2B, scanner rulesets SEC-G2C.
examples: Fixture repos RailsGoat and AspGoat default to the floating `main` branch instead of a pinned ref, and are built
Fixture image builds from unpinned mutable git branches of third-party repositories
Fixture manifest drives supply-chain-unsafe, unpinned third-party code execution during image build
SEC-E2C.name: unpinned-third-party-source-reference

SEC-E3A.criteria: Qualifies when a tool runs a build or configure step on untrusted input whose build files execute code by design (MSBuild targets, setup.py, Makefiles, npm lifecycle scripts, Gradle), which gives arbitrary code execution as the tool's user (CWE-94/829). Command injection through a string-built shell is SEC-A1A. A curl-pipe-shell of a vendor installer is SEC-E3C.
examples: MSBuild Target Injection with Runtime Command Execution
MSBuild <Exec> target performs unrestricted network egress and filesystem write on every build
roslyn-secguard runs `dotnet build` on scanned code, executing arbitrary MSBuild targets/NuGet package content
roslyn-secguard adapter executes untrusted target source via `dotnet build`
SEC-E3A.name: arbitrary-code-execution-via-untrusted-build-file

SEC-E3B.criteria: Qualifies when a binary, archive, plugin or signing key is downloaded and installed or run with no checksum or signature verification (CWE-494/345). Piping a remote script straight into a shell is SEC-E3C. Missing lockfile hashes for package-manager installs is SEC-E1C.
examples: FindSecBugs SpotBugs plugin fetched from an unauthenticated scrape URL with no checksum/signature verification
Scanner toolchain binaries and the Trivy apt signing key are downloaded with no checksum or signature verification
Static-analysis tool binaries fetched from GitHub Releases / Maven Central without checksum or signature verification
Docker scanner-tool image installs unpinned packages and unverified remote binaries with no integrity checks
SEC-E3B.name: unverified-binary-download-no-integrity-check

raise_when.condition: the download is over plain HTTP or with TLS verification disabled (curl -k, verify=False), so an on-path attacker can substitute the content

SEC-E3C.criteria: Qualifies when a remote script is fetched and run in one step (curl | sh, iwr | iex) with no checksum or signature check on its content; a version-pinned URL alone does not verify the content. Downloading a binary and then running it unverified is SEC-E3B.
examples: Piping remote script to shell (Rustup installer)
Piping remote script to shell (.NET SDK installer)
Unverified curl-pipe-to-shell installers execute remote code during panopticon-tools image build
Dockerfile.fixtures pipes dotnet-install.sh into bash without version pin or verification
SEC-E3C.name: unverified-remote-script-execution-curl-pipe-shell

lower_when.condition: the script URL is pinned to an immutable version on the vendor's HTTPS origin

raise_when.condition: the script is fetched over plain HTTP or with TLS verification disabled (curl -k)

SEC-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when attacker-influenced input can raise an unhandled exception or panic that ends the process or request worker, a denial of service (CWE-248/755). The input must come from an untrusted party: a network payload, an uploaded file, or content of a scanned target. Tool output counts only when the malformed part is shown to come from that target's content. A crash on internal data or on a trusted tool's malformed output is COD-B2A. A component that silently skips malformed input is ARC-F2D. The missing test for malformed input is TST-A2D.
examples: Unhandled ValueError in line number conversion from XML attributes
Unguarded XML Parsing Causes Crash on Malformed Output
Unguarded JSON Parsing in CargoAuditAdapter Causes Crash
Unguarded JSON Parsing in NpmAuditAdapter Causes Crash
Unhandled panics on attacker-influenced input crash the process (denial of service)
`RoslynSecGuardAdapter.is_applicable()` raises an unhandled exception on a missing/inaccessible target directory
SEC-F1A.name: crash-on-malformed-input

lower_when.condition: the crash aborts only the single CLI run or request that supplied the input, with a clear error, and no shared worker or other user is affected

raise_when.condition: a single unauthenticated request kills a long-lived shared service process that no supervisor restarts

SEC-F1B.criteria: Qualifies ONLY when the swallowed exception hides a SECURITY-relevant failure (an auth/permission/verification error silently dropped). A generic swallow with no security consequence single-homes at COD-B2C — do not route ordinary error-swallowing here (it inflates the security lens). A security/enforcement CONTROL that degrades to permit is ARC-F2E.
examples: An auth or permission check's verification error is caught and swallowed, so a request that should be rejected proceeds authorized
A signature or token-validation exception is silently discarded, so an invalid signature is treated as valid
SEC-F1B.name: silent-exception-swallowing

raise_when.condition: the swallowed failure silently skips a signature or integrity verification and the unverified content is then accepted (no access is granted)
the swallowed error comes from an authentication, authorization or signature check and execution goes on as if the check passed (a bypass is shown)

SEC-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when a response from an external server an attacker can influence is read wholly into memory with no size cap (response.read(), .json() on an unbounded body), so a hostile or compromised endpoint can exhaust memory (CWE-400/770). A missing timeout on the call is OPS-A1A. An inbound request body with no size limit is SEC-H4B. A persisted file read whole is DAT-F2B. Internal capacity overload is OPS-D1A.
examples: Unbounded Response Size in External API Lookup
SEC-F2A.name: unbounded-external-response-read

SEC-G1B.criteria: Qualifies when security tooling or a rule mapping cites an imprecise or inconsistent CWE or classification for a finding (equivalent patterns mapped to different CWEs, a parent CWE where a child applies), which degrades triage and trend fidelity. Severity hardcoded so that it ignores the tool's value is COD-C1B. Confidence conflated with severity is COD-C1A.
examples: Brakeman 'Dangerous Eval' maps to CWE-94 while the equivalent JS eval pattern maps to the more precise CWE-95
SEC-G1B.name: tool-citation-cwe-mismatch

lower_when.condition: both cited CWEs are in the same lineage (parent and child) and either is defensible; only precision differs

SEC-G2A.criteria: Qualifies when a review or scan pipeline detects a security-relevant surface (secrets config, auth code, concurrency) but never routes it to the security reviewer or lens, so that surface gets no security review at all. A tool that silently drops coverage at runtime is SEC-G2B. General asymmetric coverage across non-security domains is ARC-E3B.
examples: scout.md defines secrets_config as a detectable surface but never routes it (or concurrency-surfaced files) to the security panel/lens
SEC-G2A.name: security-surface-not-routed-to-review-lens

lower_when.condition: the unrouted surface is still covered by a deterministic security scanner in the same run; only the agentic lens misses it

SEC-G2B.criteria: Qualifies when a DETECTION or SCAN tool silently loses coverage — no-ops on missing inputs, falls back to a stale ruleset/DB, discards stderr, or drops findings — so the review under-reports with no signal. The harm is missed findings, not a permitted action: a security/enforcement control that fails open is ARC-F2E; a general component that skips malformed input is ARC-F2D.
examples: SpotBugs adapter silently no-ops (zero findings, exit 0) when compiled classes are absent
dependency-check silently falls back to a stale, unrefreshed vulnerability DB when NVD_API_KEY is unset
Tool/adapter stderr is silently discarded whenever the process exits 0/1, hiding scan failures
Fixture-noise suppression exists only for tool/SARIF findings, not for LLM agent (lens_sweep/panel_review) findings
bandit noise suppression drops B101 project-wide and all findings under any path that merely looks like a test
SEC-G2B.name: silent-scan-coverage-loss

raise_when.condition: the scan that loses coverage feeds a CI gate that reports PASS while scanning nothing

SEC-G2C.criteria: Qualifies when a security scanner loads a remote or floating ruleset or vulnerability DB (semgrep --config auto, unpinned rule packs), so results cannot be reproduced and the scan may send telemetry. A stale-DB fallback that silently loses coverage is SEC-G2B. Unpinned third-party source that is built or executed is SEC-E2C.
examples: Semgrep invocation uses `--config auto` without `--metrics=off`, introducing an unpinned remote ruleset
SEC-G2C.name: unpinned-scan-ruleset

raise_when.condition: the floating ruleset is fetched with metrics/telemetry on and uploads metadata about a private codebase

SEC-G3B.criteria: Qualifies when a security guard or control (a sandbox trigger, a fail-closed gate, a confinement check, parser hardening) has no negative or adversarial test proving it rejects the attack input it exists for. General untested malformed-input paths are TST-A2D. A security path that is unit-tested but never tested end to end is TST-G3E. A guard enforced only by assert is SEC-G3C.
examples: test_roslyn_secguard.py has no is_applicable() test, leaving the trigger for the dotnet-build RCE surface
SpotBugs adapter test suite has no coverage for malformed/adversarial XML (entity-expansion DoS, CWE-776)
No test drives dispatch's fail-closed unenforced-reviewer gate through main() with a MIXED-enforcement plan
Write-guard hook test suite never exercises non-string tool_input.file_path, hiding an uncaught TypeError
meta.parts confinement test covers relative traversal only, not an absolute-path escape
SEC-G3B.name: insufficient-negative-test-coverage-for-security-guard

raise_when.condition: the untested guard is the only control in front of a sink graded HIGH or CRITICAL in this catalog (code execution, path escape)

SEC-G3C.criteria: Qualifies when a security invariant in production code is enforced only by assert (stripped under python -O, disabled in release/NDEBUG builds), so the check disappears in optimized runs (CWE-617). Asserts in test code do not qualify. A policy that is stated but not enforced in code at all is ARC-F1E.
examples: Security-ordering invariants in TestPanelPriority are checked with bare `assert`, which `python -O` silently strips
SEC-G3C.name: security-invariant-enforced-only-via-assert

raise_when.condition: the production deployment is shown to run optimized (python -O, PYTHONOPTIMIZE set, NDEBUG release build), so the check is absent today

SEC-G3D.criteria: Qualifies when a project that ships software has no vulnerability-disclosure policy (a SECURITY.md or equivalent contact and process). When documentation promises a disclosure process whose backing file is absent, that is the doc-versus-repo gap ARC-D3B; cite one code, not both.
examples: No SECURITY.md backing the vulnerability-disclosure instruction
SEC-G3D.name: missing-vulnerability-disclosure-policy

SEC-H1A.criteria: Qualifies when the session identifier is not regenerated on authentication or privilege change, so a pre-set id that an attacker planted becomes authenticated (CWE-384). Missing cookie flags are SEC-H1B. No idle or absolute expiry is SEC-H1C.
SEC-H1A.name: session-fixation

lower_when.condition: the framework rejects session ids supplied from outside (no URL or adoption of unknown ids), so planting one needs a separate XSS or subdomain foothold

SEC-H1B.criteria: Qualifies when a session or auth cookie lacks Secure, HttpOnly, or a suitable SameSite attribute (CWE-614/1004). Missing CSRF tokens are SEC-H2A, where SameSite is a compensating control. Missing expiry is SEC-H1C.
SEC-H1B.name: missing-secure-cookie-flags

lower_when.condition: the only missing attribute is Secure on a host served solely over HTTPS with HSTS preload, or the only missing attribute is SameSite and token-based CSRF protection is present

SEC-H1C.criteria: Qualifies when server-side sessions or refresh tokens have no idle or absolute timeout, or are not invalidated on logout or password change (CWE-613). JWT exp/aud not being validated is SEC-H3C. Fixation is SEC-H1A.
SEC-H1C.name: missing-session-expiry

lower_when.condition: an idle timeout and logout invalidation exist and only the absolute lifetime cap is missing

SEC-H2A.criteria: Qualifies when a state-changing endpoint authenticated by ambient credentials (cookies) accepts cross-site requests with no anti-CSRF token, origin check, or SameSite protection (CWE-352), including a missing OAuth state parameter. A permissive CORS policy is SEC-H2B. A cookie missing SameSite on its own is SEC-H1B.
SEC-H2A.name: csrf-missing-token-protection

lower_when.condition: the forgeable state change is limited to non-sensitive user preferences (no credentials, payments, permissions, or data deletion)

SEC-H2B.criteria: Qualifies when a CORS policy reflects arbitrary origins, allows null, or uses wildcard or regex origins together with credentials, so a hostile site can read authenticated responses (CWE-942). Missing CSRF protection is SEC-H2A.
SEC-H2B.name: cors-misconfiguration

lower_when.condition: the permissive policy covers only unauthenticated, public, read-only endpoints and credentials are not allowed

raise_when.condition: an arbitrary origin is reflected together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true on endpoints that return user data

SEC-H2C.criteria: Qualifies when a server endpoint redirects to a URL taken from request input with no allow-list (CWE-601). An OAuth redirect_uri validation gap is SEC-H3B. A javascript: link in rendered content is SEC-B1B. A redirect used to launder an SSRF fetch is cited at SEC-D2A.
SEC-H2C.name: open-redirect

raise_when.condition: the redirect carries tokens, codes, or session material in the URL to the host the attacker chose

SEC-H2D.criteria: Qualifies when a served page with state-changing UI sends neither X-Frame-Options nor a CSP frame-ancestors directive (CWE-1021). A missing CSP in a static generated report is SEC-B1E.
SEC-H2D.name: missing-frame-protection-clickjacking

raise_when.condition: the frameable page performs a sensitive one-click action (payment, permission grant, account deletion)

SEC-H3A.criteria: Qualifies when JWT verification accepts the algorithm from the token header (alg=none, or HS256 verified with an RSA public key used as the HMAC secret) instead of an algorithm pinned on the server (CWE-347). Missing exp/aud/iss checks are SEC-H3C.
SEC-H3A.name: jwt-algorithm-confusion

raise_when.condition: alg=none or key confusion is accepted on tokens that authenticate internet-facing requests (forgery needs no key)

SEC-H3B.criteria: Qualifies when an OAuth/OIDC authorization server or client matches redirect_uri by prefix, substring or wildcard, or skips matching against the registration, so authorization codes or tokens can be delivered to an attacker's host (CWE-601). A general application open redirect is SEC-H2C. A missing OAuth state parameter is SEC-H2A.
SEC-H3B.name: oauth-redirect-uri-validation-gap

lower_when.condition: PKCE is enforced for every client and no response type that returns tokens in the redirect (implicit or hybrid flow) is enabled, so an intercepted redirect yields only an unredeemable code

SEC-H3C.criteria: Qualifies when JWT validation skips the exp/nbf, audience or issuer checks, so expired tokens, or tokens minted for another service, are accepted (CWE-613). Accepting an algorithm chosen by the header is SEC-H3A. Server-side session expiry is SEC-H1C.
SEC-H3C.name: jwt-missing-expiry-or-audience-validation

raise_when.condition: the audience is unchecked and the same issuer and key sign tokens for other services or tenants, so cross-service replay is possible

SEC-H4A.criteria: Qualifies when a regex with nested or overlapping quantifiers (catastrophic backtracking) runs on attacker-controlled input with a backtracking engine (CWE-1333). A regex that rejects valid input is COD-C2C. Unbounded input size alone is SEC-H4B.
SEC-H4A.name: redos-catastrophic-backtracking

lower_when.condition: the measured worst-case match time at the enforced maximum input length is under about 100 ms (e.g. polynomial-only backtracking with a tight length cap)

raise_when.condition: a single unauthenticated request is measured to block a worker past the service's request timeout, and no per-match timeout exists, so a few concurrent requests exhaust the worker pool

SEC-H4B.criteria: Qualifies when an inbound request body, upload, header or decompressed payload is accepted with no size limit, so an attacker can exhaust memory or disk (CWE-400; zip and gzip bombs included). An outbound response read with no bound is SEC-F2A. Internal load or capacity is OPS-D1A. A persisted file read whole is DAT-F2B.
SEC-H4B.name: unbounded-request-size

raise_when.condition: the payload is decompressed with no size or ratio limit on an unauthenticated endpoint (a decompression bomb is possible)

SEC.guide: SEC covers defects an adversary or untrusted input can exploit, or that weaken a security boundary or the security tooling that guards it. Choose SEC when the harm needs an attacker or untrusted input. With no adversary, a wrong result is COD and an internal or systemic capacity or timeout failure is OPS (SCHEMA OPS/SEC rule). A security control that degrades to permit on missing or malformed config is ARC-F2E, agent tool grants and prompt injection are AGT, and a generic missing test is TST. Start from the area that matches the sink: A injection, B output and data exposure, C identity/access/crypto/audit, D path and URL resolution, E supply chain, F adversarial-input robustness, G security tooling and scan integrity, H web session and request boundaries.
SEC.name: security

category_guides.1: Whole units with no test: a script (TST-A1A), a function or method (TST-A1B), a function that persists or recovers durable state (TST-A1C), or CLI flag/entrypoint wiring (TST-A1D). Choose TST-A1C over TST-A1B only when the untested unit writes or restores durable state. A single untested branch, error handler or default arm inside a tested unit is A2 (TST-A2B/TST-A2C), even when it is reported as 'untested function'.
category_guides.2: Unexercised branches inside a tested unit: error handlers (TST-A2B), fallback/default arms (TST-A2C), malformed or boundary input (TST-A2D), enum/mapping arms beyond one case (TST-A2E), the false side of a boolean gate (TST-A2F), and registry-wide invariants that new members escape (TST-A2A). TST-A2C is easily confused with TST-A2B (default vs error path), and TST-A2E with TST-A3C (mapping arms vs scenario combinations). An untested exit-code remap is currently TST-G3A, the narrow form of TST-A2B. An untested negative path of a security guard is SEC-G3B.
category_guides.3: Tests exist but in unrealistic scenarios: the integration path is only mocked (TST-A3A), a planted fixture's expected detection is never asserted (TST-A3B), or only a sliver of the supported configuration matrix runs (TST-A3C). A security-critical path tested only in-process is TST-G3E; CI never running the integration tests is ARC-C1C.
category_guides.4: Test tooling that trusts its inputs: subprocess output consumed without checking format or success (TST-A4A), tool/fixture output never validated against a schema (TST-A4B), and fixture-presence checks that silently skip (TST-A4C). TST-A4C vs TST-E1A is silence vs a loud-but-misleading I/O error; TST-A4B vs TST-G3D is output schema vs hand-built fixture shape.

A.guide: Coverage: behaviour or paths that no test exercises. Use A1 when a whole unit (script, function, entrypoint) has no test, A2 when a tested unit has an unexercised branch, A3 when tests exist but only in mocked or narrow scenarios, and A4 when test tooling consumes tool or fixture output without validating it.
