If a test exists but its assertion is weak, go to area B instead.
A.name: coverage

category_guides.1: Real but insufficient assertions: wrong property (TST-B1A), substring instead of structure (TST-B1B), presence/truthiness only (TST-B1C), mock called but key argument unchecked (TST-B1D), no positive assertion at all (TST-B1E), and a universal invariant checked on one example (TST-B1F). TST-B1C vs TST-B1E vs TST-B1A is the common confusion; TST-G3F is the residual.
category_guides.2: Assertions that cannot fail or verify nothing: tautologies (TST-B2A), tests whose every environment branch is vacuous (TST-B2B), loops that assert on only some iterations (TST-B2C), and assertions whose logic is inverted (TST-B2D). TST-B2B vs TST-F1B: B2B passes without checking anything, F1B skips.
category_guides.3: Fragile or gameable assertions: index lookups that raise instead of failing cleanly (TST-B3A), and golden snapshots with no regeneration or provenance discipline, which can be 'fixed' by editing the expected file (TST-B3B). A substring check on stringified output is TST-B1B. Hand-built fixtures never validated against an authoritative schema are TST-G3D.

B.guide: Assertion quality: a test runs the code but its assertions would not fail on a real regression. Use B1 for assertions that are real but insufficient, B2 for assertions that cannot fail or cover nothing, B3 for assertions that fail for the wrong reason or can be satisfied by editing the expectation. TST-G3F is the residual weak-assertion code when no B code fits.
B.name: assertion-quality

category_guides.1: Tests that exist but are never collected: defined after a `__main__` guard (TST-C1A) or outside the runner's discovery pattern (TST-C1B). Production code after a misplaced guard is COD-E2A. A misplaced guard after which every test is still collected by the project's supported runner is QAL-F2B, not TST-C1A.
category_guides.2: Duplication and size inside the test tree: one oversized module of unrelated cases (TST-C2A) and behavioural helpers or fakes reimplemented across cases (TST-C2B). Inert scaffolding duplicated across files is TST-G1B; duplicated literals are TST-G2D.
category_guides.3: Names and inputs that misrepresent what a test covers: an input production can never produce (TST-C3A), a test name that over-claims (TST-C3B), a helper whose name inverts its semantics (TST-C3C), and a misnamed test file or class (TST-C3D). TST-C3A vs TST-E2D: C3A is one test's input, E2D a shared fixture's realism.
category_guides.4: Test doubles: an incomplete double that silently masks behaviour (TST-C4A), inconsistent mocking idioms (TST-C4B), mocks that assert internal calls instead of outputs (TST-C4C), and doubles with no stated contract (TST-C4D). TST-C4C is the opposite failure of TST-B1D (over-specifying internals vs under-checking a critical argument).
category_guides.5: Local hygiene inside a test file: a symbol used but not imported (TST-C5A), an over-engineered fixture builder (TST-C5B), imports inside test bodies (TST-C5C), and unexplained literals (TST-C5D). Suite-wide import-convention drift is TST-G2A. In test code cite the TST code even though QAL-F1B and QAL-B1B carry test-code examples of TST-C5A and TST-C5C; the production-code forms are QAL-F1B, QAL-B1B and QAL-A2C.

C.guide: Test design: how individual tests and their doubles are built. C1 discovery (tests that never run), C2 duplication and module size, C3 names and inputs that mislead about what is tested, C4 test-double fidelity, C5 local hygiene inside test files. Suite-wide convention drift belongs in area G.
C.name: test-design

category_guides.1: State and resources not cleaned up: hand-rolled patch/restore instead of a scoped patcher (TST-D1A), file handles left open (TST-D1B), and os.environ mutated without restore (TST-D1C). The production-code leak is COD-A1A; the resulting order-coupling is TST-F2C.
category_guides.2: Paths that break hermeticity: fixture paths resolved against the invocation cwd (TST-D2A) and hardcoded shared temp paths (TST-D2B). A machine-specific absolute path baked into fixture DATA is TST-E2C; the production-code wrong-base path is COD-E2B.

D.guide: Isolation and hermeticity: a test leaks state or depends on where and how it is run. D1 is state and resources a test fails to restore or release; D2 is filesystem paths that tie the test to a cwd or a shared location. Order-dependent outcomes caused by the leak are TST-F2C.
D.name: isolation-hermeticity

category_guides.1: Fixture lifecycle: tests that assume a fixture exists and fail with a misleading I/O error (TST-E1A) and fixtures no test consumes (TST-E1B). Silent skipping on absence is TST-A4C.
category_guides.2: Fixture fidelity: degenerate empty/placeholder values (TST-E2A), lockfile drift inside fixture projects (TST-E2B), machine-specific absolute paths in fixture data (TST-E2C), and synthetic data that could never occur (TST-E2D). Hand-built fixtures never validated against the authoritative schema are TST-G3D; a single test's unreachable input is TST-C3A.

E.guide: Fixtures and test data: the files and records tests load. E1 is fixture lifecycle (missing-without-validation, orphaned); E2 is whether fixture content is faithful to what production sees. A presence check that silently skips is TST-A4C.
E.name: fixtures-test-data

category_guides.1: Skip and environment-gated execution plus nondeterministic inputs: chained skip guards that make a test near-permanently skipped (TST-F1A), a single environment/tool gate (TST-F1B), an unexpected outcome converted to a skip (TST-F1C), unseeded randomness (TST-F1D), wall-clock dependence (TST-F1E), and live calls to external services (TST-F1F). TST-F1A vs TST-F1B is a chain vs a single gate. A vacuous body that passes on every branch is TST-B2B, and a fixture-presence check that silently skips is TST-A4C. A subprocess test that can hang with no timeout is TST-G3B.
category_guides.2: Ambiguous pass signals: a test-selection filter never checked to match anything (TST-F2A), an exit code that reads 'no tests ran' as success (TST-F2B), and outcomes that depend on test execution order (TST-F2C). TST-F2A and TST-F2B often co-occur; cite F2A when the cause is the selector, F2B when it is the exit-code interpretation.

F.guide: Flakiness and determinism: whether a green result means the tests ran and passed. F1 covers skips, environment gates and nondeterministic inputs (randomness, clock, network); F2 covers pass signals that cannot tell 'passed' from 'nothing ran', or that depend on test order. A subprocess test that can hang with no timeout is currently homed at TST-G3B.
F.name: flakiness-determinism

category_guides.1: Organisation: sys.path injection to import the code under test (TST-G1A), fixture scaffolding redefined across files (TST-G1B), and unit and integration tests mixed with no separation (TST-G1C). The production-code import hack is ARC-A2C; behavioural helper duplication is TST-C2B.
category_guides.2: Consistency across test files: import convention (TST-G2A), duplicated test literals (TST-G2D), assertion style (TST-G2E), and missing module documentation (TST-G2F). Mocking-idiom drift is TST-C4B; a single file's inline import is TST-C5C.
category_guides.3: Residual verification gaps: an exit-code remap never exercised (TST-G3A), a subprocess test with no timeout (TST-G3B), hand-built fixtures never validated against the authoritative source (TST-G3D), a security path only unit-tested (TST-G3E), and the residual weak assertion (TST-G3F). Prefer TST-A2B over TST-G3A, TST-A3A over TST-G3E and the specific TST-B codes over TST-G3F when they fit.

G.guide: Suite architecture: suite-wide structure and convention rather than one test. G1 is how the suite is organised and imported, G2 is consistency across test files, G3 holds residual verification gaps (several of which have a more specific home in areas A, B, E or F; check those first).
G.name: suite-architecture

TST-A1A.criteria: Qualifies when an entire executable script or module (its main path and helpers) has no automated test at all, so any regression in it ships unseen. Evidence names the script and confirms no test imports or invokes it. When the module is tested but one function in it is not, that is TST-A1B; when only the CLI flag wiring is untested, TST-A1D; when tests exist but only against mocks, TST-A3A.
examples: smoke_adapters.py has zero automated test coverage
run_fixture_tests.py has no unit tests and no injectable subprocess seam
Untested error handling in _run_adapter.main()
TST-A1A.name: zero-coverage-script

lower_when.condition: The script is a thin wrapper whose logic lives in imported modules that are themselves covered by tests; only the wrapper's argument plumbing is untested.
The script is a diagnostic or smoke script whose output is not consumed by any other step, gate, or persisted artifact.

TST-A1B.criteria: Qualifies when a specific production function or method in an otherwise tested module is never called by any test, directly or through a tested caller. Evidence names the function and the test file that would own it. A whole untested script is TST-A1A; an untested function that writes or restores durable state is TST-A1C. A function that is called but has an error, default or mapping arm that is never reached is TST-A2B, TST-A2C or TST-A2E.
examples: cargo-audit's dict-shaped CVSS severity branch has no test coverage
No test exercises DependencyCheckAdapter.is_applicable()
is_architecture_file() function lacks unit test coverage
TST-A1B.name: uncovered-function-or-method

lower_when.condition: The function is a pure formatter, accessor, or presentation helper with no branching and its output feeds no gate, verdict, or persisted record.

TST-A1C.criteria: Qualifies when a function that persists, recovers, replays, or applies durable state (a ledger save, a recovery/restore routine, a verdict or queue builder whose output is written) has no direct test, so a regression could corrupt or lose state without a failing test. Evidence names the function and what state it writes. An untested function with no durable side effect is TST-A1B; the recovery path being lossy in fact is ARC-D1A.
examples: save_recovered_ledger() lacks direct test coverage
build_verify_queue() lacks direct test coverage
apply_verdict() lacks direct test coverage
load_verdicts_detailed() lacks direct test coverage
TST-A1C.name: untested-critical-recovery-function

lower_when.condition: The function is exercised indirectly by an end-to-end test that asserts on the state it writes, so only the direct unit test is missing.

TST-A1D.criteria: Qualifies when a CLI flag, subcommand, or entrypoint's argument wiring (parse to dispatch) is never exercised by a test, even though the handler it reaches may be unit-tested, so a mis-wired or dropped flag passes the suite. Evidence names the flag and the handler. A wholly untested script is TST-A1A; a documented flag that is not implemented at all is COD-D2B; flag documentation drifting from the parser is QAL-C2C.
examples: --tools-exclude CLI wiring in synthesize.py has no end-to-end test
dispatch.main()'s --model-lens-sweep/--model-panel-review/--model-advisor and --agents-dir CLI flags are never exercised
TST-A1D.name: untested-cli-flag-or-entrypoint-wiring

raise_when.condition: The untested flag enables or disables a containment, gating or enforcement mode (e.g. turns a write-guard or a CI gate on or off), so mis-wiring silently changes the security or gate posture.

TST-A2A.criteria: Qualifies when a test checks an invariant over a registry, list or set of stages by enumerating the members that existed when it was written, so members added later (a new adapter, a new image stage) escape the check with no failure. Evidence names the hardcoded subset and an existing member it misses. A universal property tested only on a few hand-picked inputs (not a growing registry) is TST-B1F; a production shadow registry with no enforced parity is ARC-A4C.
examples: No systemic test guards against a future adapter-prefix collision in the ADAPTERS registry
Dockerfile tests only cover a stale subset of bundled tools; several later-added tool stages have no assertion coverage
TST-A2A.name: growth-blind-invariant-check

lower_when.condition: The registry is closed: members are added only by a documented process that also updates the enumerating test.

TST-A2B.criteria: Qualifies when a tested unit's exception, timeout or error-return path is never driven by any test, so the error handling could be broken or removed with the suite still green. Evidence names the handler and the trigger no test supplies. A default/fallback arm reached on normal input is TST-A2C; malformed-input handling is TST-A2D; an untested exit-code remap is TST-G3A; a security guard's untested rejection path is SEC-G3B. Error handling that is absent altogether is COD-B2C.
examples: run_tool tests do not cover timeout exception path
roslyn_secguard.py invoke() error handling not covered
Missing exception handling tests for JSON parsing in adapter parsers
TST-A2B.name: untested-error-handling-path

lower_when.condition: The handler only logs and re-raises (no recovery, translation, or fallback logic), so a regression in it would still surface as a failure.

TST-A2C.criteria: Qualifies when a fallback or default branch (default severity, missing-key default, alternate file lookup, secondary parser) is never reached, or is reached but never asserted, by any test. Evidence names the branch and why existing fixtures do not trigger it. An exception/timeout path is TST-A2B; a mapping with several arms of which one is tested is TST-A2E; a production fallback that silently masks a failure is ARC-C2A or COD-C3B.
examples: cargo_audit.parse's default-severity branch is reached by the module's own fixture but never asserted
YAML parsing fallback in load_catalog() not tested
brakeman.py: is_applicable()'s .gemspec fallback path is unreachable by the existing tests
TST-A2C.name: untested-fallback-default-branch

lower_when.condition: The default value is a constant with no further logic and is stated in the schema or docs that a separate test validates.

TST-A2D.criteria: Qualifies when a parser or input-handling unit is never tested with empty, truncated, malformed, or boundary input (empty findings list, non-empty but truncated XML, a missing optional key), so its behaviour on those inputs is unverified. Evidence names the input class and the unit. When the missing case is a security guard's adversarial input, cite SEC-G3B; when the unit demonstrably crashes on that input, SEC-F1A; when a malformed record is silently skipped in production, ARC-F2D.
examples: BrakemanAdapter parse() lacks empty findings test
Malformed/truncated (non-empty) XML tool output is untested, unlike other adapters' tests in this codebase
No-CWE-mapping branch (citations key omitted) is never tested
TST-A2D.name: untested-malformed-or-boundary-input

lower_when.condition: The unit's input is validated against a schema by a separately tested step in the same call path before the unit reads it, so malformed input cannot reach the untested code.

TST-A2E.criteria: Qualifies when a mapping, switch, or enum translation with several arms is tested for only one (or a small minority) of its arms, so the untested arms could be wrong with the suite green. Evidence names the mapping and the count of arms tested vs total. Untested combinations of independent configuration axes are TST-A3C; a schema enum missing values is COD-D1A.
examples: SpotBugs priority-to-severity mapping only exercised for priority "1"
BrakemanAdapter._normalize_confidence only has test coverage for one of its four branches
Category-derived CWE fallback is only tested for one of twelve categories
TST-A2E.name: single-case-enum-mapping-coverage

lower_when.condition: The mapping is table-driven data with no per-arm logic and one test already iterates the whole table.

raise_when.condition: An untested arm maps directly to the threshold value that decides a required CI gate's pass/fail outcome (e.g. the arm that emits the fail-on severity), not merely a severity or label shown in a report.

TST-A2F.criteria: Qualifies when a boolean predicate (an applicability check, a filter, a feature gate) is tested only on its true path, so a regression that makes it always-true passes the suite. Evidence names the predicate and the missing false-path case. When the predicate guards a security decision, cite SEC-G3B; an untested error branch is TST-A2B.
examples: is_applicable() false-path untested in bundler-audit and cargo-audit adapter tests
is_applicable() only tested for the pom.xml true path
SpotBugsAdapter.is_applicable test coverage is asymmetric compared to every sibling adapter
TST-A2F.name: untested-negative-boolean-branch

lower_when.condition: The false path is a trivial negation of the tested true path in a single expression with no other inputs.

TST-A3A.criteria: Qualifies when the only tests of a path that talks to a real tool, filesystem, or service replace that dependency with a mock, so the integration contract (real output format, real path normalisation) is never exercised. Evidence names the mocked seam and the real behaviour left untested. When integration tests exist but CI never runs them, that is ARC-C1C; when they exist but are skipped by environment gates, TST-F1A or TST-F1B; when the path is security-critical and only unit-tested, TST-G3E.
examples: Real-tool detection assertions for the vulnerable-python/vulnerable-node/insecure-js fixtures never execute
osv-scanner is never integration-tested against the real vulnerable-python/vulnerable-node/vulnerable-rust fixtures
diff_map._mk_worktree_dir's realpath normalization is only ever mocked out, never exercised against a real filesystem
TST-A3A.name: mocked-or-absent-integration-path

lower_when.condition: The mocked dependency's output is pinned by a recorded real-output fixture that the mock replays, so only live-version drift is untested.

TST-A3B.criteria: Qualifies when a fixture deliberately plants a defect or hostile behaviour (a vulnerable dependency, a malicious build file, a containment probe) but no test asserts the expected outcome (the finding is detected, egress fails, the marker stays out), so the fixture can silently stop proving anything. Evidence names the planted item and the absent assertion. A fixture no test consumes at all is TST-E1B; when the consuming test is gated off, TST-F1A. A planted pattern that no available tool can detect is a scanner capability gap, not this code (there is no catalog home yet; record it in cross-domain notes).
examples: evil.csproj's own containment invariants (egress must fail, marker must stay off the mounted target) are asserted nowhere
main.rs's ~20 planted source-level CWE patterns have no adapter/tool able to detect them
hostile-csproj's weak-Random() fixture is opt-in-only and gated, and its consuming test never asserts a finding
TST-A3B.name: unverified-planted-fixture-detection

lower_when.condition: The planted fixture is documented as a manual demo or reviewer aid, not as an automated regression check.

TST-A3C.criteria: Qualifies when a unit with several independent configuration axes or input dimensions (mode x depth x panel, path variants) is tested in one or a few combinations, so interactions in the untested combinations are unverified. Evidence names the axes and the combinations covered. A single mapping with untested arms is TST-A2E; one test using an input production cannot produce is TST-C3A.
examples: Golden-render regression suite exercises only one (panel, depth, security_mode) combination
Limited path traversal edge case testing
Sparse dispatch integration test coverage
TST-A3C.name: narrow-scenario-matrix

lower_when.condition: The axes are shown to be independent in code (no branch reads more than one axis), so per-axis tests already cover the behaviour.

raise_when.condition: An untested combination is a documented, supported default or a mode that changes enforcement (e.g. the security_mode setting), not merely a rarely used permutation.

TST-A4A.criteria: Qualifies when test-harness or fixture tooling runs a subprocess (docker, a scanner, a build) and consumes its output without checking the exit status or the output's format, so a failed or partial run is read as valid test input. Evidence names the harness call and the unchecked assumption. The same unchecked call in production code is COD-B2C (or SEC-F1A when it crashes on malformed output); output that is checked but not against a schema is TST-A4B; a harness reading the test runner's own exit code as 'tests passed' is TST-F2B.
examples: No validation of Docker command output format; check_fixtures assumes docker run output is well-formed and never validates the command succeeded
TST-A4A.name: unvalidated-subprocess-output-format

lower_when.condition: A downstream assertion in the same test fails loudly on the malformed output, so the gap only degrades the diagnostic rather than producing a false pass.

TST-A4B.criteria: Qualifies when files produced or consumed by tests (tool output, a fixture manifest) have a defined shape but no test validates them against it, so a shape change goes unnoticed. Evidence names the file and the shape it should satisfy. Hand-built fixtures that omit schema-required fields are TST-G3D; a schema that disagrees with its producer is ARC-D1B or COD-D1A.
examples: Missing schema validation for adapter/tool output files
tests/fixtures/manifest.json has no automated validation of its own shape or content
TST-A4B.name: unvalidated-tool-output-schema

lower_when.condition: Every test that reads the unvalidated file asserts each field it relies on explicitly, so a shape change fails those tests even without schema validation.

TST-A4C.criteria: Qualifies when a test's fixture-presence check exists but SILENTLY SKIPS (or drops fixtures) on absence, so fixture rot passes unnoticed with no alert — the failure mode is silence. When there is no existence check at all and a missing fixture instead surfaces as a confusing low-level I/O error rather than a clear test failure, that is TST-E1A.
examples: Silent skip on missing fixture directory masks fixture rot with no alerting mechanism
Fixture-presence check silently drops baked fixtures instead of surfacing a check failure, degrading CI signal
TST-A4C.name: unenforced-fixture-presence-check

lower_when.condition: The skip emits a reason that the CI summary surfaces and counts, so fixture loss is visible even though it does not fail.

raise_when.condition: The silently skipped fixtures back the only test of a security or containment property, so the skip removes that property's sole verification.

TST-B1A.criteria: Qualifies when the test asserts the WRONG property — it stays green while the behaviour it purports to protect is unverified (e.g. bounds-only assertions on a value whose computation is broken). Distinct from a presence-only assertion (TST-B1C) and a tautology (TST-B2A).
examples: The only regression test for the SEC-101 HTML-injection fix in _render_provenance checks cosmetic normalization instead of the injection-blocking property itself
TST-B1A.name: regression-test-verifies-wrong-property

TST-B1B.criteria: Qualifies when a test checks a structured result (dict, list, JSON, citation record) by substring-matching its string form, so wrong structure that happens to contain the substring passes. Evidence names the substring check and the structure it stands in for. A truthy/presence-only check is TST-B1C; a byte-exact snapshot of prose is TST-B3B; tests regex-scanning documentation prose for architecture rules fall to TST-G3F.
examples: Weak assertion: checks for substring instead of validating citation structure
Fragile stringified-dict substring assertion instead of structural check on citations
TST-B1B.name: substring-instead-of-structural-assertion

lower_when.condition: The substring is unique enough that only a structurally correct result can contain it (e.g. a full serialised key-value pair with delimiters), and the result is a flat string by contract.

TST-B1C.criteria: Qualifies when the test asserts a value is present or truthy but never checks its CONTENT (`assertTrue(result)` without asserting what result is). Distinct from asserting the WRONG property (TST-B1A) and from making NO positive assertion at all (TST-B1E).
examples: Weak assertion: only checks if findings list is truthy
Minimal asset validation coverage: test_assets.py only checks for string presence, not structure or completeness
Ambiguous assertTrue usage with confusing assertion semantics
TST-B1C.name: truthy-or-presence-only-assertion

TST-B1D.criteria: Qualifies when a test asserts that a mock was called but never checks the argument that carries the behaviour under test (the comment body sent to gh, the command vector, the path written), so a wrong argument passes. Evidence names the mock and the unchecked argument. Over-specifying internal call sequences instead of outputs is the opposite failure, TST-C4C; a double that silently returns defaults for unexpected calls is TST-C4A.
examples: Test does not verify comment body argument passed to gh command
Incomplete verification of command structure in mock assertion
TST-B1D.name: unverified-critical-mock-argument

lower_when.condition: The unchecked argument is a constant or pass-through that a different test verifies at its construction site.

TST-B1E.criteria: Qualifies when the test exercises code but makes NO positive assertion about the outcome (it only runs the code / asserts it did not raise). A test that asserts presence but not content is TST-B1C.
examples: Security-critical test lacks positive assertion of expected behavior (verifies cwd != target but never asserts what cwd IS)
test_unresolvable_recurring_finding_is_omitted lacks positive assertion
TST-B1E.name: missing-positive-assertion

lower_when.condition: The test is an explicit smoke test, named and documented as checking only that the code does not raise.

raise_when.condition: The test is named or documented as verifying a security, containment, or gate property and no other test asserts that property positively.

TST-B1F.criteria: Qualifies when a property that must hold for all inputs (round-trip identity, ordering, idempotence, a sanitiser rejecting every dangerous input) is tested only with one or a few hand-picked examples, with no property-based, generated, or exhaustive check. Evidence names the universal property and the examples used. A registry invariant that misses later members is TST-A2A; a mapping with untested arms is TST-A2E. No corpus instance yet; enrich when observed.
TST-B1F.name: universal-invariant-only-example-tested

lower_when.condition: The input domain is small and finite and the examples enumerate all of it.

raise_when.condition: The universal property is a security or data-integrity invariant (sanitiser, encoder, round-trip of persisted data) over an input space that includes untrusted input.

TST-B2A.criteria: Qualifies when the assertion is tautological and cannot fail — `assert(1==1)`, `!(x != x)`, comparing a value to itself — so it verifies nothing structurally. The strongest weak-assertion form; when a test asserts something real but insufficient, use the specific TST-B1x codes; TST-G3F is the residual.
examples: Pointless assertion: self.assertTrue(True) always passes, providing no actual test coverage
TST-B2A.name: always-true-assertion

lower_when.condition: The tautological assertion sits beside real assertions in the same test, so the test still verifies something.
The always-true assertion is an explicit placeholder in a test marked skip/xfail/TODO, so it is not counted as coverage.

TST-B2B.criteria: Qualifies when a test branches on the environment (tool installed or not, platform) and every branch it can take passes without asserting the adapter's actual behaviour, so the test is green everywhere and verifies nothing anywhere. Evidence names the branches and shows none asserts real output. A test that is skipped (not run) when the environment is missing is TST-F1B; a single tautological assertion is TST-B2A.
examples: test_cargo_audit_skips_without_rust is a tautological test that never verifies adapter behavior regardless of which branch executes
TST-B2B.name: environment-branch-vacuous-test

TST-B2C.criteria: Qualifies when a test loops over cases (rule mappings, inputs) but its assertion only covers some iterations (asserts after the loop on the last value, breaks early, or asserts a redundant condition each time), so most cases are unverified despite appearing covered. Evidence names the loop and which iterations go unchecked. A mapping whose arms are simply not enumerated is TST-A2E.
examples: Test loop with redundant assertions: does not validate all rule mappings
TST-B2C.name: incomplete-loop-assertion-coverage

lower_when.condition: The unchecked iterations exercise the same code path as a checked one (table data with no per-case logic).

TST-B2D.criteria: Qualifies when an assertion's logic is inverted or negated so it passes in the failure case it was written to catch (assertNotIn where assertIn was meant, a double negation, a comparison flipped). Evidence shows the input under which the assertion passes although the behaviour is wrong. An assertion that can never fail at all is TST-B2A; a helper whose name inverts its semantics is TST-C3C.
examples: Test with inverted logic and meaningless assertion
TST-B2D.name: inverted-logic-assertion

lower_when.condition: The inverted assertion is redundant with a correct assertion in the same test.

TST-B3A.criteria: Qualifies when a test locates its target with an operation that raises on absence (list.index, a bare [i] on a possibly short list, dict[key]) so a regression surfaces as an unrelated ValueError/IndexError instead of a clear assertion failure naming the missing element. Evidence names the lookup and the assertion it should have been. The same unchecked index in production code is COD-A2C; a fixed magic index in production is QAL-A2C.
examples: Brittle test assertion using unsafe list.index(): cmd.index('--network') without error handling raises ValueError instead of a clear assertion failure
Fragile test with unsafe list indexing on command array
TST-B3A.name: unsafe-index-based-assertion

lower_when.condition: A broad except in the test or its fixture is shown to catch the lookup's ValueError/IndexError, so the regression can turn into a pass.
Nothing catches the exception: the test still errors on the regression and only the diagnostic message is poor.

TST-B3B.criteria: Qualifies when golden/snapshot fixtures are compared byte-exactly but have no regeneration tooling, no recorded provenance, or no review step, so a regression can be 'fixed' by editing the expected file and stale goldens cannot be refreshed safely. Evidence names the golden set and the missing discipline. Goldens that drift from an authoritative schema are TST-G3D; substring checks are TST-B1B; generated artifacts in the build (not tests) are ARC-C1F.
examples: Golden fixtures are hand-maintained with no regeneration tooling or documented provenance
Byte-exact prose snapshots can be satisfied by editing the fixture instead of fixing the regression
TST-B3B.name: unmanaged-golden-snapshot-assertion

lower_when.condition: Goldens are tiny and hand-written by design and the expected values are restated in the test as literals.

raise_when.condition: The snapshot is the only regression check for output a gate or security reviewer relies on (a rendered report's escaping, a verdict summary) and goldens are updated by a blind overwrite command with no diff review.

TST-C1A.criteria: Qualifies when TEST classes or functions defined after a misplaced `__main__` guard are silently excluded from discovery, so they never run and coverage is lost without signal. If the unreachable code is production code, that is COD-E2A; if the guard is merely misplaced with nothing after it actually skipped, QAL-F2B.
examples: TestRunTool is defined after the `if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()` guard
test_base.py places the __main__ guard mid-file, silently dropping TestRunTool from script-mode discovery
TST-C1A.name: test-defined-after-main-guard

TST-C1B.criteria: Qualifies when a test function or class sits where the project's runner does not collect it (a module-level function under unittest, a name missing the test_ prefix, a file outside the discovery pattern), so it never runs. Evidence names the test and the runner's rule it misses. Tests dropped because they follow a `__main__` guard are TST-C1A; tests that are collected but skipped are TST-F1A/TST-F1B.
examples: Test function defined outside unittest.TestCase class
Module-level test_multi_model_fields_in_schemas is invisible to unittest's own discovery
TST-C1B.name: undiscoverable-test-function

raise_when.condition: CI's actual runner fails to collect the test and it is the only test of the unit it exercises, so coverage of that unit is lost in CI.

TST-C2A.criteria: Qualifies when one test module bundles many unrelated concerns (dozens of independent TestCase classes, or classes for different production units) so failures are hard to localise and the file is hard to change. Evidence names the module and its unrelated groupings. The production-code analogue is ARC-A1B; unit and integration tests mixed in one directory is TST-G1C.
examples: Single 2,669-line test module conflates dozens of unrelated concerns (~46 independent TestCase classes) for synthesize.py
test_roslyn_secguard.py contains three unrelated test classes (TestRoslynSecGuardAdapter, TestSafeCopytree, TestScsOnlyFilter) with no semantic grouping
TST-C2A.name: monolithic-test-module

lower_when.condition: The module is large but tests a single production module whose structure it mirrors.
The module is large only because of data tables or parameterised cases, not distinct concerns.

TST-C2B.criteria: Qualifies when test LOGIC — a helper method or a hand-rolled fake/stub/mock class — is reimplemented near-identically across multiple test methods or cases instead of shared; the duplicated unit carries behavior. Inert fixture scaffolding (a fixture-root/path constant or setup boilerplate) duplicated across test FILES is TST-G1B. (Note: a duplicated behavioural helper can be more consequential than inert scaffolding despite this code's lower default severity — grade the instance on consequence.)
examples: Fake subprocess-result class reimplemented locally in ~8 test methods instead of one shared helper
Duplicate _target() helper method across test classes
TST-C2B.name: duplicated-test-helper-across-cases

lower_when.condition: The duplicated helper is two or three lines with no branching.

raise_when.condition: The duplicated fakes or helpers have already diverged in behaviour (different return shape, missing method), so different cases test against inconsistent doubles.

TST-C3A.criteria: Qualifies when a test feeds the unit an input that production can never produce (a shape, combination, or value unreachable from the real caller), so the test passes while the path real inputs take is untested. Evidence names the input and why production cannot produce it. A shared fixture file with implausible data is TST-E2D; a fixture with empty/placeholder values is TST-E2A.
examples: test_clean_group_is_shallow exercises a panels input that build_result can never actually produce, masking that the real code path is untested
TST-C3A.name: unrepresentative-test-input

TST-C3B.criteria: Qualifies when a test's name or docstring claims more coverage than its body provides (all four roles, but only two are pinned), so readers believe a behaviour is protected when it is not. Evidence names the claim and the gap. A helper whose name states the opposite of its behaviour is TST-C3C; a misnamed test file or class is TST-C3D; a test whose assertion checks the wrong property is TST-B1A.
examples: Test name claims coverage of all four dispatch roles but only pins tokens for two
TST-C3B.name: misleading-test-name

raise_when.condition: The over-claimed behaviour is a security or gate property and no other test covers the unclaimed part.

TST-C3C.criteria: Qualifies when a test helper's name states the opposite comparison or polarity of what it implements (a `_depth_gte` that computes less-than), so tests using it read as asserting something other than what they assert. Evidence names the helper, its name, and its actual semantics. An over-claiming test name is TST-C3B. An assertion shown to pass on the behaviour it should reject is TST-B2D.
examples: Helper function _depth_gte is named for the opposite comparison it actually implements
TST-C3C.name: misnamed-helper-inverted-semantics

lower_when.condition: The helper is used only to build inputs, and every caller passes arguments that make the inversion irrelevant.

TST-C3D.criteria: Qualifies when a test file, class, or module name refers to a scope, language, or unit it does not test (or duplicates another file's scope under a different name), misleading navigation and ownership. Evidence names the artifact and what it actually tests. An individual test's over-claiming name is TST-C3B; a production name collision is QAL-A1C.
examples: File/class name references a non-existent 'cs' scope and duplicates test_rust_integration.py
TST-C3D.name: misnamed-test-artifact

lower_when.condition: The misname is a casing or abbreviation difference that does not point to a different scope.

TST-C4A.criteria: Qualifies when a hand-written double (a fake exists(), a stub client) handles only the calls the test author expected and returns a permissive default for everything else, so unintended calls by the unit pass silently instead of failing. Evidence names the double and the default it returns for unexpected input. A double with no documented contract is TST-C4D; a mock whose critical argument is not asserted is TST-B1D; a global mock that blinds every path is TST-G3F.
examples: Incomplete mock_exists function masks unintended behavior: only explicitly returns True for the expected path, silently returning False for everything else
TST-C4A.name: incomplete-test-double-masks-behavior

TST-C4B.criteria: Qualifies when sibling tests patch the same dependency with different idioms or targets (patch.object on the module vs patch of the import path, nested vs decorator patches), so a refactor of the import path silently un-patches some tests. Evidence names the divergent patch sites. Inconsistent assertion style is TST-G2E; inconsistent imports across test files is TST-G2A; the production analogue is QAL-F1B.
examples: Inconsistent subprocess mocking pattern across test suite: patch.object(subprocess, "run") in one file vs. mock.patch("scripts.tools.base.subprocess.run") in others
A test locally does `from unittest import mock` and nests four levels of `with mock.patch(...)`, diverging from every sibling adapter test's mocking idiom
TST-C4B.name: inconsistent-mocking-pattern

lower_when.condition: All variants resolve to the same patched object today and no test patches a re-exported name, so the drift is stylistic only.

TST-C4C.criteria: Qualifies when a test verifies the unit by asserting internal calls on mocks (call order, private helper invocations) instead of its observable output, so behaviour-preserving refactors break the test while behavioural regressions with the same call pattern pass. Evidence names the internal call asserted and the output left unasserted. Failing to assert a critical argument is the opposite, TST-B1D. No corpus instance yet; enrich when observed.
TST-C4C.name: mock-asserts-internal-behavior-not-output

lower_when.condition: The asserted internal call is itself the contract (an adapter that must invoke the tool exactly once), so it is an output in disguise.

TST-C4D.criteria: Qualifies when a non-trivial test double (fake service, stub client) does not state which real interface or behaviours it mimics, so drift between the double and the real dependency cannot be checked. Evidence names the double and the real interface. A double that is demonstrably incomplete and masks behaviour is TST-C4A.
examples: Undocumented test double lacks contract specification
TST-C4D.name: undocumented-test-double-contract

lower_when.condition: The double subclasses or is spec'd from the real interface (autospec, Protocol), so its contract is enforced mechanically.

TST-C5A.criteria: Qualifies when a test file uses a symbol or submodule it never imports (unittest.mock via `import unittest`), working only because another import happened to load it, so test success depends on import order. Evidence names the symbol and the accidental provider. Imports placed inside test bodies are TST-C5C; the same import inconsistency across production modules is QAL-F1B.
examples: test_synthesize.py calls unittest.mock.patch without importing unittest.mock
TST-C5A.name: missing-import-for-referenced-symbol

TST-C5B.criteria: Qualifies when a test fixture builder carries its own conditional logic and options to the point that the builder itself needs testing, so a bug in it can make tests pass or fail for reasons unrelated to the unit under test. Evidence names the branches in the builder. A duplicated helper is TST-C2B; needless abstraction in production is QAL-H2C.
examples: Overly complex test fixture builder with conditional branching
TST-C5B.name: overengineered-fixture-builder

lower_when.condition: The builder's branches are each exercised by at least one test and produce visibly different fixtures.
The complexity is a short chain of optional keyword overrides with no branching.

TST-C5C.criteria: Qualifies when a test file imports inside test function bodies or re-imports and shadows a module-level import, for no isolation reason (no optional dependency, no import-time side effect under test). Evidence names the import site. A suite-wide divergence in import convention is TST-G2A; the same pattern in production code is QAL-B1B or QAL-B1C.
examples: Late imports: module imports inside test function
Redundant import shadowing module-level import
TST-C5C.name: nonstandard-import-placement

lower_when.condition: The inline import is mechanically flagged by a configured linter rule, so it is a free lint rather than a review finding.

TST-C5D.criteria: Qualifies when a test uses a bare literal (an expected count, timeout, offset) whose origin is not explained, so a reader cannot tell whether a change to it is a fix or a weakening. Evidence names the literal. The same literal duplicated across many test files is TST-G2D; the production form is QAL-A2C.
examples: Magic number without explanation in test
TST-C5D.name: unexplained-magic-value-in-test

lower_when.condition: The literal is the obvious expected value of the input in the same test (e.g. len of a three-item list is 3).

TST-D1A.criteria: Qualifies when a test replaces module or global state by direct assignment and restores it by hand (save original, try/finally) instead of a scoped patcher, so an early failure, a missed restore, or parallel execution leaks the replacement into other tests. Evidence names the patched attribute and the restore path. Environment-variable mutation is TST-D1C; asserting internal calls on the patched object is TST-C4C; the resulting order-dependence is TST-F2C.
examples: Test uses direct module state patching instead of context managers: saves original references then restores via try/finally
Mock patch scope too broad; test depends on internal module structure
Test mock restoration pattern creates isolation risk
TST-D1A.name: manual-state-patch-without-context-manager

TST-D1B.criteria: Qualifies when test code opens a file (often `json.load(open(p))`) without a context manager or close, leaking the handle until garbage collection and raising ResourceWarnings or exhausting descriptors in long suites. Evidence names the open call. The same leak in production code is COD-A1A; cite COD-A1A (not D1B) when the leaking helper is shared production code called by tests.
examples: Resource leak: files opened without context manager
Unclosed file handle in test assertion: json.load(open(actions_path)) without context manager
Multiple unclosed file handles in test method
TST-D1B.name: unclosed-file-handle

TST-D1C.criteria: Qualifies when a test sets or deletes os.environ entries directly without a scoped mechanism (mock.patch.dict, monkeypatch.setenv) or an unconditional restore, so the change leaks into later tests. Evidence names the variable and the missing restore. Other module/global state patched by hand is TST-D1A; production inheriting the whole environment into a subprocess is SEC-B3B.
examples: Test isolation violation: os.environ mutated without proper cleanup
test_env_override / test_cli_beats_env mutate os.environ directly instead of using mock.patch.dict
TST-D1C.name: unscoped-env-var-mutation

TST-D2A.criteria: Qualifies when a test opens a fixture or repository file by a path relative to the invocation cwd rather than anchoring it to the test file or repo root, so the test fails or reads the wrong file when run from another directory. Evidence names the relative path. Production code resolving a path against the wrong base is COD-E2B; a machine-specific absolute path in fixture data is TST-E2C; a shared /tmp path is TST-D2B.
examples: Non-hermetic test: fixture path is relative to invocation cwd, not the test file
Hard-coded relative path in test assumes repo-root execution
test_status_is_in_schema_enum opens a bare CWD-relative path instead of anchoring to __file__/repo root
TST-D2A.name: cwd-relative-fixture-path

lower_when.condition: The project's runner configuration pins the working directory (e.g. rootdir/cwd set in config) so the test cannot be invoked from elsewhere through the supported entrypoint.

TST-D2B.criteria: Qualifies when a test writes to or reads from a fixed shared path (/tmp/foo, a literal scratch directory) instead of a per-test temporary directory, so parallel runs, reruns, or other users collide. Evidence names the path. A machine-specific path in committed fixture data is TST-E2C; an unsafe symlink-following copy into such a path is SEC-D1C; durable state kept in scratch is ARC-E2A.
examples: Hardcoded /tmp path in test bypasses test isolation
TST-D2B.name: hardcoded-shared-tmp-path

lower_when.condition: The path includes a per-process unique component (pid, uuid) and is removed in cleanup, so only the base directory is shared.

TST-E1A.criteria: Qualifies when tests assume fixtures exist WITHOUT validating them, so a missing fixture surfaces as a confusing low-level I/O error instead of a clear test failure — the failure mode is loud but misleading. When a presence check exists and instead silently skips (masking fixture rot with no alert), that is TST-A4C.
examples: Tests depend on fixture files without existence validation; load_report() failures surface as confusing I/O errors rather than clear test failures
TST-E1A.name: unvalidated-fixture-existence-assumption

lower_when.condition: The error raised on absence names the missing fixture path (e.g. a FileNotFoundError with the path), so the failure is attributable without an explicit check.

TST-E1B.criteria: Qualifies when a committed fixture file is consumed by no test (no path reference, no glob that reaches it), so it rots unnoticed and misleads readers about what is covered. Evidence names the fixture and confirms no consumer. A planted fixture that is consumed but whose expected outcome is never asserted is TST-A3B; dead production code is QAL-E3A.
examples: Fixture file vulnerable-python/requirements.txt exists but is unused by specified tests
tests/fixtures/semgrep.sarif is an orphaned fixture with no consuming test
Fixture file manifest.json exists but is unused by specified tests
TST-E1B.name: orphaned-unused-fixture

lower_when.condition: The fixture is documented as an example or reserved for a manual or external harness.

TST-E2A.criteria: Qualifies when fixture records carry empty strings, zeros, or placeholder values in fields the unit branches on (severity, category, title), so tests pass on degenerate data while realistic values follow untested paths. Evidence names the fields and the branches they skip. Data that is plausible-looking but impossible is TST-E2D; a single test's unreachable input is TST-C3A.
examples: Test fixture with incomplete field values for reconciliation edge case: empty strings for severity, panel, category, title
Test fixture contains intentionally degenerate/empty findings
TST-E2A.name: degenerate-fixture-values

lower_when.condition: The degenerate values are in fields the unit only passes through without branching.
The fixture is deliberately degenerate to test empty-input handling, and its name or a comment says so.

TST-E2B.criteria: Qualifies when a fixture project's lockfile and manifest disagree (declared vs locked version), so the fixture does not represent a state a real package manager would produce and tests of lockfile-reading tools exercise an impossible input. Evidence names both versions. A production lockfile missing integrity hashes is SEC-E1C; a stale version string in docs is QAL-C1D.
examples: Cargo.lock has time version mismatch with Cargo.toml (0.1.44 declared vs. 0.1.45 locked)
TST-E2B.name: fixture-lockfile-version-drift

lower_when.condition: No test parses the drifted field (the lockfile is only scanned for package names).
The drift is deliberate to test drift detection and is documented as such.

TST-E2C.criteria: Qualifies when committed fixture DATA embeds a machine-specific absolute path (a developer's home directory, a CI workspace), so the data is non-portable and may leak workstation details. Evidence names the path and file. A hardcoded absolute path in production source is ARC-E1A; a test's runtime cwd-relative path is TST-D2A; a shared runtime /tmp path is TST-D2B.
examples: Hardcoded, machine-specific absolute path embedded in committed test fixture data
TST-E2C.name: hardcoded-machine-specific-path-in-fixture-data

lower_when.condition: The path is an opaque string the unit treats as data (e.g. a sample 'file' field in tool output) and never resolves.

raise_when.condition: A test resolves the embedded path at runtime and SKIPS or passes vacuously when it is absent, so on every machine but the author's (including CI) the test silently verifies nothing.

TST-E2D.criteria: Qualifies when shared fixture data is synthetic in a way the real ecosystem could not produce (a dependency edge that does not exist, a structure a tool never emits), so tests may pass against data the real input never resembles. Evidence names the impossible element. Empty or placeholder values are TST-E2A; lockfile/manifest version disagreement is TST-E2B; a single test's unreachable input is TST-C3A.
examples: Synthetic dependency in Cargo.lock fixture may not reflect realistic resolution behavior (serde depending on a package that isn't a real dependency)
TST-E2D.name: unrealistic-synthetic-fixture-data

lower_when.condition: The unrealistic element is in a part of the fixture no assertion or branch depends on.

TST-F1A.criteria: Qualifies when a test sits behind two or more chained skip conditions (tool present, image built, network reachable, env flag set) such that in practice it skips on every CI runner and most developer machines, so the coverage it claims is near-permanently absent while the suite reports green. Evidence lists the guards and an environment where all hold. A single environment gate is TST-F1B; an unexpected tool outcome converted to a skip is TST-F1C; integration tests CI never schedules are ARC-C1C.
examples: Integration tests have cascading skipTest guards making coverage uncertain
Five cascading skip conditions plus an implicit network dependency reduce this test to a near-permanent skip
Containment probe test has multiple exit paths that skip validation
TST-F1A.name: cascading-skip-guard-chain

lower_when.condition: At least one CI job satisfies every guard and runs the test (verified in the workflow config), so only local runs skip.
Skips are reported with reasons in the CI summary and a scheduled job is documented as the place they run.

TST-F1B.criteria: Qualifies when a test runs only if a single environmental condition holds (a tool installed, Docker available, an optional library importable) and otherwise skips, so whether it executes depends on the machine. Evidence names the gate and whether CI satisfies it. Two or more chained gates that make the test near-permanently skipped is TST-F1A; a test that runs on every branch but asserts nothing is TST-B2B; an unexpected tool result turned into a skip is TST-F1C.
examples: Docker availability tests depend on runtime environment
Conditional test execution based on external tool availability
Schema validation tests skipped when jsonschema not installed
TST-F1B.name: environment-gated-test-execution

lower_when.condition: The required CI job provides the gated dependency, so the test always runs in CI and only skips locally.
The gate is an optional extra documented as such and the gated behaviour is also covered by a non-gated unit test.

TST-F1C.criteria: Qualifies when a test treats an unexpected outcome from the system under test (an unrecognised exit code, an error result) as a reason to skip rather than fail, so genuine regressions are reported as skips. Evidence names the outcome and the skip. A skip because a prerequisite is absent is TST-F1B; a fixture-presence check that silently skips is TST-A4C; a production fallback that masks failure is ARC-C2A.
examples: Unexpected cargo-audit exit codes are silently skipped instead of failing the test
TST-F1C.name: unexpected-outcome-silently-skipped

lower_when.condition: The unexpected outcomes skipped are documented tool-environment failures (e.g. a registry outage code) distinct from the codes the unit under test produces.

TST-F1D.criteria: Qualifies when a test's input or expected value depends on an unseeded random source (random, uuid4, hash ordering of a randomised set) so it can pass or fail between runs on identical code. Evidence names the random source and the assertion it affects. Time-dependent behaviour is TST-F1E; dependence on execution order is TST-F2C; a weak PRNG in production security code is SEC-C3A. No corpus instance yet; enrich when observed.
TST-F1D.name: unseeded-randomness-dependent-test

TST-F1E.criteria: Qualifies when a test's outcome depends on the real clock (current date, elapsed-time thresholds, timezone of the runner, a sleep-based wait) with no frozen or injected time, so it fails at certain times, on slow runners, or in other timezones. Evidence names the time read and the assertion. Production code using wall-clock for elapsed time is COD-G1D; unseeded randomness is TST-F1D. No corpus instance yet; enrich when observed.
TST-F1E.name: wall-clock-dependent-test

lower_when.condition: The time dependence has a margin of minutes or more and no date/timezone boundary is involved, so failure requires an extreme runner stall.

TST-F1F.criteria: Qualifies when a test makes live calls to a third-party service or registry (package audit APIs, a remote advisory DB) with no recorded response, mock, or opt-in marker, so results depend on network and the service's current data. Evidence names the call and the absent isolation. Missing timeouts on the call are OPS-A1A; gating such tests on network availability is TST-F1B.
examples: pip-audit/npm-audit integration tests make live network calls to third-party services with no opt-out marker
TST-F1F.name: unisolated-external-service-call

lower_when.condition: The test is behind an explicit opt-in marker excluded from the default and CI runs.

raise_when.condition: The test runs in a required CI check, so a third-party outage or data change blocks or flips merges.

TST-F2A.criteria: Qualifies when a harness selects tests by a filter (pytest -k, a name pattern, a marker) and never verifies that the filter matched at least one test, so a renamed or missing test makes the run select nothing and still pass. Evidence names the filter and the missing count check. When the cause is reading the runner's exit code as pass without distinguishing 'no tests collected', that is TST-F2B; a test the runner never collects at all is TST-C1B.
examples: Fragile test discovery with assumed pytest naming convention: pytest -k 'test_{test}_integration' never validates that matching tests exist
TST-F2A.name: unverified-test-selection-filter

lower_when.condition: The filtered run is not a required gate (advisory or local helper only).
The runner is configured to fail on zero collected tests (e.g. pytest exit code 5 is treated as failure), so an empty selection already fails.

TST-F2B.criteria: Qualifies when a harness treats the test runner's exit code 0 (or any non-failure code) as proof the tests passed, though that code is also returned when nothing ran (no tests collected, all skipped, filter matched nothing). Evidence names the exit-code check. When the root cause is an unvalidated selection filter, cite TST-F2A; an untested non-zero exit path in production code is TST-A2B; a CI step whose failure is swallowed is ARC-C2B.
examples: No validation that tests actually executed: a returncode of 0 could mean tests passed OR pytest -k matched nothing
Non-zero exit code handling in run_adapters not fully tested
TST-F2B.name: exit-code-conflates-pass-with-no-op

lower_when.condition: The harness also checks a collected/passed count from the runner's report, so only the exit-code reading is redundant.

raise_when.condition: The exit code is the sole pass/fail signal of a required CI gate AND the harness is shown to accept the runner's 'no tests collected/all deselected' result (e.g. pytest exit 5 treated as success, or a runner that returns 0 on an empty selection), so a zero-test run merges green.

TST-F2C.criteria: Qualifies when a test passes only if another test ran first (it relies on state, files, or patched globals left behind) or fails only after a particular predecessor, so reordering, selection, or parallelism changes the result. Evidence names the two tests and the shared state. The leaking cause is TST-D1A, TST-D1C, or TST-D1B; randomness-driven flakiness is TST-F1D. No corpus instance yet; enrich when observed.
TST-F2C.name: test-order-coupling

lower_when.condition: The coupling only causes a spurious failure (never a spurious pass) when order changes.

TST-G1A.criteria: Qualifies when the TEST SUITE imports the code under test by injecting directories into sys.path at module level (across many test files) instead of installing or packaging the project, so tests exercise an import layout the shipped package does not have. Evidence names the injection and its spread. The same hack in production entrypoints is ARC-A2C; a single module relying on an implicit path someone else set is QAL-F1A.
examples: All 18-43 test files inject the skill directory via sys.path.insert(0, ...) at module level instead of relying on an installable package
TST-G1A.name: test-suite-sys-path-import-hack

lower_when.condition: The project is also installed in CI and at least one job runs the tests against the installed package.
The injection is centralised in one conftest/bootstrap file rather than repeated, and points at the same root the package installs from.

TST-G1B.criteria: Qualifies when inert fixture SCAFFOLDING — a fixture-root/path constant, environment/directory setup, or config boilerplate — is redefined identically across multiple test FILES instead of a shared fixture module; the duplicated unit is not behavior. A duplicated behavioral helper method or fake/stub class across cases is TST-C2B.
examples: FIXTURE_ROOT is redefined identically across every integration test file (Java, C#, Ruby, Rust) instead of a shared fixture module
An identical _touch fixture helper is copy-pasted verbatim into three separate TestCase classes
TST-G1B.name: test-fixture-scaffolding-duplicated-across-files

TST-G1C.criteria: Qualifies when fast unit tests and slow real-tool or end-to-end tests share a directory and runner selection with no marker or structural split, so developers cannot run the fast set alone and CI cannot schedule them differently. Evidence names the directory and examples of each kind. One oversized module of unrelated cases is TST-C2A; CI never running the integration subset is ARC-C1C.
examples: tests/tools/ mixes fast unit tests and slower real-tool integration tests in one directory with no structural separation
TST-G1C.name: unit-and-integration-tests-not-separated

lower_when.condition: The whole suite, integration tests included, runs in a few minutes in CI, so the lack of separation has no scheduling cost.

TST-G2A.criteria: Qualifies when the test suite as a whole uses two or more competing import conventions for the same modules (module-level vs in-method, `import x` vs `from x import y`) with no rule, so readers and patchers cannot rely on one. Evidence names files on each side. A single file importing inside a test body is TST-C5C; production-code inconsistency is QAL-F1B.
examples: test_dependency_check.py imports unittest.mock inside a test method body while every other test file imports it at module level
TST-G2A.name: inconsistent-import-convention-in-test-methods

lower_when.condition: A configured import-sorting linter already enforces one style and the instance is a lint finding.

TST-G2D.criteria: Qualifies when the same expected value (a timeout, a limit, an exit code) is hardcoded as a literal in assertions across many test files instead of imported from the production constant or a shared test constant, so changing the production value requires a scattered test edit. Evidence names the literal and its spread. Duplicated fixture scaffolding is TST-G1B; a single unexplained literal is TST-C5D; production duplicated constants are QAL-D1B.
examples: The subprocess timeout value 300 is hardcoded identically as a literal in test assertions across a dozen adapter test files
TST-G2D.name: hardcoded-test-constant-duplicated

lower_when.condition: The literal is part of an external contract that must not change silently, so restating it in tests is deliberate pinning.

TST-G2E.criteria: Qualifies when tests in the same framework mix assertion styles (bare assert inside unittest.TestCase vs self.assert*) without reason, degrading failure messages and consistency. Evidence names the divergent tests. When the bare asserts guard a security invariant in production code (stripped by -O), that is SEC-G3C; inconsistent mocking idioms are TST-C4B.
examples: TestPanelPriority uses bare assert statements instead of self.assertEqual/self.assertIn inside a unittest.TestCase, unlike every other test method in the suite
TST-G2E.name: inconsistent-assertion-style-in-test-suite

lower_when.condition: The runner is pytest, which rewrites bare asserts with full introspection, so failure messages do not degrade.

TST-G2F.criteria: Qualifies when most test modules or classes have no docstring stating what unit or behaviour they cover, so ownership and intent must be reverse-engineered. Evidence gives the proportion lacking documentation. A docstring that misstates what the test covers is TST-C3B.
examples: Only 2 of 15 assigned test files contain a meaningful module- or class-level docstring
TST-G2F.name: missing-test-module-documentation

lower_when.condition: Test file and class names map one-to-one to production modules, so intent is evident without docstrings.

TST-G3A.criteria: Qualifies when an adapter remaps a tool's exit codes (treating some non-zero codes as success) and no test drives those codes through the remap and the runner's ok-codes wiring. Evidence names the remap and the untested codes. The general untested error path is TST-A2B; reading exit 0 as 'tests passed' is TST-F2B.
examples: BrakemanAdapter's exit-code remap (2/3 -> 0) and its ok_codes=(0,1,2,3) wiring into run_tool are never exercised by any test
TST-G3A.name: exit-code-remap-path-never-exercised-by-tests

lower_when.condition: The remapped codes are documented by the tool as informational (e.g. 'findings present') and the adapter's parse step is tested on output produced under those codes.

TST-G3B.criteria: Qualifies when a test shells out to a real entrypoint or tool via subprocess with no timeout, so a hang in the child hangs the whole suite or CI job until an outer kill. Evidence names the subprocess call. A missing timeout on a production external call is OPS-A1A; a live call to a third-party service is TST-F1F.
examples: TestEndToEnd shells out to the real orchestrator.py and synthesize.py entry points via subprocess.run with no timeout, so a hang in either script hangs the whole test suite/CI
TST-G3B.name: long-running-subprocess-test-has-no-timeout

lower_when.condition: A per-test timeout (pytest-timeout or equivalent) is configured for the suite that runs this test, so a hang fails that test instead of stalling the job.

TST-G3D.criteria: Qualifies when hand-built test fixtures stand in for data that has an authoritative definition (a JSON schema, a real producer) but are never validated against it, so fixtures can omit required fields or carry shapes production never emits while tests stay green. Evidence names the fixture and the authoritative source. Tool-output files lacking schema validation are TST-A4B; a single test's unreachable input is TST-C3A.
examples: Hand-built ScopeProfile test fixtures omit schema-required fields and are never validated against scope-profile-schema.json
Model-resolution precedence tests can't distinguish the YAML-config tier from the hardcoded-fallback tier because fixtures don't isolate them
TST-G3D.name: test-fixture-not-validated-against-authoritative-source

lower_when.condition: The omitted fields are optional in the schema or not read by the unit under test.

TST-G3E.criteria: Qualifies when a security or enforcement mechanism (a write-guard hook, a sandbox policy) is tested only by calling its decision function in-process, never through the harness that actually wires and enforces it, so a broken registration or wiring leaves all tests green. Evidence names the in-process test and the untested wiring. Non-security integration paths only mocked are TST-A3A; missing negative tests for the guard's decision logic are SEC-G3B; an enforcement gap in the control itself is AGT-B1A.
examples: The write-guard hook's live enforcement path is only exercised via its in-process decide() function - the harness actually denying an out-of-scope Write call is never tested end-to-end
TST-G3E.name: security-critical-path-only-unit-tested-never-e2e

lower_when.condition: A static test validates the registration/config that wires the in-process function, so only the live harness round-trip is untested.

TST-G3F.criteria: The residual home for a weak assertion that verifies little of the real behaviour. Grade by CONSEQUENCE, and cite the specific member first when it fits — tautology TST-B2A, presence-only TST-B1C, wrong-property TST-B1A, no-assertion TST-B1E; use G3F only when none of those applies.
examples: A test mocks builtins.open globally via mock_open, so it can never detect a wrong report path or misread content
Tests enforce architectural conventions by regex-scanning SKILL.md's prose instead of checking actual code structure
Dockerfile 'bundles core tools' tests only assert case-insensitive substring presence, not that the tools actually run
TST-G3F.name: weak-test-assertion-doesnt-verify-real-behavior

raise_when.condition: The weakly asserted behaviour is a security, gate, or data-integrity property and no other test asserts it more strongly.

TST.guide: TST covers defects in test code and test infrastructure: behaviour no test exercises, assertions too weak to fail, tests that are non-hermetic, nondeterministic or silently skipped, fixtures that rot or misrepresent reality, and suite organisation that hides or drops tests. Choose TST when the question is whether the tests would catch a regression. When the production code is itself wrong, cite COD or SEC (a security guard's missing negative test is SEC-G3B); when CI never schedules a test path, cite ARC-C1C. When a defect that also has a production-code home (an unclosed handle COD-A1A, a missing timeout OPS-A1A, an inline import QAL-B1B) is found in test code, cite the TST code and do not cite the production code plus a test-scope modifier. Look in A (what is untested), B (what assertions check), C (test structure and doubles), D (cleanup and paths), E (fixtures), F (skips, determinism, pass signals) and G (suite-wide organisation; G3 is a residual, so check A, B, E and F first).
TST.name: testing
